News.title: Donald Trump son’s wedding party was paid for by top Vladimir Putin ally - including private islands
News.content:
Donald Trump son’s wedding party was paid for by top Vladimir Putin ally - including private islands

Donald Trump said the arrangement - which saw Vladimir Putin ally Umar Kremlev pay for two private islands and a huge fireworks display after the wedding - was 'very common'

View 3 Images Donald Trump said the arrangement was 'totally allowed' (Image: Samuel Corum - Pool via CNP/Shutterstock)

Donald Trump has hit back after it emerged his son's wedding party was paid for by a Russian oligarch with close ties to Vladimir Putin.

‌



Umar Kremlev, a gambling magnate and head of the International Boxing Association, bankrolled the celebrations that followed Donald Trump Jr and wife Bettina's ceremony in the Bahamas in May, an investigation by ProPublica found this week.

‌



It included paying hundreds of thousands of dollars to rent out one of two private islands where the three-day party was held, and a huge fireworks show.

‌



In a joint statement on Monday, the couple wrote: "Our dear friend Umar very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us AFTER our wedding. It was an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful".

View 3 Images Donald Trump Jr and his wife Bettina said the Russian billionaire 'hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us' (Image: NEIL HALL/EPA/Shutterstock)

Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office last night, the US president defended the arrangement - and claimed for the first time that the couple had "paid him back".

‌



Trump said: "It’s totally allowed. And a lot of people have parties and all. But, as I understand it, he paid them back."

He described the arrangement as "very common", adding: "I’ve given wedding parties to numerous people."

View 3 Images Vladimir Putin and Umar Kremlev pictured together in Moscow in 2022 (Image: SPUTNIK/AFP via Getty Images)

‌



Who is Umar Kremlev?

Originally a biker gang member from the ex-Soviet state of Tajikistan, 43-year-old Kremlev has built a vast network within Russian business over the past three decades - helped by his cosy relationship with the Kremlin.

In 2021, Putin signed a decree making Kremlev's company, TSUPIS, the sole operator for all sports betting in Russia, giving it an effective monopoly over the sector. The firm is currently valued at $300million (£224m), according to international estimates.

Three years later, when Russian authorities confiscated Rolf, Russia's largest car dealership network, from its previous owner Sergei Petrov, the state handed ownership of the enterprise over to Kremlev at a reduced price.

Article continues below

Kremlev is also head of the International Boxing Association (IBA), the sport's historical governing body which was banned from the Olympic movement a year before the Paris games over allegations of corruption and bout-rigging.

After taking over the IBA in 2020, Kremlev moved much of the organisation's operations to Russia, installing the state-owned energy giant Gazprom as its primary sponsor.

He frequently appears alongside Putin at major events, including the opening of the International Boxing Centre in Moscow.

News.title: 'I'm telling the truth': Earl Spencer defends Diana book claims about Charles in BBC interview
News.content:
Reacting to the rare statement from the Palace, Earl Spencer said: "Well, is he furious? Is he furious or is he embarrassed?"

Speaking to the BBC at his Althorp estate, he added: "I've only ever had two calls on the line with Prince Charles at any stage of my life.

"I was hyper alert to what he was saying and those are precisely the words that he said and I promise that to you now. Genuinely, that is what he said. I don't hear him saying he didn't say that."

Pressed on whether he had evidence to back up the claim, he said he told family and friends at the time what had been said "because it was so monstrous".

In response to the Palace disputing his account, Earl Spencer, who shares his first name with the King, said: "They've sort of smudged that one, haven't they? They've said that recollections may vary."

When asked which Charles the public was meant to believe, he said: "I'm telling the truth."

Buckingham Palace declined to give a response to Earl Spencer's fresh comments.

The remarks may bring a renewed focus to the war of words between the Palace and the King's former brother-in-law.

News.title: Watch: Diana's brother says Charles 'went ballistic' in phone call after her death
News.content:
Princess Diana's brother said King Charles "went ballistic" during a phone call with him in the days after his sister's death.

Earl Spencer spoke exclusively with the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg about claims he has made in a new book, alleging the then-Prince of Wales said "we'll forget her soon enough" during an argument over whether Princes William and Harry should walk in Diana's funeral procession.

In a strongly-worded response to the book claims, Buckingham Palace said the King was "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgement and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss".

Read more about Laura Kuenssberg's interview with Earl Spencer.

News.title: Billionaire Man United owner says he has lost confidence in the UK
News.content:
One of Britain's richest people, Sir Jim Ratcliffe, says he has lost confidence in the UK, describing the country as "on the slide".

The founder of petrochemical giant Ineos, who also owns a large stake in Manchester United, said the UK was in decline due to a combination of high taxes and high immigration.

He told the BBC failing to invest further in North Sea oil and gas amounted to "insanity" and warned gas storage was so low that the UK could "run out of gas" if there was a cold snap this winter.

In response to the billionaire's criticism, the government said it was working to deliver growth and that business investment had increased in the last two years.

A spokesperson said they did not foresee any problems with gas supply: "We have a diverse energy mix and are confident in our security of supply."

Sir Jim, whose wealth is estimated to be around Â£15bn, has prompted controversy in the past with his comments on immigration. He was a supporter of Brexit but has been a tax resident in Monaco since 2020.

The businessman's UK exit has been followed by other high-profile billionaires, including steel tycoon Lakshmi Mittal and most recently hedge-fund boss Chris Rokos.

Sir Jim said the politics of envy was driving people away from the UK.

"In America they applaud people who create wealth," he said. "Unfortunately the UK has got a bit of a green eye towards wealth at the moment."

He said for him to return to the UK "things would have to get better".

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will take a "pragmatic approach" to oil and gas, but one of the biggest decisions facing the government, whether to give the go-ahead to further development of the oil and gas fields at Rosebank and Jackdaw, is still waiting to be resolved.

Sir Jim criticised the hesitation and suggested high taxes on North Sea operators were threatening the sector's viability. Tax on energy company profits is being reformed, but won't be fully implemented until 2030.

Ineos operates the Forties pipeline which transports about 30% of the UK's North Sea oil.

"You would expect [the government] to exploit our natural resources and we're clearly not doing that. We're shutting it down.

"If you tax everybody to death, they're all going to leave. And that's what's happening."

Recent climate data combined with record heatwaves have given weight to the argument against further exploitation of fossil fuels. However, political pressure has grown on the government to proceed with Rosebank and Jackdaw to support UK jobs, tax revenues and boost energy security.

Sir Jim backed those calls, saying it was "absurd" to import more energy than necessary.

The government spokesperson said that oil and gas would play an important role in the UK "for decades to come", but they added: "The transition to homegrown clean power is the only way to deliver energy and financial security for families and businesses."

News.title: Parents could lose benefits or face prison for child's crimes, minister says
News.content:
Parents could lose their benefits or face prison sentences for their children's crimes under reforms to the youth justice system, a minister has said.

Youth Justice Minister Jake Richards told the Times newspaper the system "should hold parents to account in a proportionate way for ensuring that they play their role in keeping communities safe".

His comments come after the government set out plans in May to strengthen and expand Parenting Orders, which can currently compel parents or guardians to address their child's behaviour by attending counselling sessions or face fines.

Richards said prison sentences would only apply "in the most extreme cases" and would be up to judges' discretion.

He described the proposed changes in England and Wales as part of a "carrot-and-stick" approach.

"Parenting orders are going to make sure that parents are more involved in the process by which we try to turn around young offenders," Richards told the Times.

"Yes, that will have some stick. It could be custodial, or docking benefits - ultimately it will be up to a judge. But we want them to be more involved and that comes with responsibilities as well."

Critics of the proposals say engaging with parents on a voluntary basis is generally more effective in building trusting relationships and providing support.

Jess Mullen, chief executive of the Alliance for Youth Justice which represents more than 70 organisations that advocate for children, previously questioned how putting parents in prison would provide "stability or support for the child".

When the government white paper was announced in May, then Justice Secretary David Lammy said that strengthening parenting orders would mean "there are real consequences for parents and carers who wilfully fail to support efforts to address their children's behaviour."

He told BBC Breakfast at the time that if a parent was struggling, then the "judge can intervene to make sure that the young person is getting the support that they need and the parent is doing the best that they can".

He also said he expected the power to jail parents to be used "very, very rarely".

Courts are currently required to consider issuing a Parenting Order where a child under 16 has been convicted of an offence.

They can also consider an order for 16 and 17-year-olds if they believe this would help prevent further offences.

The term of the order must not exceed 12 months and breach of a parenting order is a criminal offence with a maximum Â£1,000 fine, according to the Sentencing Council.

However, government statistics show the use of parenting orders has declined in recent years, from more than 1,000 orders in 2009/10 to just 33 in 2022/23.

The government's youth justice reform plans come after Phase One of the Southport Inquiry report found "catastrophic" failures by the parents of the Southport killer Axel Rudakubana and various agencies meant clear chances to prevent the 2024 child murders were missed.

In the interview with the Times, Richards also rejected calls from lawyers to raise the age of criminal responsibility from 10, saying it would undermine "public faith" in the justice system and it was "not a priority at all".

In June, the Bar Council, the representative body for barristers in England and Wales, said the threshold should rise to 14 due to criminalisation at such an early age not being an "effective, proportionate or just response".

The United Nations has previously pointed out the UK has some of the lowest ages of criminal responsibility in the world and that it should rise it to the UN recommendation of at least 14.

Additional reporting by AndrÃ© Rhoden-Paul

News.title: Daisy Edgar-Jones: I try and bury my emotion when it comes to love
News.content:
Daisy Edgar-Jones has been well cast in her new film.

She plays Elinor, the rational elder sister in Sense and Sensibility, opposite the younger, more romantic sister Marianne.

Speaking to the BBC, Edgar-Jones says that in her personal life, she really is like her character.

"When it comes to love, I think I am very much more Elinor in every sort of way," she says.

"I definitely lead a lot with my head and try and push aside, bury my emotion."

But she notes that one of the joys of the film is seeing Elinor learn to enjoy a "wilder, passionate side" of herself. "And I feel like I learnt to do that too," she says.

Best known for starring in hit TV series Normal People with Paul Mescal, Edgar-Jones, 28, is now taking on a lead role in the latest adaptation of Jane Austen's book.

Ahead of its release, sheâs been talking to me about whether we really need another Sense and Sensibility film (spoiler: yes. âThe more the merrier, in my opinion.â)

She also told me why young people today can still see themselves in Jane Austen's stories - and gave me her take on whether her friend and former co-star Mescal should be the next James Bond.

News.title: Bitter row over Diana book brings back unhappy times for royals
News.content:
At issue is Earl Spencer's account of a conversation with the then Prince Charles after the death of Diana, with the prince accused of telling Earl Spencer: "We'll forget her soon enough."

He is accused of sounding "giddily elated" and like a "lottery winner" after the news of her death.

Buckingham Palace hit back with a response, which although dressed in courtier-like politeness, was essentially saying the conversation had never happened like that.

The King was said to be "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways that others do not recognise".

Anyone who has lost someone knows how feelings can run high, people can hear different things about the same conversations - and families can fall out, or come together, in the wake of a death.

Psychotherapist Nick Hatter says he doesn't have a view on which version of events is correct, but he says that during traumatic events memories can be "distorted". A phone call doesn't have any of the visual clues or body language to give a fuller picture, he adds.

Hatter says there can be very different and unpredictable responses to grief, including a condition known as "bereavement mania" where someone can seem inappropriately hyper or even euphoric after the loss of a loved one.

The first opinion poll on who to believe has been published by YouGov - and it suggests a very split view, with 31% believing Earl Spencer's allegations, 36% suspecting it's not true and 33% saying they don't know.

Low thinks the book is unlikely to change many opinions, as "people have settled into their camps about how they regard Charles, how they look back on the Diana years".

There could also be a feeling that it's "tawdry" to rake up these claims so many years later, he says.

That's echoed by historian and author Sir Anthony Seldon who says Earl Spencer showed great courage at the time of Diana's funeral, but says his memoir is a "sad and unnecessary publication".

Royal commentator Richard Palmer says the book threatens to take the royals back to the difficult days of 1997.

"This book and the run-up to next year's 30th anniversary of Diana's death threaten to undermine the Royal Household's three decades of work to rehabilitate Charles and Camilla's image," he says.

Veteran broadcaster David Dimbleby, who led the BBC's coverage of Diana's funeral, said it seemed "odd" Earl Spencer would release the book now.

"Why 30 years later for god sake you should do it, well again you have to ask him," he said, adding he wished the appetite for the "cycle of gossip" would decline and instead focus would shift to what kind of monarchy the country needs.

News.title: A four-minute warning isn't enough: Russia's new relentless missile tactics exhaust Kyiv residents
News.content:
For much of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Daria was not afraid of the shelling.

Even on nights of heavy bombardment, the 27-year-old could sleep through the explosions in her apartment in Kyiv. Like many Ukrainians, she relied on the "two-wall rule": staying safe by keeping two walls between herself and the outside world.

But this year that has changed.

In recent months, Russia has scaled up the intensity and frequency of its attacks against the Ukrainian capital.

In the first 10 days of July alone, the Russians launched dozens of ballistic missiles in three major attacks, killing nearly 60 civilians, according to official figures. Similar large scale attacks took place in August and September.

A BBC Verify analysis of government figures found Kyiv is now suffering more daily air raid alerts than at any time since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.

It was during an attack one night in May that Daria realised she no longer felt safe in her home.

She and her boyfriend were in the corridor of their ninth-floor apartment, watching a boxing match, as explosions went off around them, the blast waves causing the windows to repeatedly slam open and shut.

When the fight ended, "there was no longer anything to distract me," Daria says. "That's when I realised I was really scared."

At first, she thought she would start using a nearby bomb shelter during attacks.

But in June, when a young mother was killed running to a shelter in Kyiv, Daria decided she needed to leave the city altogether.

She returned to her family's country house, 30km (18.6 miles) away in Romankiv, and now spends a total of four hours a day commuting to and from Kyiv, where she works in the defence sector.

News.title: When a beloved tree began withering away, locals suspected a killer in their midst
News.content:
Every summer, Seoul turns a deep green, growing dense and lush under humid skies.

But this year, one tree was visibly suffering.

"Green leaves were falling to the ground, which shouldn't happen at that time of year," recalls Jung, who lives near the streetside ginkgo in Buam-dong, a largely residential neighbourhood in the north of Seoul.

The tree is beloved by locals, who believe it has occupied its spot for more than 100 years. So Jung couldn't ignore what she was seeing. With each passing day, her curiosity turned to concern.

A rotting carpet of familiar fan-shaped leaves soon surrounded the tree, a sight so alarming Jung and her neighbours formed a crew of amateur detectives to solve the mystery: what was ailing their hardy ginkgo?

The whodunnit engrossed Buam-dong and piqued the country's interest, making national headlines. But the attention unsettled Jung, who spearheaded the campaign but has since requested anonymity - we are using a pseudonym.

"Imagine a grandfather who silently embraces you every day, listens to you, and has always been strong and full of life," she says. "Suddenly, he begins to die.

"How heartbreaking would that be?"

So began one community's fight to save a cherished symbol of their neighbourhood. Their unlikely enemy, who they believe plotted a surreptitious attack, was a museum built to honour a pioneering, nature-loving Korean artist.

News.title: Flight chaos caused by 'millisecond' software defect, report says
News.content:
An air traffic control failure that sparked widespread travel chaos earlier this month was caused by a "software defect" affecting the system underpinning UK air space management, the national air traffic service Nats has said.

The problem happened "in the space of a millisecond", Nats said, leading to the system producing corrupted data.

The failure led to more than 2,000 flights being cancelled and hundreds of thousands of passengers affected, with some sleeping on airport floors or getting stuck overseas.

Nats chief executive Martin Rolfe told the BBC he would not resign, saying the software defect was "very, very obscure."

"You can fly to almost anywhere from almost any airport at almost any time. If that stops, even for a moment, then you get huge disruption.

"My job is to make sure that we have this happen as infrequently as possible," he added.

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander called the disruption "completely unacceptable", while industry body Airlines UK is writing to Nats to demand immediate compensation for costs incurred.

The incident prompted questions over the resilience of Nats' systems, and some airlines questioned the position of Mr Rolfe.

There has also been anger from passengers about how much support they got from airlines, and about the fact that they are unlikely to be entitled to compensation because the regulator judges the situation was extraordinary circumstances.

In an initial report, external, Nats said the software defect meant air traffic controllers had reduced information available, so restrictions were put in place to limit air traffic to maintain safety.

The defect occurred at 10:00am on 8 September, but it did not become apparent this was a serious problem for another two and a half hours.

The system restart did not start until just after 3:15pm, and restrictions on UK airspace were not lifted until 7:30pm.

Flights in and out of the UK's main airports were affected, including Heathrow, Gatwick, Luton and Glasgow.

The disruption took days to completely resolve because of the number of planes and crew left out of place.

Mr Rolfe apologised to those affected by the disruption, saying Nats was "devastated".

"However, our primary role is to keep our skies safe, and everyone who flies through them. At no point last week was safety in question."

Nats has "tested these systems so much," he added.

"We spent so much time making sure they work that anything that does happen of this nature is, by its very nature, going to be incredibly complicated and probably difficult to understand at the time," he said.

Reacting to the Nats report, the transport secretary described the disruption as "completely unacceptable" and "frustrating" for passengers, airlines and airports.

"It's clear we need to urgently understand why this issue was not discovered and fixed before it caused chaos," Alexander said, adding that a Civil Aviation Authority review was underway.

This is the third national air traffic incident in the past three years.

In 2023, a computer shutdown over the August bank holiday weekend caused chaos for 700,000 passengers.

There was another, smaller Nats outage in 2025, which caused 150 cancellations.

Tim Alderslade, chief executive of Airlines UK, said: "Once again, it is passengers who have suffered and airlines who have picked up the pieces - and the tab - of an ATC [Air Traffic Control] system failure, while Nats itself faces no real consequences."

He added that passengers deserved "commitment and proof that the system is being fixed".

Alderslade also said Airlines UK was writing to NATS "to demand immediate compensation for the costs incurred and a credible plan to improve resilience."

News.title: Temperatures could peak at 26C as summerlike warmth returns next week
News.content:
Temperatures could peak at 26C next week as late summer warmth returns to parts of the UK.

Southern areas will experience the highest temperatures, but most locations will be warmer than normal for late September.

Warmth could last all week for some in England and Wales, but it might only be a short-lived boost for Scotland and Northern Ireland.

The high pressure, which is responsible for the warmth, will also mean little rain for places continuing to experience drought conditions.

News.title: 'Fast, furious and dangerous' - a city's quad bike menace
News.content:
Sitting in his Birmingham city centre apartment, one resident says he can often hear them before he sees them.

The sound of revving engines is followed by groups of quad bikes and off-road motorcycles weaving through traffic, performing wheelies and riding through some of the busiest streets in the city.

"It's only a matter of time until something serious happens," he said.

Videos shared on social media over recent months have captured groups of riders travelling through areas including Hurst Street, Bristol Road and Corporation Street, often with faces covered and no visible number plates.

One video filmed by the resident showed a pedestrian narrowly avoiding being struck as a group rode through the city centre.

"I've watched them and they go through red lights, they just totally ignore the red lights," he said.

"People still cross when the pedestrian lights are green, but they don't even slow down to check.

"They're zigzagging in the middle of cars. No number-plates. It's bad because nobody sees any action happening and it's only a matter of time until something serious happens."

News.title: A village familiar with tragedy mourns Noah Woods
News.content:
Canon Yvonne Tulloch founded the charity Ataloss after the death of her husband in 2008. As chief executive, she campaigns for more support for those navigating grief.

She said that as a society, we are not good at acknowledging grief - preferring to convince ourselves that we will live until old age; because of this, emotions can be suppressed and come to the fore following high-profile cases.

"We assume it's next of kin who will be the grievers and, while that is correct, it is not the whole picture.

"There are these ripples, there will be people who will grieve who we wouldn't assume would be doing so.

"Because we've been so poor at understanding grief, what can happen even more is when there is a tragedy that is near to us it makes us think it could have been us - particularly when it involves a child and you're a parent who can relate to it."

Tulloch added this can be "confusing" because those removed from a tragedy can feel they do not have a right to grieve.

She said: "Those who helped with the search have done so because they felt helpless. Equally there will be those who did not help and feel they should have done more.

"In most cases people will have made their decision for sensible reasons and you have to release yourself from guilt and realise you did the best you could."

For the family, there is a balance between appreciating the community support, but not being overwhelmed by it, she said.

"The important thing is not to isolate the family because you do not know what to say.

"People fear saying the wrong thing, but it takes nothing more than acknowledging somebody and saying, 'I'm so sorry, I just want you to know I care'.

"It can mean even more coming from a stranger."

Annie Owen, who volunteers at Ipswich and East Suffolk Samaritans, said that in the modern world, the overload of information can anaesthetise people to many tragedies.

"But for this pure innocent child, there is nowhere to put our reactions or our grief," she said.

Owen said it was important that people do not "beat themselves up" over what they did or did not do.

"So if anybody can find the way of looking at themselves and just thinking, this hurts right now because I'm decent, because I'm caring, because I have a heart. And I think that's a way of easing ourselves through it."

If you, or someone you know, have been affected by child bereavement, details of help and support in the UK are available at BBC Action Line

News.title: About 280 people evacuated after fire at seaside hotel
News.content:
About 280 people have been evacuated from a seaside hotel after a fire broke out overnight.

Kent Fire and Rescue Service said 26 fire engines were sent to the Grand Burstin Hotel in Folkestone at about 01:05 BST.

In an update at 08:30, it said 10 fire engines remained at the scene "dampening down any remaining hotspots".

The fire service said the blaze was believed to have started in the basement of the building, adding that the cause was not yet known. No fire-related injuries have been reported.

Folkestone and Hythe District Council has set up a welfare centre at the Three Hills Sports Park and nearby residents have been advised to avoid the area of the fire and close windows and doors.

"We are supporting all emergency services involved in the response and their efforts to get people to safety", said the council.

A spokesperson for Britannia Hotels Group, which runs the Grand Burstin, said it was "taking immediate action to ensure the safety and wellbeing of all guests and team members".

"Emergency services are on site and we are fully cooperating with the authorities to support those affected and assist with the ongoing response", it added.

News.title: 'Our flat has been for sale for four years': Why is the market so weak?
News.content:
In 2015, thousands of people queued overnight in the rain to reserve and buy studio apartments selling for under Â£200,000 in Hounslow, west London.

It's in stark contrast to today's appetite for flats, with property portals reporting a slump in sales.

But why, when the country is in a housing crisis with a desperate need for affordable homes, are flats now struggling to sell?

According to the property site Zoopla, 88% of flats listed for sale in inner London on its website in 2025 did not find a buyer within six months. The company also says the gap between the value of a flat and a house is the widest it has been for 30 years.

Executive director Richard Donnell points to post-pandemic social changes with "people looking for space, prioritising houses, working from home".

He also points to higher mortgage rates, people concerned about "all the costs and liabilities of owning a property" including service charges and ground rents.

In September, nearly all the major mortgage lenders in the UK announced increases in the cost of home loans.

Donnell says flats in inner London are struggling in particular as they are more expensive, the service charges are higher, and "there's greater complexity - it's highly likely it's a bigger building, maybe more of a complex building, so less are selling within six months".

News.title: RNLI video receives 'pure hatred' after anti-migrant protests
News.content:
A woman who shared an RNLI video on social media says she has received "pure hatred" following anti-migrant protests in England.

Councillor Elizabeth Evans, who represents Aberaeron and Aberarth in Ceredigion, shared a video on Facebook which showed New Quay's RNLI lifeboat leaving the station on a training day.

According to Evans, the post - which attracted 30,000 views - drew comments of hatred, some of which she described as "really, really bad".

It comes after RNLI volunteers in Portsmouth were targeted by protesters following the charity's role in helping to bring migrants on a small boat to shore earlier this month.

The RNLI said it existed "to save lives at sea".

Evans said she was "really shocked" by the reaction to the video.

"I couldn't believe it," she said.

"And it wasn't a few. It took me a good half hour to get rid of those comments, just one after the other. With that thread of hatred."

Describing the comments, Evans continued: "The comment thread was 'traitors', 'taxis for migrants', they were some of the politest ones."

She said one of the comments was suggestive of violence, adding: "I don't want to go on because I don't want to give those comments oxygen but they were really, really bad."

Evans said she deleted the comments but was subsequently criticised for "shutting down discussion".

"I wasn't shutting down discussion because there was no discussion available to be had," she said. "I was shutting down hatred."

News.title: 'Not an easy inbox' for new Scottish Labour leader
News.content:
There's an old joke involving someone asking for directions, and the reply comes: "Well, if I were you, I wouldn't start from here."

And that's probably the (unhelpful) advice a lot of people would give the next Scottish Labour leader.

It's a job that will go to one of two MSPs this weekend - Michael Marra or Joe Fagan.

The victor will inherit a party that had a historically bad result in May's Scottish Parliament election. They will lead a group of just 17 MSPs.

That makes them the joint second-largest party at Holyrood, tied with Reform UK, but there remains a gulf between Labour and their SNP rivals.

The second series of excerpts from Earl Spencer’s book about Princess Diana have been released as he doubled down on his claims in a fresh interview.

In his highly anticipated memoir, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, the Earl has made bombshell allegations about King Charles’ conduct around his ex-wife Princess Diana up to and following her death.

Revelations from the book, currently being serialised by the Daily Mail before it is published next Tuesday, have so far focused on the King’s behaviour, from statements he made to Diana before their marriage to comments he made to the Earl before her funeral.

Earl Spencer gave an interview to the BBC ahead of the book’s publication in which he insisted everything he said was true amid backlash.

Prior to the serialisation, Buckingham Palace responded directly to the allegations, saying the King was mindful that “grief can cloud reason” in reference to the Earl.

Here are the latest bombshell allegations made in the memoir.

open image in gallery The latest extract from Earl Spencer’s book declares Prince Charles ‘had no place’ at Diana’s funeral ( PA Archive )

Prince Charles ‘had no place at his his ex’s funeral’

Earl Spencer recalled his sister’s funeral as a “a form of mental torture,” stating that he believed neither Prince Charles, or Princes William and Harry should have been in attendance.

Sharing his feelings on the funeral procession, one passage read: “What was Prince Charles actually doing there? I thought at one moment.

“This ex-husband, from a marriage that had collapsed so bitterly four years before and finally ended in divorce a year earlier, surely had no place at his ex’s funeral.

“Supporting his sons was the reason given for his prominent place, but what were the boys doing there, anyway? It all seemed mad to me.

“I was anxious that I could not look sideways to check how Harry was doing. But at one point I found us marching briefly out of sight, under a massive arch. Relieved that nobody could see us here, I quickly leant across to Harry, and gave him an encouraging hug. ‘Well done, Harry!’ I said. ‘You’re doing bloody brilliantly!’”

open image in gallery The Earl recalled his concerns surrounding then-Prince Charles’ decision to include William and Harry in the funeral procession ( AFP/Getty )

Diana’s fraught relationship with the Royals at the time of her death

Excerpts published on Friday reveal further details about Diana’s fraught relationship with the Palace at the time of her death.

The book read: “I saw the face of Princess Michael, whom Diana had considered her ‘nightmare neighbour’ at Kensington Palace. She had accosted my sister after she was deprived of her HRH title, and said, with feigned kindness: ‘Don’t worry, Diana – you only need to curtsy to me when we are in public !’

“There was Princess Margaret, who had been a good ally of Diana till the Panorama interview had taken place. Margaret could never forgive what she viewed as an unforgivable act of treachery against the Royal Family and had chosen not to bow to Diana’s coffin when it had passed her that morning”.

open image in gallery The then Duke of Edinburgh, William, Earl Spencer, Harry and Charles during the funeral procession to Westminster Abbey ( PA Archive )

After Diana’s death, there was ‘a lack of obvious care’ for Prince Harry

In other passages of the book, Earl Spencer spoke of his concern for Prince Harry.

He wrote: “My chief memory of that train journey is of being concerned at the lack of obvious care for Harry, as he decompressed from the ghastliness of the morning.

“He needed Diana’s hugs, of course, and they would forever be denied him. But instead of calm and nurture, he was allowed to spin out of control.

“I have often looked back, reckoning that a more caring hand at such points as this would have helped him enormously in the future. Instead, he seemed so very alone in his despair and torment”.

The Queen’s offer to restore her honorifics posthumously

open image in gallery Diana, Princess of Wales, wearing Paul Costelloe in 1991 ( Alamy/PA )

The Earl wrote he rejected the late Queen’s “well-meaning” gesture to restore Diana’s HRH title posthumously as it felt like a “consolation award”. He claimed his sister was “dreadfully hurt” by the “petty and vindictive” decision to remove her title, and just hours after her funeral she offered to restore it.

“I felt that I knew in my bones how she would view this posthumous award,” he writes. “That's very kind of the Queen, of course. But what's the point, Robert? Now? I mean – Diana's dead.”

He said that just hours after his eulogy at Diana’s funeral, the late Queen’s private secretary Robert Fellowes beckoned me to follow him into a quiet corner of the carriage.

“I have just received a call from Her Majesty… and she would like to offer Diana her HRH title back,” he wrote Mr Fellowes as saying.

While the Earl later wondered if he was right to reject the award, he felt “the title should never have been removed during her life, in which case it would not have been necessary to offer it to her in death.”

Prince Charles plucked a ‘single stem’ to drop on Diana’s coffin

open image in gallery Earl Spencer, William, Harry and Charles waiting as the hearse carrying the coffin of Diana, Princess of Wales prepared to leave Westminster Abbey following her funeral ( PA Archive )

The Earl also recalled his anger at Prince Charles on the day of Diana's funeral.

He wrote: “Diana was lowered into the ground as the vicar offered his sentences of Christian comfort.

“Several of us threw in our flowers on top of the coffin. Prince Charles plucked a single stem from my bouquet for Diana and let it drop on his ex-wife’s coffin.

“How very generous, I thought, angry now on Diana’s behalf, as she began to disappear under the soil.

“But anger was very much a secondary emotion at such a moment of profound loss. The burial was both incredibly painful and utterly exquisite.”

Earl doubles down on claims in fresh interview - and says Queen reacted ‘tetchily’ to news of fatal crash

The latest serialisation of the Earl’s book was released alongside a teaser clip of an interview he gave to the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg, in which he insists everything he has said is true.

Speaking about an alleged row over Diana’s funeral arrangements involving her sons, the earl said: “(The King) went ballistic, would be the right term, and started really going for my family as a whole, about their sense of duty, not being adequate enough, and ranted for a while, I have no idea how long, but it was a significant period, and I just listened.

“And then he stopped, and I thought, ‘Oh now he’s going to pull himself together and say something more appropriate’.

“And then he said, ‘We’ll forget her soon enough’.”

Asked whether he has “evidence” of the King’s comments, the earl told the BBC: “I told friends and family straight away, close friends and family, about what had been said, because it was so monstrous.”

He added: “I’m telling the truth.”

Earl Spencer further claimed Elizabeth reacted “tetchily” to news of his sister having been in a car accident.

He said: “When the Queen had heard the first news of Diana’s being in a traffic accident, she had asked tetchily, ‘What is she up to now?’

“This, before the seriousness of it all became clear.”

His full interview with Laura Kuenssberg will be available to watch on BBC iPlayer on Sunday from 4pm and broadcast on BBC One at 6.30pm.

On a Wednesday afternoon in September, Borough Market is still as busy as ever. It is not difficult to see why – with offerings ranging from juniper-cured ham to chilli-stuffed Lebanese olives, it is one of London’s most-loved culinary hotspots.

The central London market promises to act as a beacon for sustainable food production and champion independent producers. But beneath it all, traders across the market suggest there is a growing sense of unease.

The feeling stems from the news that Bread Ahead – the famed artisan bakehouse – has been told to leave on the grounds of being “too successful”, according to founder Matthew Jones.

open image in gallery Bread Ahead has attracted global attention for its unique takes on classic baked goods ( The Independent )

The bakery, which first appeared in this part of Southwark 13 years ago, was founded by the popularly termed ‘King of Doughnuts’, Mr Jones.

Specialising in avant-garde takes on classic baked goods, ranging from peach melba doughnuts to fig and roquefort sourdough pizzas, Bread Ahead has both garnered and sustained global attention for its decadent creations.

open image in gallery Bread Ahead’s goods have received international attention ( Bread Ahead )

For many, the decision to shut down the bakery’s operations in its flagship brick-and-mortar location has sparked varying combinations of confusion, fear, and frustration.

Speaking to The Independent, Mr Jones warned of the precedent the move sets for local vendors.

“I think the decision sends a really strange message to the market,” Jones said. “That's what a lot of the other traders here have been saying – 'What about me? If I grow my business and become successful, does it mean I get thrown out?'

“Traders here are worried because a lot of them have got short-term leases, and they're always in fear of losing their lease.”

Other vendors who spoke to The Independent anonymously echoed a similarly stomach-churning question: how can a stall be closed for being “too popular”?

open image in gallery Matthew Jones questioned what the decision means for the rest of the market ( Bread Ahead )

Dating back more than a millennium, Borough Market is run by a charitable trust governed by a board of volunteer trustees.

Traditionally dedicated to wholesale trade and independent food craft, securing a trader spot is notoriously competitive – applicants are vetted through a rigorous selection process that prioritises artisanal production, local sourcing, and environmental sustainability.

But in more recent years, the market has found itself managing increasing levels of congestion, massive queues, and a shifting consumer demographic looking for the next viral bite.

open image in gallery Borough Market has surged in popularity as viral food trends have taken the internet by storm ( AFP/Getty )

While long-term residents like Neal’s Yard Dairy and Kappacasein have anchored the market for decades, turnover among smaller pitches is built into the business model to encourage fresh talent and rotas of guest traders.

In market terms, Bread Ahead’s decade-plus tenure has placed it well beyond the category of a temporary guest pop-up. For Mr Jones, “Borough Market is home. It is where Bread Ahead began, and we want to stay.”

The sentiment is widespread.

Oskar Threlfall, a student visiting the market, was in the middle of biting into a creme brûlée doughnut when he said: “It does seem like they’re punishing someone for being successful – there must be something else behind it because why else would they get rid of something just for being too good?”

open image in gallery Oskar Threlfall, right, questioned the logic behind the market’s plans to close the bakery ( The Independent )

Nichola Collete, a regular who has watched the market evolve, was equally baffled: “It seems like such a shame – it’s quite sad. I thought the whole point of Borough Market was to host independent places that make really good things. I just don’t get it; surely the market should want their stalls to be doing well?”

But for Amaan Faisal, another Bread Ahead customer, the proposed closing was less of a blow: “I do love Bread Ahead, but there’s quite a few of them around London.

“It’s sad they’ll have to close down, but it might give another independent place a chance to become just as popular.”

But not all customers agreed.

Adinda Vandeyken, a Belgian tourist who stumbled upon Bread Ahead’s doughy creations with her family on holiday, said: “It just sounds really weird. Why would it be shut down just because it’s doing well?”

open image in gallery Bread Ahead when it first appeared at Borough Market ( Bread Ahead )

Looking around, she added: “It’s not as if Bread Ahead is taking over the entire market. People come here to sample different stalls and walk around. It doesn't look like they're taking business away from anyone else.”

For Mr Jones, who started Bread Ahead as a small stand, the growing popularity of his bakery – which now hosts locations in Dubai, Riyadh, and Bangkok as well as seven branches in London – cannot be called anything but a success story.

But in Borough Market, a space that traders across the market say has built its reputation on independent hustle, something has changed. Success, it seems, may no longer be the recipe for survival.

open image in gallery Adinda Vandeyken, right, expressed surprise at the market’s decision ( The Independent )

Borough Market told The Independent its terms do not allow its traders to enter franchises, or offer franchised goods for sale, and that a formal process is communicated to traders well in advance of a lease expiry date.

In a statement, the market added: “We apply this process fairly and consistently.

“The Borough Market Charitable Trust remains in contact with Bread Ahead, both directly and through its respective legal representatives, and discussions are ongoing about the business’s future at the market, including a potential departure date in 2028.

“We remain committed to engaging constructively with Bread Ahead as discussions about its future at the market continue.”

Harry Kane has rewritten German football history by becoming the fastest player to reach 100 Bundesliga goals, achieving the milestone in just his 98th league appearance during Bayern Munich’s 7-0 victory over Union Berlin.

The England captain broke a mark set 49 years ago by Cologne’s Dieter Muller, who required 129 matches in 1977. Kane’s remarkable efficiency — averaging a league goal every 78.5 minutes since arriving in 2023 — ensured the record was long inevitable.

He now has 152 goals in 154 appearances in all competitions, including 61 in 51 games last term.

He secured the landmark with a 39th-minute penalty before heading in a Michael Olise cross early in the second half, putting Bayern top of the table ahead of the weekend matches.

The feat upstaged Olise, who scored his first Bayern hat-trick, and Jamal Musiala, who also scored a goal worthy of winning the game.

open image in gallery Bayern's Harry Kane celebrates after scoring his side's fourth goal between Bayern Munich and 1. FC Union Berlin ( AP )

“I’m very proud to have now scored 100 and 101 Bundesliga goals. I haven’t been around that long. I’ve loved every second of it,” he told Sky Germany.

“With Michael, Lucho (Luis Diaz) and Jamal I naturally get chances and today was no exception.

“So I just want to thank the team, the club, the coach, and the staff – everyone who has helped me achieve this.

“Let’s keep going like this. Scoring more goals in games is obviously a big step. Of course, there have been many important goals among them. I can only say that I’m enjoying every minute of it. Just like today.”

The 33-year-old is the bookmakers’ favourite to win the Ballon d’Or in October after scoring 73 goals for club and country last term, beating Cristiano Ronaldo’s career-best single-season record of 69 set in 2011-12, and only being surpassed by Lionel Messi’s record 82 goals from the same season.

open image in gallery The England captain admitted to being 'amazed' to find his name alongside Messi and Ronaldo, two figures widely considered the game’s greatest ever ( Getty )

Should Kane claim the prize, he would become just the fifth Englishman to receive it, following Sir Stanley Matthews, Sir Bobby Charlton, Kevin Keegan and Michael Owen, and the first since Owen’s success in 2001.

In an interview with Owen Hargreaves for TNT Sports, the Bayern Munich striker said: "I’m extremely proud of the season I put up, for sure.

"Not that long ago, I was that fan wanting to become a professional footballer and I am here now and winning awards and the Ballon d’Or is the same.

"Of course, now it is out of my hands, it is down to the voters and the people who decide it. The season I had was my best season by far and we’ll have to wait and see."

Once a distant ambition for technology researchers, the prospect of artificial intelligence models teaching themselves autonomously to be more efficient and capable appears ever closer to reality.

As the technology advances, developers say it is approaching “recursive self-improvement,” or RSI, in which AI models find ways to improve themselves and build their successor. It could bring the promise of advances in science and medicine, tech company executives say, but also risks.

The uncertainty over where it all could lead is at the heart of growing fears about AI evading human control, and possible threats to humanity, which led several AI moguls to join last weekend in a call to slow down the technology’s pace of growth.

Anthropic this week detailed how its model Claude is helping the company to develop the next, more intelligent version of itself. Claude is now leading 26% of Anthropic’s model research and development, which the company said means it can complete most of a given task “end-to-end from a high-level prompt” while still being under human supervision. The models are not working completely autonomously — at least not yet.

Here are some key points about recursive self-improvement.

What is recursive self-improvement?

Leading AI companies have different definitions for recursive self-improvement. Some define it as when there is any feedback from AI on model improvement, while others define it as AI working toward that goal fully autonomously.

Autonomous recursive self-improvement essentially means AI that can improve itself designing the next version of the system, then the next version, and so on, said Anthony Aguirre, president and CEO of the nonprofit Future of Life Institute and a physics professor at the University of California, Santa Cruz.

“The really important thing here is that as AI is doing more of it, it gets faster, because AI operates just much, much more quickly than the humans do," he said.

The fear around RSI is based largely on a runaway superintelligence emerging from that process, said John Thickstun, an assistant professor of computer science at Cornell University who studies methods that control the behavior of AI models. But he said a more grounded view suggests a kind of recursive self-improvement has been going on in AI development for a while now.

"We have already, for years, been using these models in supportive roles for creating the next version of these models. So people use the past generation of models to write code for the AI systems that then create the next generation," he said.

For years, prominent AI researchers such as OpenAI co-founder Andrej Karpathy have experimented with trying to get AI models to train and improve new AI systems. Those efforts have brought minor improvements, but not big creative leaps, Thickstun said.

But AI companies today, Aguirre said, are much closer to pulling off those bigger leaps in improvement.

“You can see in these plots from Anthropic over time, more and more of research is being done by the AI and it’s becoming closer and closer to fully autonomous,” he said. “And the result of that success, ultimately is something that is, I think, extremely scary. I think this is probably the worst idea in the history of humanity to do this. And yes, they’re doing it.”

Some AI labs say RSI is not far off

Anthropic's recent announcement provided the public — and other labs — with some insight into RSI progress, and it encouraged its competitors to share similar metrics. Still, the company has not expressly said how close it is to achieving fully autonomous model improvement.

ChatGPT maker OpenAI announced this month that it has developed an automated “research intern,” which it defines as a system that can carry out well-defined research tasks under human direction, including “tasks that would take a skilled researcher a few days.” The company has said it is moving forward with the goal of creating an automated AI “researcher” by March 2028.

The company said in that announcement that while RSI can help align models' actions with human values and intentions, that doesn't mean “rapid RSI is necessarily an outcome we should pursue.”

“Whether and how to proceed must depend on our ability to preserve human control and on informed democratic choices about the benefits and risks,” the company said in a blog post.

Elon Musk seems more eager to forge ahead. He said in March that for xAI's Grok models, “humans are gradually getting less and less in the loop” on model improvement and that “every successive model is built by the one before it,” but clarified that the process was not yet fully automated. That target might be reached by the end of this year, he added, “but not later" than 2027.

Microsoft and some other leading AI companies seem to be taking a different approach.

Mustafa Suleyman, the CEO of Microsoft AI, has said the company is moving toward “humanist superintelligence,” or advanced AI capabilities that are in service of people and humanity at large. Suleyman said in a 2025 essay that this would not mean “an unbounded and unlimited entity with high degrees of autonomy,” but rather AI that is “carefully calibrated, contextualized, within limits.”

How development slowdown talks could impact RSI

A key challenge labs face — and have been facing essentially since the technology’s inception — is ensuring their safety measures advance alongside the models' capabilities.

Divisions have emerged in the tech industry over calls for a coordinated AI slowdown for safety, and not every major player in the AI space has specifically commented on their path forward with RSI.

Anthropic, which has been a leading voice in the calls for pacing, has said it would slow or temporarily pause its development work — assuming its global competitors also did so, and in a "verifiable manner.”

OpenAI explicitly said this month it does not yet know how to “safely get all the way to aligned, full RSI,” adding that the company “cannot assume that progress in alignment and safety will keep pace.” More capable systems can become harder to monitor, it continued, but pursuing RSI is still a goal it says it values because an “automated AI researcher can also be an automated safety or alignment researcher.”

Hundreds of people have been evacuated after a huge fire broke out at an iconic hotel in Kent.

Emergency services raced to the Grand Burstin Hotel in The Harbour, Folkestone, to tackle the blaze, which fire crews said started in the basement in the early hours of Saturday morning.

About 280 people were evacuated as dramatic pictures showed plumes of smoke billowing over the harbour. Residents living nearby have been urged to close all windows and doors and “avoid the area” as firefighters continue to tackle the blaze.

No injuries relating to the fire have been reported and the cause of the blaze is not yet known.

open image in gallery A blaze broke out at the Grand Burstin Hotel in Folklestone ( PA Archive )

At its height, 26 fire engines were at the scene, the fire service said.

Folkestone and Hythe District Council posted on X saying: “A fire is currently ongoing at the Folkestone Grand Burstin Hotel.

“We are operating a welfare centre at Three Hills Sports Park for people being evacuated from the site, where we are providing support to those affected. We are supporting all emergency services involved in the response and their efforts to get people to safety.

“Our advice to residents living nearby is to: close all windows and doors; avoid the area and do not attempt to approach the hotel; follow the instructions of emergency services; keep roads clear to allow emergency vehicles to access the area.

“We will provide further updates as information becomes available.”

Kent Fire and Rescue Service said 10 fire engines currently remain at the scene.

“Crews wearing breathing apparatus have worked hard to bring the fire under control and are now dampening down any remaining hotspots,” the service said in an update.

“It’s believed the fire started in the basement of the property, but the cause is not yet known. Around 280 people evacuated the building, and a welfare centre has been organised by Folkestone and Hythe District Council.

“No fire-related injuries have been reported.”

It added: “Members of KFRS’ Volunteer Response Team are on-hand to offer advice and support, and The Salvation Army is providing welfare to crews. Road closures remain in place while emergency services continue to work at the scene.”

A spokesperson for Kent Police said: “Kent Police was called at around 1.20am on Saturday September 19 2026 to reports of a fire at a hotel on Marine Parade, Folkestone.

“Officers remain in attendance to assist traffic flow while our Kent Fire and Rescue Service colleagues work to tackle the fire.”

A spokesperson for Britannia Hotels Group said: “We can confirm there has been an incident at the Grand Burstin Hotel in Folkestone and we are taking immediate action to ensure the safety and wellbeing of all guests and team members.

“Emergency services are on site and we are fully cooperating with the authorities to support those affected and assist with the ongoing response.”

Parts of the UK are set to be hotter than Athens next week as temperatures will soar to 26C as late summer warmth returns.

Greece’s capital city will struggle to see temperatures above 24C at the start of next week, while large swathes of England are forecast to bask in the mid-20s.

While the south will get the best of the sun, most areas will experience warmer temperatures than usual for late September.

Met Office forecasts show Tuesday will be the hottest day of the week, with the mercury soaring to 26C across the south-east of England.

Monday and Wednesday will also see temperatures above 20C across most of England, with the mercury only taking a slight dip towards the end of the week.

Temperatures are set to soar to the mid-20s next week ( Met Office )

A build up of high pressure across the UK is responsible for the temperatures creeping up compared to the milder weekend.

The Met Office said: “The change begins with developments over the Atlantic. A deep area of low pressure is expected to form well to the west of the UK. Although this system is not forecast to move directly across the country, it is likely to drag warmer air up from the continent and subtropical Atlantic.

“High pressure will then build across the UK alongside this warmer air during the latter part of the weekend and into next week. This would mean a transition to predominantly dry and bright conditions, with sunny spells becoming more widespread.”

However, the Met Office also said the warmer weather could also be cut short by the expected arrival of a colder front from the west, the timing of which remains uncertain.

After this, conditions are likely to become “changeable”, according to the Met Office’s longer-term forecast, “with spells of rain and showers interspersed with some short-lived spells of more settled weather and temperatures returning to near normal overall”.

It comes after an unbearably hot summer this year, marking the UK’s hottest on record.

The consecutive heatwaves had a devastating impact on the country, resulting in droughts and wildfires, and despite recent rainfall and fresher conditions, the nation is still paying the price.

Met Office five day forecast

Today:

A cloudy start in the south with outbreaks of rain. Staying largely cloudy in southern England and Wales with rain at times. Sunny spells elsewhere and showers across Scotland. Another windy day but feeling warm in any sunshine.

Tonight:

Staying cloudy and mild in the south tonight with a few outbreaks of rain possible. A fresher feel in the north with clear spells. Winds easing.

Sunday:

Rain clears to the south by morning, leaving a drier and brighter day with lighter winds. A few showers continue in Scotland. Feeling pleasant in the sunshine.

Outlook for Monday to Wednesday:

Sunny spells on Monday and Tuesday, and turning warmer. A brief spell of rain moves into the north on Wednesday, but staying dry for many.

News.title: ‘Caged like an animal, it could only end one way’: New prisons crisis as segregation deaths soar
News.content:

Read our Privacy notice

Almost 50 people have died in segregation in Britain’s prisons over the past decade, The Independent can reveal, as governors face calls to stop putting vulnerable inmates in isolation.

Matthew Osborne, 39, had spent 54 days in a segregation unit when he took his own life at scandal-hit HMP Lowdham Grange in November 2023.

His sister said his death had left the family “broken” and believes his mental health severely deteriorated in isolation. He was supposed to be closely monitored but at one point he received just three minutes of human contact in a three-day period.

“I think most people wouldn’t last 54 days by themselves with nothing,” Jasmine Osborne told The Independent, adding it would have been “torture”.

“I think even the most healthy minds would have fractured at some point.”

She demanded a review of the use of segregation after freedom of information requests showed her brother was among 49 people to die in isolation in prisons in England and Wales between 2015 to 2025.

In 2024, as the prison overcrowding crisis was taking hold, deaths in segregation units soared to 12 – the equivalent of one a month.

“I do feel like there’s a clear correlation between segregation and his deterioration that led to his passing,” she added. “Long periods of isolation would be enough to tip anyone over the top.”

An inquest into his death concluded multiple failings and neglect contributed to Mr Osborne’s suicide in the Care and Separation Unit (CSU) at the then privately-run prison in Nottinghamshire, which was later taken over by the Ministry of Justice after a string of tragedies.

The prisons and probation ombudsman, Adrian Usher, believes some of the recent deaths in segregation were avoidable.

He has previously warned that segregation should only be used for struggling prisoners in exceptional circumstances. He issued a bulletin earlier this year after discovering that eight out of 11 recent deaths in segregation involved prisoners who were being monitored under suicide and self-harm procedures.

“Our data shows that the number of deaths recorded in segregation units have been higher in the past two years, particularly due to the marked increase in 2024,” he told The Independent.

“Some of these deaths would have been avoidable and vulnerable people should not be held in segregation unless absolutely necessary”.

The charity Inquest, which supported Ms Osborne, said segregation creates a “prison within a prison” which isolates people from vital human contact and its use must be phased out.

“Inquest's casework repeatedly lays bare that people with mental ill health are being inappropriately segregated against prison rules, with fatal consequences,” added Jessica Pandian, senior policy and communications officer.

“Almost 50 deaths in segregation over the past decade are an indictment of its overuse. Segregation must be phased out, and reliance on it indicates a failing system."

open image in gallery Matthew Osborne died after 54 days in segregation ( Jasmine Osborne )

Mr Osborne, 39, was moved to the segregation unit in October 2023 after he was involved in a number of altercations, which staff believed he initiated as a form of self-harm. He had already made three attempts on his own life at the category B prison, which had recently undergone the first ever private-to-private transfer as Sodexo took over operations.

Governors have the power to confine prisoners to segregation for up to 72 hours for discipline or for the prisoner’s protection, after which cases must be reviewed every 14 days by a Segregation Review Board. Segregating a prisoner beyond 42 days must be authorised by senior leadership, usually a prison group director.

Policies also state that inmates like Mr Osborne, who was being monitored under suicide and self-harm procedures called Assessment, Care in Custody and Teamwork (ACCT), should only be segregated in “exceptional circumstances”.

The inquest jury found Mr Osborne was segregated unlawfully for the last nine days of his life because the exceptional circumstances were not met.

His sister said Mr Osborne, who used to love staying active and enjoyed meeting new people, rapidly declined as he was shut off from human contact.

“In his time in segregation, Matthew was described as shouting in his cell saying things that didn’t make sense,” she told The Independent. “He was found under his bed. These aren’t scenes of someone who’s well.

“I do find it quite hard to understand why he wasn’t given the proper support that he needed. I do feel that everything that I heard at the inquest, Matthew was treated as a disciplinary problem more than someone who was losing his mind.”

open image in gallery The MoJ stepped in to take HMP Lowdham Grange back into public management ( Google )

The inquest found the prison falsified records of his ACCT monitoring checks, which were supposed to take place three times an hour.

On 25 November, there were no observations of him between 2.32pm and 4.22pm, during which time ended his life. The segregation staff who were supposed to be monitoring him were watching television to “keep track of the football reporting”, the inquest heard.

He was also housed in a cell which did not meet basic standards, including a lack of mattress, the coroner said in a prevention of future deaths report.

Although prison rules state that inmates must never be subjected to a regime which amounts to solitary confinement – being confined alone for 22 hours a day without human contact – Mr Osborne’s cell door was open for less than three minutes in the three days before his death.

Neither was he provided with adequate distraction materials. He had no radio, TV or reading or writing material and was last seen staring at the cell wall before he died.

Ms Osborne, 39, said her brother was deprived of care and human comfort while he was “locked in four small walls while he’s mentally unravelling”.

“Matthew wasn’t given meaningful interaction,” she said. “At one point he only had three minutes in a period of three days. What would you expect the outcome to be? It’s like having a caged animal.”

She said suicidal prisoners should not be isolated and called for greater transparency around the use of segregation. Currently, the prisons service does not publish any data about the number of prisoners in segregation or how long they are held.

Paying tribute, she said her brother was someone who used to “love to adventure”. “He was just a big brother who will be missed greatly,” she added.

open image in gallery Prisons and Probation Ombudsman Adrian Usher says prisoners on an ACCT should only be segregated in ‘exceptional circumstances’ ( Design102/PPO )

A spokesperson for Sodexo said they continue to extend their “deepest sympathies and sincere apologies” to Mr Osborne’s family and all those affected by his death.

"As we commented at the conclusion of the inquest into Mr Osborne's death, we have accepted the findings of the jury in full and continue to take this matter seriously,” they added.

A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: “The government is gripping the prison crisis it inherited, and progress is being made at across the prisons estate to strengthen safety measures and improve support for prisoners.

“The safety of prisoners and staff is our top priority, and the use of segregation is only ever a last resort. We are taking further steps to protect prisoners at risk of self-harm by improving case management, enhancing staff training and providing targeted support for those with the most complex needs.”

News.title: GPs summoned in Frankfurt as third malaria death reported
News.content:
While malaria is treatable if caught early, the patients were likely not considered to have the disease because they lacked travel history to countries where malaria typically circulates, meaning treatment was delayed.

“This is why we alerted the medical people in Frankfurt, if you have odd cases presenting at your clinic, please also consider that there might be malaria around,” Dr Tinnemann said.

“There is this assumption that people who get sick with a nasty fever in places like Frankfurt and elsewhere that have not travelled cannot have malaria, and we don’t bother to investigate. That’s got to stop. That’s why these people die,” Joe Lines, Professor of Malaria Control and Vector Biology at the London School of Tropical Hygiene and Medicine, told The Telegraph.

Before the two cases in Schwanheim – both of which occurred at least 3 miles from the airport where the first malaria cases were reported – investigators were working on the hypothesis that just a single mosquito was responsible for the outbreak, but the new cases have cast doubt on that theory.

“We expect mosquitoes to live between one and three weeks on average,” said Dr Tinnemann.

“We had five cases in the beginning of July, then another in August - at that point, there was a good chance that potentially it could just be one bug. But now it seems at least there must be one other,” he said.

Frankfurt’s public health board have now shipped blood samples from all eight patients to a specialised lab in Antwerp, Belgium, where scientists can carry out DNA analysis to indicate if the infections came from one or multiple mosquitoes, and are awaiting results.

As temperatures warm, experts fear that several tropical mosquito-borne diseases – including malaria, dengue fever, Zika virus, and chikungunya could become established across Europe.

Earlier this month, a colony of Aedes aeypti mosquitoes – the bugs responsible for transmitting dengue and Zika virus – were found breeding in a residential area in East London for the first time.

Airfinity, the disease-monitoring company, said of the malaria outbreak in Frankfurt: “the risk to the wider public remains low but non-zero.”

“Continued vector surveillance, rapid diagnosis, and ready access to antimalarials are critical to prevent further severe outcomes.”
