Sports.title: UEFA and CONCACAF demand Gianni Infantino hands over £7m to all FIFA members
Sports.content:
UEFA and CONCACAF have written a joint letter to Gianni Infantino calling for at least $10million from its reserves to be paid to FIFA's 211 Member Associations.

It follows Infantino's failed FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) plans, which intended to part-privatise world football's governing body.

4 UEFA and CONCACAF have called on Infantino and FIFA to pay their 211 members using money in their reserves Credit: Getty

The letter is signed by UEFA President Aleksander Ceferin and CONCACAF President Victor Montagliani. The latter is a potential candidate to run against Infantino in next March's election even though he has not yet publicly come forward.

"FIFA is on course to close 2023-26 with reserves of approximately $6billion," reads the letter, seen by talkSPORT. "[This is] considerably more than is required."

Infantino is asked to "make at least $10m available to each of [FIFA's] 211 member associations over the 2027-30 cycle". This would cost $2.11bn with pre-planned funding on top.

The letter backs up a belief from senior UEFA and CONCACAF figures that FIFA should invest using far more of its own reserves.

It was not lost on critics of FFE that Infantino was seeking $4.2bn from investors, including Joshua Kushner, and yet FIFA's own reserves following the 2022 World Cup were almost exactly this number.

Given the investment was offered on such favourable terms to private investors, there appears no reason why FIFA couldn’t have just used its own reserves to fund FFE allowing for 100 per cent of any profits to stay within the organisation. It’s a moot point now FFE has been shelved, but one that has led to a wider debate over how FIFA should use its reserves.

Several federations, including the English Football Association, are in favour of FIFA depleting their reserves in order to better fund members. This is due to FIFA being a not-for-profit organisation and a confidence that the organisation's revenue streams will continue to grow.

Infantino had promised federations who endorsed FFE two joining bonuses: an initial payment worth $20m, and a secondary one for the same amount.

Ceferin and Montagliani argue FIFA has more than enough money to self-fund without the need for private investors.

"FIFA currently holds billions of dollars in accumulated reserves," the letter goes on to read. "These resources belong to football and exist to serve the game and its 211 Member Associations.

4 FIFA have been told to stop withholding 'billions' that currently sit in its reserves Credit: AFP

"Prudence should not prevent a careful examination of whether a portion could responsibly be released to the extent those reserves exceed FIFA's foreseeable needs.

"Releasing part of these reserves would demonstrate that member associations should not have to choose between development and good governance; between investment and integrity; or between financial support and the ability to consider proposals on their merits.

"Development is an institutional responsibility of FIFA – not a matter of individual discretion."

UEFA and CONCACAF have been lobbying other confederations to support their motion ahead of the next FIFA Council meeting on October 15 in Zurich.

Meanwhile, Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt has called on Infantino and FIFA Secretary General Mattias Grafström to release all documents relating to FFE, and to publish the reasoning behind why US striker Flo Balogun's red card against Bosnia was suspended making him eligible to play in the World Cup last sixteen tie with Belgium.

As talkSPORT exclusively revealed, Infantino was lobbied by US President Donald Trump to review the ban.

4 Infantino is under huge pressure after a controversy-filled World Cup and due to his FFE plans Credit: Getty

Infantino has been under significant pressure to stand down following both that incident and the ill-fated FFE proposal. Yet the FIFA President has vowed to fight on, and no candidate has yet come forward to stand against him.

That could change between now and the November 18 deadline, according to UEFA vice-president Laura McAllister. The former Wales international has been one of the leading voices within UEFA pushing for FIFA reforms, including a new president.

'There has to be a challenger for Infantino'

"In the weeks since the exposure of FFE, we have seen a gradual seeping lack of confidence in the leadership of Gianni Infantino," McAllister told talkSPORT's Ben Jacobs at the World Football Summit in Madrid.

"It wasn't just about that initiative, there have been a series of episodes or incidents over recent months and years that have undermined the confidence in his leadership.

"Most recently, there was the overturning of the red card of Balogun at the World Cup, and the FIFA Peace Prize over which there was no consultation… despite it being hugely political.

"There has to be a challenger to Infantino because he will certainly, as he already said, be a candidate in the election unless something dramatic happens in the coming weeks. Of course, it could do, but legal processes [including UEFA putting together a criminal case against Infantino and FIFA] take a long time, so let's not hold our breath over that.

4 UEFA's vice president, McAllister, believes a candidate has to rival Infantino for FIFA presidency Credit: Getty

"There has to be a candidate who, first of all, can command the support of all modernisers beyond just Europe. Football doesn't belong to Europe. Yes, we [UEFA] are a very powerful confederation and, yes, we generate a lot of funds, but football belongs to every single federation and club across the world. On this, I agree with Infantino that football doesn't belong to anyone in any geographical location.

"We have to unite people around a candidate, or maybe more than one candidate, and that candidate, whoever he or she is, has to stand on a manifesto of agreed reform: of greater transparency or greater accountability, of less political interference and must recognise the role of the FIFA President should be to run football, and not [like Infantino] to involve himself in other ventures, whether that's via the private or political sectors.

"I hope very much there will be a candidate [to rival Infantino] and I think that's where we are at the moment. Lots of work is happening behind the scenes. But we need a candidate with an ethos of credibility and modernisation, showing why they should win the election next March."

Behind the scenes, both Infantino and prospective candidates, including Montagliani, are doing the maths to determine where the votes lie.

Infantino went into the 2026 World Cup with 200+ letters of endorsement. Several of these have been revoked, but the FIFA President currently still has more than 106 Member Associations on side despite a wave of withdrawals of support from Europe.

That’s why Infantino remains so bullish about winning another term, but the landscape could yet change if another candidate emerges to rival him.

Sports.title: Harry Kane creates Bundesliga history as he smashes 49-year record for Bayern Munich
Sports.content:
Harry Kane creates Bundesliga history as he smashes 49-year record for Bayern Munich

Harry Kane has become the fastest Bundesliga player in history to hit 100 goals.

The England captain scored twice for Bayern Munich in a 7-0 win over Union Berlin on Friday night to set a German top-flight record.

3 Kane tucked away a penalty for Bayern to reach 100 Bundesliga goals on Friday night Credit: AFP

Kane found the target for the 100th time in the Bundesliga since his 2023 move from Tottenham Hotspur.

He managed to reach a century of goals in just 98 appearances by tucking away a penalty in the 39th minute of the game.

This has smashed the record previously held by German icon Dieter Muller, who took 129 matches to score 100 in 1977 for FC Cologne.

He then went on to score a second time and reach 101 goals, netting another after 54 minutes at the Allianz Arena.

Since joining Bayern three years ago, Kane has remarkably scored a goal every 78.5 minutes in the Bundesliga.

That is a better rate than Erling Haaland and Robert Lewandowski.

In Bayern's last match, a 2-1 win over Elversberg, Kane became the fastest player in their history to hit 150 goals too.

The 33-year-old managed to do so in his 153rd Bayern appearance.

Last season, he scored 61 goals in 51 matches across all competitions and won the European Golden Boot with 36 league strikes.

Closing in on the Ballon d'Or?

Kane is in a strong position for the Ballon d'Or title, with the striker one of the favourites to be crowned at next month's ceremony.

3 Kane smashed home from the spot to reach a century faster than any other player Credit: Getty

Should he win, he would become the first English player since Michael Owen in 2001 to receive the honour.

And his record-breaking strike is sure to have increased his chances of pipping Kylian Mbappe and Lamine Yamal to the post.

However, speaking ahead of Friday night's game, where he has made history, he wasn't keen on speaking about the award.

Kane told Marca: “I don’t like to speak about myself… 73 goals speak for themselves.

“It’s been the best season of my life, by far.”

Bayern led 3-0 at half time against Union Berlin, with Kane's penalty the second of the evening in Munich.

3 Kane and Bayern thrashed Union Berlin at the Allianz Arena, with Olise scoring a hat-trick Credit: Getty

Jamal Musiala opened the scoring after 18 minutes before Michael Olise added the third just before the break.

And then Kane added another to double his tally and put Bayern 4-0 up and cruising - but the scoring didn't stop there.

Olise would go on to score a hat-trick and Ismael Saibari also got in on the act, as Bayern thrashed Union Berlin 7-0.

Sports.title: History-making WSL side building new training ground ‘better than most Premier League clubs’
Sports.content:
London City Lionesses owner Michele Kang believes their new training ground will be better than Premier League teams' facilities.

The WSL club, who are the first-ever team not affiliated with a men's side to reach the top flight, are building a new training centre.

3 London City Lionesses are building a new state-of-the-art training ground that will compete with Premier League clubs' Credit: Getty

It is expected to open within the next year, as they continue to take big strides in the women's game under Kang's ownership.

Kang has invested a huge amount of money into the women's football sphere and has transformed London City Lionesses.

Within 18 months of taking over in 2023, they achieved promotion to the WSL, and they've gone from strength to strength since.

Last summer, they broke the women's transfer world record by signing Grace Geyoro from Paris Saint-Germain, before going on to bring in multiple other new superstars this year.

London City Lionesses incredibly brought two-time Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas to the club from Barcelona, also signing her teammate Mapi Leon and ex-England goalkeeper Mary Earps.

As well as investing on the pitch, the club are now in the process of building a new training ground - and it's going to be special.

New training ground 'better than Premier League clubs'

Kang told BBC Sport: "We're building a state-of-the-art training centre for our female athletes dedicated to them, built and designed for them, which will open in less than a year.

"Our architect, who has built several Premier League training centres, told me that by the time the London City training centre is up and running, it would be better than the majority of Premier League men's teams' training centres."

On the importance of making sure the women's game is equal to the men's, she added: "We have to take care of our female players better so that they can train, perform, and thrive as female athletes, not small men.

"You drive your boy to a state-of-the-art training centre and then, if you're lucky enough to have a facility nearby, you drive your girl somewhere else. Why would you accept that?"

3 Two-time Ballon d'Or winner Putellas is London City Lionesses' captain amid investment on and off the pitch Credit: Getty

3 Owner Kang believes the club's new facility will rival some of the best in English football as a whole Credit: Getty

London City Lionesses' new training facility will also help in research into injury rates in the women's game going forward.

"There are more ACL injuries among female players. Two or three times more female players get ACL injuries than male players," Kang continued.

"Something like 94 per cent of all science medical research is dedicated to men. So there's just fundamentally so little known about the female body."

How are London City Lionesses doing this season?

Two games into the WSL season, London City Lionesses are sitting seventh in the table and three points off the top.

They have won one and lost one of their opening games.

In their first game of the league campaign, they beat Manchester United 2-1, as Putellas made her WSL debut.

But a defeat to West Ham followed and now they're preparing to take on Charlton Athletic on Saturday afternoon.

Sports.title: RIATH AL-SAMARRAI: It's all very well Howard Webb sending his VAR bunglers to the naughty step - but those that know him tell me 'back-stabbing' referee supremo must look in the mirror
Sports.content:
Matt Donohue and Blake Antrobus will have a sharper grasp of what it means to interfere with play this weekend. On account of their VAR blunders at the Manchester derby, Howard Webb has decreed they won’t have that option in the Premier League for the foreseeable future.

We know enough by now about their journey to the naughty step. But what about their boss? What about Webb?

How many of these malfunctions need occur before the guy in charge of refereeing takes a look closer to home?

He gave his opinion on Tuesday, which is to say he took a dim view of how his best official, Michael Oliver, saw a correct decision to disallow Erling Haaland’s winner overruled by his eyes in the sky. When Webb reviewed it all, he blamed Donohue’s ‘tunnel vision’ on Haaland and Antrobus was guilty of following Donohue down the same hole.

Neither of them factored for the obvious, that Enzo Fernandez was offside and interfering, and each of them will spend some time below ground as a consequence.

‘They'll not be officiating again until after the international break,’ said Webb.

Howard Webb may have a few questions of his own to answer if the Premier League refereeing standards keep slipping

Enzo Fernandez clearly interferes with play in the Manchester derby but it was missed by the VAR officials, who have now been stood down by Webb

I chatted over a few of these sentiments with a former Premier League referee on Friday and there was no disagreement about standing down the officials. Donohue, the VAR, and Antrobus, his assistant, had committed a cock-up in a high-profile game. Of course they should be benched for a while, we agreed.

But the issue was the man whose organisation put them there in the first place. That being the man who was also responsible for the training and refinement of Michael Salisbury, Lee Mason, John Brooks, Darren England and Dan Cook.

What do they have in common? They have all been in the VAR booth since Webb took over at what was then known as the PGMOL in late 2022 and they have all sat on that naughty step for human errors in their handling of the machine era. Salisbury has visited it more than once.

Errors will happen. That is fine. And it is also fine to view VAR as the worst encroachment in the recent history of the game; a joy-sucking, time-wasting, immensely flawed attempt to find a level of perfection that sport never needed and won’t be delivered. That’s my view and immediate abolition is my wish.

But so long as it exists, where is the accountability from Webb for its botched application in the Premier League? How many people have to be stood down for huge mistakes on his watch before Webb himself stands down?

To follow my conversations with those who have worked with him is to construct a complicated portrait. ‘He’s a clever man and he can be very charming,’ one former official tells me. ‘He can be very impressive, but he is also a master politician and will stab you in the back if it suits him.’

We can take those thoughts or leave them – refereeing is a competitive world. They can bitch and moan about a colleague as well as the best of us.

But other observations go deeper, namely around his key appointments, which include the import of Kevin Blom from the Dutch Eredivisie as performance coach and Hugh Dallas as manager of Pro Ref’s select group.

Erling Haaland celebrates the goal that should not have stood but that won the Manchester derby

Referee Michael Oliver takes his instructions from the VAR in Stockley Park

Dallas was fourth official in the 2002 World Cup final, so his credentials have merit; Blom is perhaps more famous in Scotland over a bad penalty decision that favoured Czech Republic in a Euro 2012 qualifier.

The latter is part of the tit-for-tat of football, but there is a perception in some quarters that they do not pose enough of a challenge to Webb’s leadership. In other words, who is keeping the boss in check?

As a former Premier League referee put it: ‘As ex-referees, we are asking: “Really, are you really surrounding yourself with these people?” It’s so Howard can be comfortable. I think he will always want people who he can be above.’

Only Webb will know if that’s true. But it is hard to deny that a vast amount of Premier League expertise has been lost to the migration of officials elsewhere once they leave the frontline.

Martin Atkinson refereed in the Premier League for more than 20 years, and then led the select group, but he is now the VAR manager for the Scottish FA. Jon Moss oversaw almost 300 top-flight games and left Webb’s PGMOL in 2024 – he is now head of refereeing at Football Australia. Mark Clattenburg presided over a Champions League final and today works on Gladiators.

All of them will have their reasons for being where they are and all of them dropped the occasional clanger. That’s football. That’s refereeing.

But it also looks a little like a drain of know-how that would doubtless help in the English game, where the quirks and rhythms are a unique challenge to officials.

I tend to doubt the idea that the VAR system is better implemented abroad, because statistics around the error rates across the major European leagues are fairly consistent.

Why is former referee Mark Clattenburg working on Gladiators and not helping out in the Premier League?

Martin Atkinson refereed in the Premier League for more than 20 years but he is now the VAR manager for the Scottish FA

I would also suggest that Webb is hardly the face of gross incompetence – one former colleague of his says that he is a better manager than his predecessor, Mike Riley, and worse at training referees.

Equally, some applaud the greater transparency he has pursued with video analysis on television; others say the referees ‘hate’ it.

It’s a tricky picture to study. It’s certainly far tougher to interpret than the one showing Enzo Fernandez interfering with play in front of the Manchester United goalkeeper. But one thing is clear – Webb cannot persist with the charade of blaming everyone except himself.

Sports.title: Goalkeeping icon reveals SIX secrets to David Raya's success: The Arsenal No 1's 'K-block', his spring, how he compensates for his height, the area he's always prided himself on... and where he can still improve
Sports.content:
Goalkeeping icon reveals SIX secrets to David Raya's success: The Arsenal No 1's 'K-block', his spring, how he compensates for his height, the area he's always prided himself on... and where he can still improve

Gravity-defying leaps, match-winning blocks, brilliant distribution and calming catches are just some of the attributes that have helped David Raya become one of the most important lieutenants in Mikel Arteta's Arsenal.

The Spaniard has won three consecutive Premier League Golden Gloves (awarded to the goalkeeper with the most clean sheets) and was instrumental in last season's title glory.

Only Petr Cech and Joe Hart have more Golden Gloves, on four apiece, and Raya is hunting them down. He is also in the running for the Yashin Trophy – the Ballon d’Or for goalkeeper of the year.

Daily Mail Sport has enlisted the help of Asmir Begovic, the former Chelsea Premier League-winning goalkeeper with more than 300 appearances in the top flight, to break down Raya’s strengths, weaknesses and development across six key areas.

The result is a portrait of a goalkeeper whose game is not simply about spectacular saves, but about making the right decision, at the right time, again and again.

Arsenal goalkeeper David Raya is a three-time Premier League Golden Glove winner

Raya's consistency has seen him become one of the key lieutenants in Mikel Arteta's Arsenal

ONE-ON-ONES

There is probably no better example of Raya’s proficiency at this element of goalkeeping than his wonder save against West Ham in May. With the score at 0-0, Mateus Fernandes was one-on-one against Raya with plenty of time on his side and a huge portion of the goal to aim at.

Yet Raya refused to commit early, standing tall and making himself as big as possible, forcing Fernandes to take the near-post option. When the shot finally came, Raya reacted brilliantly at point-blank range to block it with his body and keep the scores level.

It was that save that sent Arsenal on their way to the title, a stop made under intense pressure. Rather than gambling on where a striker will finish, he stays patient to narrow the angle and make the attacker beat him.

‘This is where he comes to life,’ says Begovic, who runs a goalkeeping academy specialising in coaching and educating young keepers.

‘He’s very good in terms of his decision-making, which techniques to use, when to go out, how to go. He's excelled in this part of the game. You can use different techniques. You can use a full spread: a smother where you throw your body and chest at the ball and go with your hands first.

‘You can use the K-block, which is something some goalkeepers use when you get really close to an attacker – when a keeper goes on his knee and puts his arms out like a K sign.

‘There's different ways you can challenge the attackers in a one-v-one situation. He has all those techniques. He's really good and selective as to when to use them.

‘The best (keepers) have different strings to their bow and are able to use different techniques and use them really well in times they need to.’

Begovic's verdict: 9/10

Raya pulls off his crucial one-on-one save against West Ham's Mateus Fernandes last season

Asmir Begovic, a Premier League winner with Chelsea, is hugely impressed by Raya's all-round game

SHOT-STOPPING

Raya’s reflexes are super sharp. And there are plenty of examples. There’s the save against Atalanta in the Champions League in September 2024 where he first sprang low to his right to parry Mateo Retegui’s penalty before somehow scrambling back to his feet and throwing himself in the opposite direction to claw the striker’s header off the line from the rebound. It was a remarkable display of agility and recovery.

Most recently, of course, he denied Enzo Le Fee from the penalty spot against Sunderland, diving sharply to his left and pushing the midfielder’s effort on to the post.

‘His shot-stopping has been one of the best (in the world), absolutely tremendous,’ says Begovic. ‘When you play for a team like Arsenal, it's not so much multiple shots a game, it's about having to make that one save.

'And he's been able to do that. He's showed up in big moments and helped them win many, many games.

‘There's many things in shot-stopping. Of course, years of practice and training, your physicality, your power, your speed. So I think balance, technique, many different factors go into it.

‘In particular, if you look at his power, his spring is able to really cover the goal. That's what's needed. If you look at goalkeepers (like Raya) that are slightly shorter in height, then they need a lot of power and push to be able to go and cover the goal.

‘Goalkeepers that are a bit taller, bigger, they have a bigger wingspan, they can get away with maybe not having as much power. So his spring and power is second to none. You have to compensate.’

Begovic's verdict: 9/10

Raya makes a remarkable double save against Atalanta in the Champions League

And he gets down brilliantly to tip Enzo Le Fee's penalty on to the post in last weekend's win over Sunderland

AERIAL ABILITY

Of Raya’s many strengths, it’s in the air where a chink in the armour can be found. He is still very good, no doubt, just not superhuman like he is in most other categories.

At 6ft tall, he is one of the smaller goalkeepers in the Premier League, so can’t easily rise above everyone else on crosses and corners to steal the ball away from giants trying to score. Rather than simply plucking the ball out of the air, Raya often has to rely on his positioning.

‘He copes well but it’s the trade-off,’ says Begovic. ‘If you're at a certain height, and obviously you can't do everything, you have to rely on your team-mates to help in the air.

‘He competes, he punches, he uses different techniques. He might not be able to catch often because he might not be able to reach a certain place (due to his height), but he certainly makes good decisions as to when to go, when not to go for crosses.’

His size does, however, force Raya to compensate in other ways. It leaves him making use of his goalline more, instead of always coming out to catch the ball. ‘His main strength will be on the goalline and that's where he'll always look to revert to and make the save as and when he needs to,’ Begovic says. ‘People might assume that is not being aggressive, but actually sometimes it's being more sensible.

'Because if you can't get the ball, you still give yourself a chance to make a save if you stay on the line. But if you go out and miss it, then you're usually in a world of trouble.

‘The best thing about Arsenal is they've built that relationship over time where they know what Raya’s strengths are and what they aren't, and when he's going to do things. He knows when to rely on his defenders (on aerial balls), and help them out in different ways.

‘It's very difficult to find goalkeepers who do absolutely everything. You have to pick and choose your battles.’

Begovic's verdict: 6/10

At 6ft tall, Raya is one of the smaller goalkeepers in the league, so can’t easily rise above everyone else on crosses and corners

DISTRIBUTION

Raya is amazing at distributing the ball quickly to set up counter-attacks through long throws and pinpoint kicks down field.

It helps make Arsenal deadly in transition. Raya can turn a defensive situation into an attacking opportunity within seconds. His long throws are particularly useful after corners, allowing Arsenal to bypass the first line of pressure and release players into space before the opposition can reorganise.

His solid distribution extends to a confidence in playing short passes under pressure, making him an important part of Arsenal's build-up from the back when they don't want to go long.

Begovic sees this as a real strength of Raya’s. ‘Making sure his distribution is spot on is something he's always prided himself on,’ he says.

‘He doesn't get into too many uncomfortable situations because of Arsenal’s backline but when he does, he has the different range of passing, which he also had at Brentford and Blackburn. It was always one of the strengths of his game.

‘There's the distribution with your feet, out of your hands, goal kicks. Obviously then in live play there’s dealing with pressure and dealing with different presses. Looking at his body type and the way he presents himself, it's something that he's quite comfortable in doing.

‘If I look now at Raya and Aston Villa’s Zion Suzuki and Jordan Pickford. They are very, very good at distribution. But Raya is right up there.’

Begovic's verdict: 9/10

Raya's distribution with his feet is superb and he often starts Arsenal's attacks with pinpoint passing

PERSONALITY

Raya is not a goalkeeper who hides from the spotlight. He is an assured and vocal presence behind Arsenal’s defence, demanding concentration from those in front of him while taking responsibility when the pressure is on.

He is also highly competitive and animated, his frustration quick to rise when things go wrong. Most importantly, Raya has shown a strong mentality when he has made mistakes, continuing to demand the ball and play out from the back, for example, rather than allowing errors to affect his confidence.

Begovic says: ‘He seems really well-balanced in how he approaches the game, great composure. He's been so reliable and that's the sort of presence you need at any club, but especially at a big club.

‘It's important to convey that sense of calmness. We call it being almost emotionally neutral, never get too high, never get too low, being consistent. They (the backline) look around and see you're very assured in what you're doing, very safe, very comfortable and that gives a lot of confidence to the other players.’

Begovic's verdict: 8/10

‘Raya seems really well balanced in how he approaches the game, great composure,' says Begovic

THE 'BIG' MOMENTS

From all of Raya’s strengths, there is one area Begovic believes the Spaniard has improved most in.

‘That ability to make the big saves,' says Begovic. 'In Arsenal's progression, he's not had to make as many saves, but we can look at many games where he makes those big, crucial saves.

‘That's a skill because it takes concentration, it takes focus, a save that happens in the 75th minute after maybe not having had an awful lot to do. So that's definitely something where he's progressed his game and again, it shows why he’s one of the world's best. The other thing is consistency. His consistency at the highest level has definitely improved.’

For Begovic, Raya should win the Yashin Trophy. ‘Yes, he’s been the best all-round goalkeeper in the season and the most consistent in his performances,’ he says.

Raya will certainly have earned the accolade.

Begovic's verdict: 9/10

Follow this link https://ab1academy.com/ to find details of Asmir Begovic’s goalkeeping academy which has five centres in the UK and is inspiring the next generation of keepers

Sports.title: 'At a big club it's our house, our rules': Inside the challenge Andoni Iraola faces in making the leap to Liverpool, as sources reveal the fatal errors made by Hodgson, Frank and Moyes - and the shocking player power they were up against
Sports.content:
'At a big club it's our house, our rules': Inside the challenge Andoni Iraola faces in making the leap to Liverpool, as sources reveal the fatal errors made by Hodgson, Frank and Moyes - and the shocking player power they were up against

When Roy Hodgson made the step up from Fulham to manage Liverpool, he was reigning Manager of the Year and understandably sure of himself as a coach.

His reputation for tactical knowledge and intelligence had been built across two-and-a-half decades and more than half-a-dozen countries. What he was not prepared for was working at a club like Liverpool.

‘He didn’t understand it when he walked in and he still didn’t fully understand it when he was asked to walk out again a few months later,’ a source who was there at the time tells Daily Mail Sport.

‘It’s different at a really big club and it’s especially different at a club like Liverpool. It’s not just about the football. It’s about what you do, what you say and how you carry yourself.

‘It’s nuanced and every part of it matters. That sounds daft and exaggerated. But it’s true. Roy thought his football pedigree and coaching was all that mattered and he was wrong.’

As Liverpool manager, the spotlight is on Andoni Iraola in a way he will never have experienced before

Roy Hodgson could not handle the Liverpool job despite his vast experience. ‘He didn’t understand it when he walked in and he didn’t understand it when he walked out,’ a source tells Daily Mail Sport

Taking the step up in football management always feels like a defining moment in a career. Sir Alex Ferguson at Manchester United managed it, eventually. So did Arsene Wenger. Eddie Howe’s switch from Bournemouth to Newcastle was seamless.

Others, more recently, have struggled.

Graham Potter fell on his face at Chelsea after leaving Brighton. Thomas Frank’s transition from Brentford to Tottenham proved too much. Ruben Amorim swapped Lisbon for United and drowned.

And now it’s Andoni Iraola’s turn. The 44-year-old Spaniard returns to his old club Bournemouth on Sunday still feeling his way as manager of Liverpool. Three wins and three draws from six opening games is an acceptable return but the size of the step up cannot be overstated.

For Liverpool’s opening pre-season game against Sunderland in Nashville – Iraola’s first as manager – there were 25,000 fans present. That’s twice as many as ever watched Bournemouth at their tiny stadium on the south coast. The level of expectation and scrutiny is incomparable.

‘That’s the key difference,’ says a source who watched Frank’s struggles at Tottenham closely. ‘At Brentford, every Premier League win Thomas gave them was a gift. They were grateful. It’s a bonus.

‘At Tottenham and other top clubs, it’s not like that. Three points are a minimum requirement. And then you have to play the right kind of football and say the right things. By the time Thomas started to get to grips with that, it was too late.’

For Liverpool’s opening pre-season game against Sunderland in Nashville – Iraola’s first as manager – there were 25,000 fans present

Thomas Frank could not make the step up from Brentford to Tottenham and eventually lost his job

Iraola is a well-respected and talented coach. His two previous postings have been successful, at Bournemouth – who he took into Europe – and Rayo Vallecano in Spain.

On that tour of America, Liverpool players were impressed with his sessions and expressed surprise at just how much time he spent with them on the grass, ball in hand and whistle in mouth.

Those on the trip talk of an easy charm and natural sense of calm. What is yet to emerge – simply because it hasn’t had to – is the depth and strength of his personality, steel and emotional intelligence.

‘There are some strong characters in that Liverpool dressing room,’ explains one agent to a first-team player. ‘There are egos. Others may use stronger words.

'Look what happened between Mo Salah and Arne Slot. That’s where the power balance can shift. At Bournemouth his word will have been law. Here, he may have to earn that right a little bit.’

Players are more powerful than ever in modern football. What they say and do matters more than it ideally should and they are not always rational judges.

Frank, for example, asked one first-team player to apologise for being late to a Champions League team meeting last season only to be met with refusal. At Chelsea, some of the club’s bloated squad called Potter ‘Harry’ behind his back.

On one occasion, a member of the Stamford Bridge ownership tried to pick the team for a talented coach. He had never even attended a Champions League match before selecting a Chelsea XI for one.

In the post-Ferguson era at United, meanwhile, David Moyes – hired from Everton – was suffocated by a combination of player scepticism, modest results and a lack of understanding of how you were expected to talk and behave at the biggest club in the land.

At Chelsea, some of the club’s bloated squad called Graham Potter ‘Harry’ behind his back

At Old Trafford back in 2013, players used to joke that the infamous Portuguese flop Bebe had more medals than the new manager. On a plane back from a European game, meanwhile, they chuckled when they saw Moyes reading a book on management.

‘The players were in charge,’ left back Patrice Evra told Daily Mail Sport at his book launch five years ago.

These things really shouldn’t matter but unfortunately they do and to what extent depends in part on the standing of the manager who came before. Iraola is replacing Slot who was sacked but only after winning the Premier League. The memory of Jurgen Klopp still lingers, meanwhile.

Klopp possessed a charisma, turn of phrase and political outlook that fell neatly in step with those on the Kop. He was smart, too. One of his first tactics, for example, was to reduce the very size of the football club in his head by learning the name of every single person who worked at the training ground. That was for them. But it was for him, too.

Again the contrast with the unfortunate Hodgson – sacked after taking 25 points from a possible 60 in the 2010-11 season – is stark. Hodgson, remember, was no ingenue. He had previously managed Inter Milan and the Swiss national team and had taken Fulham to the final of the Europa League only weeks before his appointment. He was an elite coach. Liverpool, however, is just different.

‘Klopp just understood the club and its quirks,’ explains another source. ‘Rafael Benitez – Roy’s predecessor – did too. And indeed Brendan Rodgers later on. At Liverpool, the media need to be indulged, as do certain fans’ groups. Your language needs to reflect that, too.

‘Iraola, for example, will be examined in a different way to how Enzo Maresca will be by Manchester City fans. Even though his job is, on the surface, a significantly harder one.

‘How many people were listening to what he said at Bournemouth? At Liverpool, everybody is listening to it. Every word of it. And they will soon be dissecting it on podcasts and looking for hidden meanings that often are not even there.

‘One of Roy’s most memorable errors came when Ferguson accused Fernando Torres of diving and he didn’t bite back. He basically said he wasn’t getting involved. Torres was his best player and a Kop idol. To the fans, Roy left him hanging there after a verbal assault by our greatest rival. As Liverpool manager you just can’t do that.’

David Moyes found the step up from Everton manager to boss of Manchester United too great

Manchester City fans call on United to keep the faith with Moyes - for their own selfish reasons

Liverpool’s style of football will also be interesting to observe under Iraola. At Bournemouth, his team were smart. Counter-pressing became an art form and they were, at times, comfortable not to have the ball even at home.

His team’s average possession, for example, was less than 50 per cent. That’s OK for a club looking to punch above its weight by way of its results. It’s not for a club like Liverpool. Klopp’s teams averaged 62 per cent while Slot’s sat at 59 per cent.

So far Iraola’s metrics are good. Only in the 2-1 home win over Atletico Madrid did the number drop below 50 per cent while even in draws against Newcastle and Nottingham Forest they were comfortably on the right side of 50 per cent.

This was one of the things that did for Frank at Spurs, according to those close to the club. ‘The players liked Thomas,’ says a source. ‘It’s impossible not to like Thomas. But they thought his football was too often built around what he thought the opposition would do.

‘Sometimes his team’s xG (expected goals) was almost minus. That may occasionally be OK at Brentford but never at Tottenham. At a club like this one you have to get on the front foot. Our house, our rules.’

Iraola seems to have avoided any obvious banana skins so far but he has not yet been placed under real pressure.

When asked about the step up in Friday's press conference, he said: 'For me the demands on the players are the same. I don’t give different instructions to one player because he is more expensive than another player because he has cost us less money.

'The demands are the same. The strengths and weaknesses of players are different, so we have to always adapt the team to try and maximise the collective side of this. In Bournemouth, we had players who could run forever and other players who could not do it.

'When you draw 2-2 at Newcastle with Bournemouth, it is a good result, but I understand that with Liverpool it is not. The goals of the team are different and so are the expectations.'

Last season under Slot was so miserable that his successor is working with some afforded leeway. That will only last so long. Two or three poor results would soon change the atmosphere and narrative, especially given the fast start made at the top of the Premier League by Arsenal and City.

It was interesting to hear Iraola say how hard it was for his team to face Fulham on Saturday having played in Europe in midweek. As we know, that is the way of life at the sharp end of our game. It simply will not wash as mitigation.

It was interesting to hear Iraola say how hard it was for his team to face Fulham on Saturday having played in Europe in midweek

Tottenham fans show their frustrations at the club during Frank's time in charge

There are always uncontrollable reasons contributing to failure, of course. Managers by and large inherit problems.

Potter’s Chelsea was a madhouse while Frank’s Tottenham finished 17th the season before. This season’s Spurs manager – Roberto De Zerbi – has been given £300million of new players for a reason.

Back in the day at United meanwhile, Moyes was dealt an almost impossible hand once Ferguson left the building with all the club’s recruitment processes buried in the back of his head. Some experienced players simply didn’t try hard enough while Old Trafford executives have since acknowledged they failed the Scot.

‘We should have helped him more,’ said former CEO Ed Woodward and it’s not by co-incidence that Moyes and indeed Hodgson have gone on to prove their enduring worth elsewhere.

Undoubtedly, though, there were some spectacular errors. Moyes’ decision to lead his squad for a walk on Sydney’s Bondi Beach on his one and only pre-season tour was taken despite warnings of impending chaos by club security.

‘It’s fine, I did it with Everton,’ said Moyes. By the time the United party had required a hastily-convened police escort to get them safely back to the team hotel, Moyes had come to understand that Everton was one kind of football club – with one kind of global standing – and United was quite another.

Such colourful tales make for great podcast chat and help to sell books. Equally, they matter. Perception matters.

Still with United, the recently departed Ruben Amorim couldn’t understand why he was required to do so many media interviews each week. Hodgson, meanwhile, once bit back at a young journalist asking about his tactics with all the patience of a surgeon who had just been told he was holding his scalpel the wrong way.

At United, Moyes was dealt an almost impossible hand once Sir Alex Ferguson left the building with all the club’s recruitment processes buried in the back of his head

Ruben Amorim couldn’t understand why he was required to do so many media interviews each week while he was manager of Manchester United

‘I just don’t understand what it has to do with them,’ he subsequently told a staffer. And that’s the point. You either instinctively get it at a big club or you don’t. And if you need to learn, you must do so quickly.

Potter – still coming to terms with what happened at Chelsea and indeed West Ham if some of his recent social media exchanges are anything to go by – said philosophically recently that: ‘You are never quite as good or quite as bad as people say.'

He is absolutely right about that. But how a manager goes about influencing those judgments at a big club really does matter.

Slot – endlessly respectful of his predecessor’s achievements - got it right for a while at Liverpool. It was his results that got him in the end and they will be the prime metric for Iraola. But Hodgson departed a decade-and-a-half ago lamenting that he never got to feel the famous love from the Kop.

The point is that you have to know how to earn it.

Sports.title: Raheem Sterling vows to be 'better than yesterday' as former England footballer, 31, breaks his silence after pleading guilty to dangerous driving and drug possession following £270,000 Lamborghini car crash
Sports.content:
Raheem Sterling says he is seeking 'progress over perfection' after pleading guilty to dangerous driving and drug possession.

In his first Instagram post since bodycam footage of his May arrest was released, Sterling says his goal is to 'be better than yesterday'.

On Tuesday, Sterling pleaded guilty at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court after crashing his £270,000 Lamborghini while driving under the influence of laughing gas.

Sterling told police he had 'a problem' with the drug after submitting rush hour motorists to a terrifying 90 minutes of dangerous driving, in which he zig-zagged on the M25 and M3 motorways before swerving onto a slip road and crashing into a metal gate.

The 31-year-old former England international was arrested by police who claim he tried to hide nitrous oxide, or laughing gas, from them by moving it to the back seat of his black Lamborghini Urus SUV.

Police bodycam footage shows the moment that Sterling was arrested with canisters and a deflated balloon on his lap. An officer can be heard saying 'you can put that down' to the footballer after opening his car door.

He can then be seen taking the items from his lap and putting them behind his seat.

Raheem Sterling says he is seeking 'progress over perfection' following his court case

Sterling pleaded guilty to dangerous driving and drug possession after crashing his £270,000 Lamborghini in May

The 31-year-old was charged with dangerous driving and possession of laughing gas after swerving his car on the M25 and M3

Sterling is asked 'can you jump out for me' and who was at the wheel at the time of the crash, but does not reply.

The officer adds: 'So you refuse to answer, okay.'

Sterling is told to get out of the car, asked his name and age at the roadside and to 'put the phone down, stop playing games. Stop tensing up.'

The former Manchester City and Chelsea star, who won the PFA Young Player of the Year award in 2018-19, is then read his rights as he is arrested after being asked to put his arms behind his back.

His arrest, near the Minley interchange on the M3 in Hampshire, happened four weeks after he had returned to the UK following the end of an abortive attempt to revive his football career at Dutch club Feyenoord. He remains without a club.

Sterling, from Berkshire, pleaded guilty on Tuesday to dangerous driving, possession of nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation and failing to provide a specimen after a single vehicle collision at 8.45am on May 28. Police found six cannisters of nitrous oxide in his car.

Basingstoke Magistrates' Court heard that Sterling was so impaired by the laughing gas that he was unable to perform basic police station tests like placing his finger on his nose or placing one foot in front of another.

Barrister Simon Jones, prosecuting, said of Sterling: 'He appeared to be quiet, withdrawn and lethargic and actively fidgeting. Eye lids drooping consistent with fatigue or drug impairment. He said he was feeling very cold, despite this being in the middle of a heatwave with 33-degree temperatures.'

Motorist Fiona Jennings told police she had looked across to witness the driver of the Lamborghini with a balloon in front of his face which was so big she thought it was an air bag.

Image issued by the Crown Prosecution Service shows the damage to the Lamborghini Urus being driven by Sterling

The former England international was pictured arriving in court today to face charges following a car crash in May

Sterling, from Berkshire, pleaded guilty on Tuesday to dangerous driving, possession of nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation and failing to provide a specimen

It was so big that 'she had no idea how the driver would have been able to see the road ahead,' Mr Jones said. Ms Jennings described Sterling's driving as 'absolutely horrendous' and expressed 'genuine concern that the driver may kill someone.'

Evidence presented to court suggested Sterling was also inhaling laughing gas while at the wheel of the Lamborghini a full seven hours before his arrest.

A concerned witness called police after seeing the driver of the same car entering a McDonalds car park alarmingly fast at 1.10am the same morning and seeing the driver holding up 'a pink, inflated balloon.'

By 7.45am that morning, another motorist concerned by the Lamborghini erratically changing lanes, saw the driver placing a white balloon to his mouth and inhaling its contents. For 30 minutes, that motorist watched the vehicle weave from inside to outside lane and back and come close to smashing into the central reservation.

It was after Sterling had left the M3 near Farnborough, Hampshire, hit the gate and come to halt with the tyres of his wheels ripped up, that police found him sitting in T-shirt and shorts in the passenger seat of the car.

One officer told him to 'stop tensing up' after he had stepped out of the car. Sterling replied: 'I'm not tensing up.' Sterling provided breath tests, which established he was not under the influence of cannabis, cocaine or alcohol. But he later refused requests for a blood test, insisting that a lawyer of his choosing must be present, having rejected the offer of a duty solicitor. He also refused to answer any police questions.

Mr Jones said of Sterling's conduct: 'He was attempting to impose a condition on provision of a specimen. He was told the investigation could not be delayed for that reason. At the roadside, there was cooperation without the need for legal advice. When the search for the presence of drugs started, the cooperation ended.'

Sterling's barrister, Jason Bartfeld QC, told the court that there was 'extensive personal mitigation' in his case and that the footballer had taken 'voluntary steps to mitigate his difficulties.'

Mr Bartfeld agreed that this was a 'top category case' because it was a prolonged period of dangerous driving and Sterling was suffering 'serious impairment'. But he said the nitrous oxide would only have caused impairment in 'short periods' and that the chemical did not pose the same risks as cannabis or alcohol.

He claimed police had left Sterling confused about the blood sample. Sterling later told police in a statement: 'I asked for a solicitor. I did not fully understand I had not slept all night and was tired and confused.'

Sterling could face a maximum two years' imprisonment. The case was adjourned until November for pre-sentencing reports.

Sports.title: The recurring problem Chelsea are failing to solve, the struggling £75m star who has rarely looked worth the price tag and why Estevao is right to be frustrated as concerns mount for Xabi Alonso
Sports.content:
The recurring problem Chelsea are failing to solve, the struggling £75m star who has rarely looked worth the price tag and why Estevao is right to be frustrated as concerns mount for Xabi Alonso

If Chelsea's defenders have clean sheet bonuses written into their contracts, they are not doing much to earn their extra pocket money out of their club. Rather, the dearth of determination to stop the opposition from scoring is getting silly now.

For the 21st Premier League match in succession, Chelsea failed to secure a clean sheet. Their last one came against Brentford coincidentally, and that was in January, Liam Rosenior's first game in charge. Since then, opposition attacks have considered them there for the taking.

How Chelsea surrendered their latest shot at a shutout involved a little charity. It came from a Brentford corner, the fifth set-piece goal conceded by Xabi Alonso's side this season.

Austin MacPhee was hired from Aston Villa in the summer, specifically to help solve these situations. He is making minor changes here and there. For example, Chelsea attempted a new kick-off routine here, with Cole Palmer booting the ball straight out of play for a Brentford throw-in by their corner flag, in a bid to pin them back from the get-go.

However, when it comes to defending set-pieces, little seems to have changed on MacPhee's watch as of yet. Mikkel Damsgaard sent his corner to the back of the six-yard box. Jannik Schuster headed it back across. Jaidon Anthony nodded it in, unmarked with Wesley Fofana having drifted to stand on the line and watch it all unfold.

He was not the only one at fault, but it did have at least some Fofana fingerprints on it, and rarely has the 25-year-old Frenchman looked like the defender that Chelsea – or Todd Boehly – hoped they were signing in 2022 for £75million from Leicester City.

Chelsea continue to struggle defensively and suffered a 3-0 defeat by Brentford on Friday

Boehly was acting as interim sporting director when Chelsea committed to bringing in Fofana. His injury history was naturally a concern, and so Chelsea's chairman had an idea.

Boehly sent his prospective purchase to New York rather than London so he could have a more thorough medical via the team doctor of the Los Angeles Lakers, the NBA team that he also co-owned. That medical lasted more than ten hours, but Fofana eventually got the green light, and Boehly his man.

Chelsea saw something special in him at that time, but he is still not standing up to the elite standards that the club want of him. Hardly any of the back line are.

Chelsea's defence is a problem which Alonso must solve if he wants to be troubling towards the top of the Premier League. They are leaking a glut of goals, and this time, they did not have the attack to save them with Joao Pedro sidelined and replaced by Danny Welbeck.

SUBSTITUTION SCRUTINY

Alonso cannot escape scrutiny for his substitutions, including his ignorance of Estevao Willian.

The Brazilian is a terrific young talent. He is still only 19, but has shown enough since arriving at Chelsea that he can have an impact if allowed the opportunity.

Indeed, it is hard not to think he is deserving of more minutes than he is receiving. Before this trip to Brentford, his Premier League season involved being an 83rd-minute substitute; unused substitute; 81st-minute substitute; 86th-minute substitute.

Here, Chelsea were already losing 2-0 when Estevao was brought on in the 87th minute.

Reports in Brazil have continued to emerge suggesting the starlet is frustrated. It is hard to blame him if so. With the very last kick of this game, Estevao swung in a corner which went straight out of play. In a way, that summed up his sorry season.

Xabi Alonso has received backlash for his substitutions, with some stars seemingly deserving of more game time

Reports in Brazil suggest that Estevao is growing frustrated with his role in the squad

A SURPRISE STAR

The bar was set low, but Jordan Henderson was one of the few that impressed for Chelsea, especially in the first half in what was his first appearance in more than three months.

The 36-year-old added experience into the centre of the pitch, and made the visitors seem a little less soft at least. That has been an accusation levelled at this young Chelsea side. But Henderson was forever having a word with our referee, Andrew Madley, when something did not go his side's way.

A year or two ago, when Chelsea were in the thick of their focus on youth, nobody would have believed us if we said Henderson and Welbeck would soon be starting for this club. Yet here they were, contributing to a line-up that carried an average age of 27 years and 349 days – Chelsea's oldest since a 2023 league trip to Arsenal.

It helped in the first-half, but all unravelled in the second after conceding from a cheap set-piece.

Sports.title: Xabi Alonso hits out at Chelsea stars for dropping their 'competitive mentality' as Blues boss sends warning after dismal 3-0 defeat by Brentford
Sports.content:
Xabi Alonso hits out at Chelsea stars for dropping their 'competitive mentality' as Blues boss sends warning after dismal 3-0 defeat by Brentford

Xabi Alonso bemoaned his misfiring Chelsea team after they lost their drive at Brentford – shipping three goals in a drab second-half showing.

Defeat leaves Chelsea winless in three games before the three-week international break, losing away to west London neighbours Brentford for the first time since their promotion to the Premier League in 2021.

Chelsea were undone by three second half goals as Alonso's side failed to test Caoimhin Kelleher after the interval, failing to score for the first time this season.

Speaking post-match, Blues boss Alonso accused his team of lacking 'competitive mentality' – admitting he has a tough job on his hands.

'We dropped our consistency and competitive mentality in the second half,' said Alonso.

'The small details can be decisive. You don't have to give advantage in these kind of games where they do with little, they get a lot and credit to them.

Xabi Alonso hit out at his Chelsea players for dropping their 'competitive mentality' in their 3-0 defeat by Brentford

The Blues go into the international break on the back of no win in three and were second best in west London

'It's about 90 minutes and we have not been able to keep that level throughout these few games at the start of the season. It's something we have to do better.

'It's a process and it's still five games in a competitive Premier League where each game is really hard. We knew it was going to be hard, so (the job) is not going to be easy at all.'

Meanwhile, Brentford boss Keith Andrews believes his side showed the determination which Chelsea lacked.

'We've shown different kind of attributes in the last few weeks where we've had to dig deep, show real great resilience,' said Andrews.

'Our opposition are setting up in a very respectful way to try and nullify what we do then the onus is on us to try and overcome that.

'I felt there was a performance bubbling; I could see it in the players' eyes over the last couple of days.

'The approach has been really focused and I thought in the second half we showed exactly what we are.

'I think there's a really nice connection between the fans and the players and the club in general that is growing all the time. Everyone is enjoying the journey that we're on, especially me.

'I just love watching us play. I love being here. I love feeling that energy from the crowd and the way we play it.'

Sports.title: Chelsea lacked the commitment, intelligence and energy of supposed title challengers in 3-0 defeat by Brentford: Familiar failings haunt Xabi Alonso as we have seen this softness before, writes IAN LADYMAN
Sports.content:
Chelsea may have started their Premier League life under Xabi Alonso with a hint of promise but it’s at places like Brentford’s Gtech Stadium where flaws tend to emerge. Here under west London’s Friday Night Lights, Alonso’s players came up short in a fashion that has become rather familiar.

There is a new coach and some new players at Stamford Bridge but we have seen this softness before. In a poor game that saw Brentford simply more familiar with each other and indeed the details of the task in hand, Chelsea lacked cohesion, intelligence and, most crucially of all, the levels of commitment and energy required of a team supposedly with title aspirations.

Brentford took time to get going themselves but once they did, late in the first half, they were the better team for a distance. Cleverer, quicker, hungrier. Keith Andrews’ team head into the weekend in third spot and will reflect on two goals that come straight from their training ground.

The set piece routine that gave Jaidon Anthony his first Brentford goal looked simple but takes practice. Then, late on, Chelsea were hit with the kind of rapid counter attack that has downed big teams in this part of London before.

Chelsea had some injuries and, as such, both Jordan Henderson and Danny Welbeck played. They were territorially superior for a while. But they faded dismally as the night wore on and after three games without a win – a draw and two defeats – they may well be in the bottom half by Sunday night

It was a surprise to see Henderson in the Chelsea team. Only hours earlier at Wembley, the England manager had declared him unfit for international duty.

Brentford took time to get going but once they did, late in the first half, they were the better team for a distance

Fabio Carvalho buried Brentford's third in a rampant second half against Alonso' side

Regardless, it was the 36-year-old’s Chelsea debut and the fact he was making it against the team he left in the summer led to a rather predictable reaction from the home fans.

Mind you, he wasn’t the only one. With Chelsea’s Emi Martinez and Valentin Barco being booed simply for being Argentinean, this was not a quiet first half in west London even if the football did nothing to stir the soul.

MATCH FACTS Brentford (4-2-3-1): Kelleher 7; Kayode 6 (Hickey 68, 6), Schuster 8, Ajer 6, Lewis-Potter 7.5 (Malick Diouf 80); Yarmoliuk 6 (Sangare 68, 6), Janelt 6; Anthony 6.5 (Ouattara 81, 6), Damsgaard 6 (Carvalho 87, 7), Schade 6.5; Thiago 6.5. Booked: Igor Thiago. Goals: Anthony 61, Thiago 83, Carvalho 90+3. Manager: Keith Andrew 7. Chelsea (3-4-2-1): Martinez 6; Fofana 6 (Acheampong 71mins 6), Lacroix 6.5, Colwill 6; Neto 6 (Estevao 87mins 6), Henderson 6.5, Barco 6 (Nicoll-Jazuli 97mins), Chavarria 6; Palmer 6.5, Rogers 6.5; Welbeck 6 (Quenda 71mins 6) Manager: Xabi Alonso 5 Referee: Andrew Madley 6

This was, in fact, an awful game in the first half and even the stadium announcer appeared to have a little sarcasm in his voice when he declared at the interval that the score is ‘exactly the same as it was at the beginning’.

With Alonso’s team involved in so many high scoring games so far this season, this had to happen at some point. It was surprising that it was here, though. Games at the Gtech don’t tend to be dull.

Chelsea – missing Reece James and Joao Pedro through injury – also had Danny Welbeck in the team and he and Henderson were among Chelsea’s better players during an open half an hour they shaded. Cole Palmer – back in the England squad – was also prominent.

Brentford goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher was required to save well to his right when a mistake from Keane Lewis Potter allowed Pedro Neto to shoot in the 10th minute. At the back end of the half, meanwhile, Morgan Rogers shot powerfully after a run and low cross from Pep Chavarria set him up. Jannik Schuster stood firm to take the shot in his midriff.

At the other end, Brentford took an age to get going. There was none of the home team’s usual energy. On the touchline manager Keith Andrews conducted a constant dialogue with the fourth official. Maybe he was asking him if he fancied a run in the centre of midfield.

As half-time neared there were some Brentford flurries. They found some momentum. Martinez dropped easily enough on a low shot from Yehor Yarmoluik before Kevin Schade's effort was blocked, allowing Lewis-Potter to curl an effort that was well anticipated by the Chelsea goalkeeper.

It was a surprise to see Henderson in the Chelsea team as only hours earlier at Wembley, the England manager had declared him unfit for international duty

Brentford managed to take some of that momentum into the second half and for a while Chelsea were becalmed. Henderson had been like a fulcrum in the first half as his team ticked over but the veteran’s influence waned as Brentford’s energy began to surge and with it their confidence.

Lewis Potter caused Chelsea particular problems with his scurrying runs down the left and it was from a corner on his side that Brentford took the lead.

There was nothing overly fancy about. A delivery to the far post, a header back across from Schuster and a nod from a yard from Anthony. Just shows what happens when you actually keep your eyes on the ball.

Chelsea tried to rally but couldn’t. Barco’s appeal for a penalty with fourteen minutes left was weak and when Schuster sent Kevin Schade clear in the 83rd minute, he was denied by Martinez only for Thiago to gobble up the rebound.

Fabio Carvalho wrapped up proceedings with Brentford's third in the fourth minute of stoppage time. A just reward for the 24-year-old, who spent the last year recovering from a knee injury.

Sports.title: Harry Kane smashes ANOTHER record as Bayern Munich star scores 100th Bundesliga goal - 31 GAMES faster than previous holder
Sports.content:
Harry Kane smashes ANOTHER record as Bayern Munich star scores 100th Bundesliga goal - 31 GAMES faster than previous holder

England captain Harry Kane is continuing to break records – now becoming the fastest-ever player to score 100 goals in the German Bundesliga.

Kane's penalty against Union Berlin on Friday night took him to treble figures in the country in 98 games – a staggering 31 games faster than the previous record holder.

German legend Dieter Muller took 129 matches to score 100 for FC Cologne, with his record coming in 1977.

He also recently became the fastest player in Bayern history to net 150 goals for the club, taking 153 games.

Only one player has reached 150 goals for one club quicker – Cristiano Ronaldo with Real Madrid. He took 149 games.

Kane has scored a goal every 78.5 minutes in the Bundesliga, which is a better rate than both Erling Haaland and Robert Lewandowski.

Harry Kane became the fastest-ever player to 150 Bundesliga goals on Friday evening

Kane would later score his 101st goal in a 7-0 win for his side.

He said upon achieving the feat: 'I'm very proud, scoring 101 Bundesliga goals in such a short time. I've loved every second of it. Playing with Michael (Olise), Lucho (Luis Dias), Jamal (Musiala), I know I'll get chances. Thank you to the team and the club. It's a great stat to have. Let's keep it going.'

The Three Lions skipper, who will next week join up with his country for the first international break since the World Cup, has been a revelation since moving to Germany from Tottenham in 2023.

He cost the Bundesliga giants £100million, and has been their anchorman ever since.

Now 33, many had wondered if he would ever return to England to try and break the record for the most Premier League goals. He is on 213 goals, with Alan Shearer leading the way on 260.

But that seems in doubt, with the forward admitting earlier this year that he is in 'no rush' to depart Bayern.

'No, not for me, I'm very happy,' he said before the World Cup. 'I made that clear to you guys. I'm really settled here. We have a fantastic team - one of the best, if not the best in the world at the moment.

'We have a top, top coach. I'm enjoying my time. The situation is calm.'

Sports.title: Michael Carrick provides Carlos Baleba injury update before Man Utd's trip to Fulham
Sports.content:
Michael Carrick provides Carlos Baleba injury update before Man Utd's trip to Fulham

Manchester United midfielder Carlos Baleba is yet to make his debut for the Red Devils after suffering an ankle ligament injury during pre-season

View 2 Images Carlos Baleba is working his way back to full fitness (Image: Manchester United via Getty Images)

Michael Carrick has confirmed that Carlos Baleba is making positive strides towards a potential Manchester United debut at Fulham on Sunday (4:30pm). The midfielder made the move to Old Trafford during the summer window from Brighton and Hove Albion.

‌



United secured a £65million deal, plus £5m in add-ons, having first shown interest in the Cameroon international the previous summer. The club were desperately short in midfield following Casemiro's departure after his contract expired, and Manuel Ugarte's serious injury while on World Cup duty with Uruguay.

‌



United brought in Andrey Santos from Chelsea before Youri Tielemans completed a switch from Aston Villa, with Baleba subsequently arriving after Brighton agreed to accept a reduced fee.

‌



Erik ten Hag's first signing at Man Utd finally joins new club after leaving for nothing READ MORE :

The 22-year-old endured a dip in form last season, yet United's hierarchy are reportedly thrilled with the deal they struck, some 12 months after first registering their interest. Baleba is yet to pull on a United shirt, having sustained an ankle ligament injury during pre-season preparations.

However, Carrick has offered an encouraging fitness update to MUTV, via the club's official website, ahead of this weekend's clash at Craven Cottage.

FOLLOW OUR MAN UTD FB PAGE! Latest United news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

‌



He said: "We're looking good. Everyone's up and running Over the last week or so, pretty much everyone has played and [been] fit and we're trying to get Carlos back in.

"Well, I say back in, actually introducing him into the group. So he's done a bit of training this week and, hopefully, we'll get Luke [Shaw] back in and around it this week and look forward to a strong game on the weekend."

View 2 Images Carlos Baleba could finally make his first Manchester United appearance this weekend (Image: Manchester United via Getty Images)

‌



Baleba is clearly raring to go as he looks to prove his worth in a United shirt.

Carrick added: "Yeah, he's desperate to get started. He's bouncing around the place.

"It's not always easy, I think, when you come into a new club and you're not right fully in with the group, with the training.

‌



"But he's dealt with that ever so well, I have to say. He's got great personality and he's full of enthusiasm around [the place] and pushing to get back as quickly as possible. So it's great to have him back."

United are crying out for three points this weekend following a torrid run of results. The Reds conceded a stoppage-time equaliser at Everton, before going down in the Manchester derby — despite playing the majority of the match against 10 men — in a defeat that hinged on a wrongly-awarded goal.

Carrick's side then blew a two-goal advantage to suffer a 3-2 home defeat to Brighton on Wednesday night, crashing out of the League Cup at the first hurdle for the second successive season. United now face a Fulham side still searching for their first league victory under new manager Alvaro Arbeloa, the former Real Madrid player and manager.

Alexandre Pato consortium agrees deal with EFL club as official statement released

Northampton Town are set for fresh backing after striking an agreement with Sports Alpha Capital - the consortium featuring ex‑Chelsea star Alexandre Pato.

Northampton Town have confirmed they have reached an agreement with consortium Sports Alpha Capital (SAC), which former Chelsea and Brazil forward Alexandre Pato is part of. The UK/Brazilian investment group is involved in a 'proposed shareholding acquisition' in the League Two club.

‌



Chairman Kelvin Thomas confirmed: "As we always said, we will keep supporters updated as we progress and we are pleased that we have finalised agreements and now move to closing. Football club transactions always have many moving parts and often take a little longer than you would hope, but we are thrilled to be moving forward.

‌



"We all saw the excitement and enthusiasm from both the supporters and Sports Alpha themselves when Pato and others from the group were at the Newport game, and we think that excitement will just build."

‌



Ex-Chelsea star Alexandre Pato has takeover deal approved as EFL club release statement READ MORE :

On behalf of the investors, Hugh Strange concluded: "All the investors are very excited about the opportunity to build on the excellent foundations in place to take the club forward and are looking forward to enjoying more days like the Newport game together with the supporters."

‌

Sports.title: Virgil van Dijk causing a stir as 'huge debate' breaks out over Liverpool star
Sports.content:
Virgil van Dijk causing a stir as 'huge debate' breaks out over Liverpool star

Virgil van Dijk will holds talks with his manager during the international break

View 3 Images Virgil van Dijk has been named in the Netherlands squad (Image: Getty Images)

Virgil van Dijk is at the centre of a "huge" debate over his future in international football. The Liverpool captain, 35, will turn 37 during Euro 2028, which will be staged in the UK and Ireland.

‌



As he enters the twilight of his career, there are widespread calls in the Netherlands for him to quit the national side or for new manager Xavi Hernandez to make the decision for him and build for the future.

‌



Dutch legend Ruud Gullit says there is a 50/50 split between Dutch fans over whether he should extend his international career. The former Chelsea player and manager told Comeon.com: "I don't know how Virgil Van Dijk is feeling at the moment.

‌



"There is a huge debate in Holland over whether he should retire. Yes or no? Some people think that he should.

FOLLOW OUR LIVERPOOL FB PAGE! Latest Reds news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

"Others say that he shouldn't. I think it’s most important to see how Xavi feels about him and it depends on how Virgil feels about it. If he still feels fit enough, then he should make his decision about it, and that's up to him."

‌



Alexis Mac Allister's dad delivers honest truth about Liverpool exit talk as Real Madrid eye deal READ MORE :

If Van Dijk does step away from the international scene, it would presumably be welcomed by Liverpool and potentially extend his club career. His current contract with the Reds expires next summer.

Gullit added: "I'm sure that Liverpool would say yes but that's not fair to him because maybe he thinks he can still do both. And it comes back to how he feels about what he can offer.

View 3 Images Van Dijk's international future is in doubt (Image: Getty Images)

‌



"We will have to wait and see what happens in the international break because I think Virgil and Xavi will have had a conversation. He went to watch Van Dijk. I'm curious to see what’s going to happen too."

Xavi is sticking with Van Dijk for now after naming him in his squad for the upcoming round of Nations League games, with the pair due to hold talks. The Netherlands face old rivals Germany at home first before taking on Serbia twice and Greece away.

View 3 Images Xavi has a big decision to make over Van Dijk's future (Image: Getty Images)

Article continues below

He replaced Ronald Koeman, who stepped down following the last-32 defeat by Morocco at this summer's World Cup. Former Barcelona midfielder Xavi won the World Cup with Spain in 2010 and lifted the European Championship in 2008 and 2012.

Xavi's appointment marked his first return to management since leaving Barcelona in 2024. After beginning his managerial career with Qatari club Al Sadd, he took over the Catalan giants in November 2021, also succeeding Koeman, and led the team to the La Liga title in 2023.

That’s where the stars really become who they really are – disciplined, morals. Everything. That’s what boxing truly is. All I care about is showing them kids that have come from nothing like I myself can get here as well."

Article continues below

John Hedges: "For me personally, listen, coming here, Co-op Live, this is absolutely crazy. I’ll be real with you. Life-long dream to get anywhere close to this let alone doing it myself. I’ve been in the game a lot of years. I’ve done it since I’ve been five years old. Like I say, people have different dreams in the boxing world in what they want to achieve. Genuinely when I say I was happy to fight on the telly and walk away, that’s the sort of mentality I have. I’ve always never really backed myself a lot. Slowly slowly I’ve just started winning fights, getting through them with ease and now look, I’m here. These are nights you dream of. I’ve had 12 fights now and I’ve barely lost a round. I turn up on the night and that’s exactly what I’ll do on Saturday night."

Sports.title: 'Ricky Hatton was my hero and I hope, for a small moment, I was a hero of his'
Sports.content:
'Ricky Hatton was my hero and I hope, for a small moment, I was a hero of his'

Darren Barker cycled and swam almost 2,000 miles and has raised almost £50,000 for charity CALM in honour of Ricky Hatton

Darren Barker knew he had to go big or go home.

‌



Nothing short of epic would be a fitting tribute to a man whose larger-than-life character had dominated British boxing. Barker, 44, was the last person to interview Ricky Hatton, just five days before he was found dead 12 months ago. And by February he had decided words were not enough to honour the sporting legend.

‌



The former world champion planned to cycle and swim almost 2,000 miles from Edinburgh to Morocco. In doing so he would raise money for suicide prevention charity CALM for whom Hatton was an ambassador. "As I get older, I've understood time is the most valuable commodity we're given," Barker said.

‌



Donate to The Longest Round at https://www.justgiving.com/page/thelongestround

View Image Darren Barker at The Rock of Gibraltar

‌



"Ricky gave up his time that day for me and I was just desperate to do something for him. I knew it had to be something quite extreme, because I wanted to grab people's attention. There are so many amazing things going on in the world as far as challenges are concerned and if mine wasn't epic, then it wouldn't do the job."

Supported by his brother, a friend and a documentary maker, Barker set out to cycle from Edinburgh to Dover before swimming the English Channel to France. But the weather scuppered his open-water plans and he instead swam the 21-mile distance along the coastline.

He then hopped on a ferry to Calais and cycled to Gibraltar where another swim - this time to Morocco - was cancelled. Scrambling for an alternative route, Barker was given a crash course in sailing and navigated a boat solo to Ceuta before a final bike ride into Africa. As fate would have it, he crossed the border last Monday, exactly a year after Hatton had passed.

Article continues below

He has raised almost £50,000, enough to help more than 3,000 people through the CALM helpline. "We were fully aware that the anniversary of Ricky's death was in September, but I was never looking at a date," Barker added. "I knew how fitting it would be to be in September but to actually finish it on the anniversary of his passing was unreal. I hope I've done Ricky proud.

"He said once that whilst he's here, he wanted to help as many people as he can, and I hope I've helped continue to do that for him. My big thing was just being able to complete it for him. I was just desperate not to fail; not for me, but for him. I didn't want to let Ricky down. He was a hero of mine and will always be a hero of mine, and I hope, for a small moment, I was a hero of his."
