World.title: FM: Alamein Africa Forum unites African business, financial institutions
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty said the Alamein Africa Forum will serve as a pan-African platform bringing together the private sector, investment and financial institutions, and representatives of various productive and service sectors, to strengthen direct links between companies and markets and promote cross-border partnerships.

Abdelatty made the remarks during a meeting with African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank) President George Elombi at the Foreign Ministry headquarters, where they discussed preparations for Egypt’s hosting of the Alamein Africa Forum, scheduled to be held in El Alamein on October 2-3.

The meeting also covered preparations for the summit of the founding member states of the African Union Development Agency (AUDA-NEPAD), scheduled for October 3, and the eighth African Union Mid-Year Coordination Meeting, set for October 4.

The two sides also reviewed the organizational and substantive arrangements for the upcoming events.

Abdelatty said the Alamein Africa Forum is part of a series of high-level African events that Egypt will host in early October, stressing that holding the forum reflects Egypt’s commitment to advancing continental economic cooperation.

He noted that Egypt is hosting the forum pursuant to a decision adopted by the African Union Summit in February 2026 to convene the forum every two years in El Alamein.

The Minister said the events are expected to draw broad presidential participation, alongside business leaders and representatives of the public and private sectors, reflecting Egypt’s integrated approach to linking the political, economic and institutional dimensions of African cooperation.

He explained that the forum seeks to move beyond the formulation of continental priorities toward mobilizing resources, forging partnerships and translating those priorities into concrete projects and tangible outcomes.

For his part, Elombi highlighted the importance of the Alamein Africa Forum as a pan-African platform for promoting intra-African trade and investment and connecting the business community and financial institutions with priority projects and investment opportunities in the continent.

He said the forum provides an important opportunity to mobilize resources, build partnerships and support the implementation of projects that contribute to Africa’s economic integration and sustainable development.

Following the meeting, Abdelatty and Elombi held a press conference during which they reviewed the organizational and substantive preparations for the upcoming high-level African events, with particular focus on the forum, its program and key sessions.

World.title: Petroleum sector reports 63 discoveries, 28 mln tons of crude refined
World.content:
The petroleum sector recorded 63 new oil and gas discoveries and refined 28 million tons of crude during fiscal year 2025/26, meeting domestic demand for petroleum products, the Ministry of Petroleum and Mineral Resources said Thursday, September 17, 2026.

The results were announced at a meeting chaired by Petroleum Minister Karim Badawi to approve the Egyptian General Petroleum Corporation’s (EGPC) fiscal year 2025/26 results.

The meeting was attended by Electricity and Renewable Energy Minister Mahmoud Esmat, Local Development and Environment Minister Manal Awad, Investment and Foreign Trade Minister Mohamed Farid, and EGPC CEO Salah Abdel Karim.

Badawi said the settlement of outstanding dues to investment partners marked a turning point in restoring investor confidence and encouraging new investments.

He added that crude oil production had begun to gradually recover after offsetting the natural decline in output.

Refinery utilization rose to more than 80 percent, helping maximize production capacity and increase diesel and gasoline output.

Badawi also praised continued coordination with the Ministry of Electricity to secure power plants’ fuel needs during the summer.

EGPC CEO Salah Abdel Karim said the corporation signed eight new oil and gas exploration agreements with investments of $377 million and recorded 48 oil discoveries and 15 gas discoveries.

Total investments in the exploration and production sector reached $4.5 billion.

The CEO said the Assiut Diesel Production Complex is about 90 percent complete and is scheduled to begin operations in the first quarter of 2027.

He confirmed that the petroleum sector met all domestic demand for petroleum products.

The sector also implemented mechanisms to encourage renewable-energy projects at oilfield sites, generating 1,927 megawatts of electricity.

In addition, 109 community-responsibility projects were carried out in areas surrounding petroleum facilities, benefiting around 300,000 people.

World.title: PM reviews National Economic Transformation Programme
World.content:
Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly said the government, in full coordination with the Central Bank of Egypt, was continuing work to finalize the National Economic Transformation Programme, which is based on an integrated vision reflecting the state’s economic priorities for the coming period.

“The programme is being prepared in line with President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi’s directives and aims to ensure the integration of economic, fiscal, monetary and sectoral policies and measures, while generating a tangible impact on citizens and the national economy,” Madbouly said.

He stressed the importance of Thursday’s meeting, which comes as the government reviews and verifies data and figures provided by various ministries in order to finalize the programme’s targets and prepare its final draft for submission to President Sisi ahead of its official launch.

Madbouly made the remarks during an expanded meeting to follow up on preparations for the programme, attended by Health and Population Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar, Electricity and Renewable Energy Minister Mahmoud Esmat, Finance Minister Ahmed Kouchouk, Social Solidarity Minister Maya Morsy, Agriculture and Land Reclamation Minister Alaa Farouk, Education and Technical Education Minister Mohamed Abdel Latif, Petroleum and Mineral Resources Minister Karim Badawi, Higher Education and Scientific Research Minister Abdel Aziz Konsowa, who is also acting Culture Minister, Labour Minister Hassan Raddad, Planning and Economic Development Minister Ahmed Rostom, Industry Minister Khaled Hashem, Deputy Finance Minister for Fiscal Policies Yasser Sobhy and officials from relevant ministries and government agencies. Investment and Foreign Trade Minister Mohamed Farid Saleh also participated via videoconference.

Madbouly said the government sought through the programme to establish an integrated framework for the next phase, focusing on strengthening the Egyptian economy’s capacity for sustainable growth, raising productivity and competitiveness and supporting sectors capable of creating jobs and increasing the added value, in line with regional and international economic developments.

At the beginning of the meeting, a number of economic performance indicators were reviewed, showing that the Egyptian economy had demonstrated resilience in the face of various regional and international challenges. Economic growth rose to 5.1 percent in fiscal year 2025/2026, compared with 4.4 percent the previous year, exceeding forecasts by major international institutions.

The growth was driven by several sectors, including industry and services such as telecommunications and information technology. Monthly inflation also declined in August to 12.7 percent, compared with 13 percent in the same month a year earlier.

The government’s targets go beyond achieving high growth rates to implementing a comprehensive economic transformation programme based on competitiveness and expanding private investment in five key sectors: industry; agriculture and food processing; tourism; telecommunications and information technology; and energy security.

The aim is to translate macroeconomic stability into sustainable growth that generates exports and improves living standards nationwide.

Planning and Economic Development Minister Ahmed Rostom presented the programme’s implementation status and proposed timeline. He said previous initiatives and programmes implemented before the National Economic Transformation Programme had been reviewed over recent months, while consultations had been held with relevant ministries and agencies on the new programme’s pillars.

Detailed data is currently being verified in coordination with various ministries following the preparation of the programme’s initial draft, with the final version to be completed before being submitted to the political leadership and then officially launched.

Rostom said 11 meetings had been held with relevant ministers, in addition to more than 34 technical meetings to discuss reform measures and priorities across different sectors. These meetings examined the current economic situation and the key challenges facing the Egyptian economy, including its structure and productivity, public finances and financing capacity, external indicators and global challenges, human capital and demographics, as well as institutional economic reform.

He said the methodology of the National Economic Transformation Programme was based on several pillars, including strengthening resilience and stability and addressing crises, empowering a productive and competitive private sector, expanding job opportunities and improving quality of life.

“The programme also builds on previous experience gained through the National Dialogue, the national narrative and structural reforms, among other initiatives. It sets economic and sectoral priorities while taking humanitarian considerations into account,” he added.

At the conclusion of the meeting, Madbouly stressed the need for thorough verification and review of the data to finalize the programme and submit it to the president in the coming period.

World.title: Egypt, Uzbekistan discuss expanding food security cooperation
World.content:
Agriculture and Land Reclamation Minister Alaa Farouk said on Friday, September 18, 2026, Egypt and Uzbekistan have strong historic ties and that political leadership has exerted efforts to expand economic and agricultural cooperation and promote investment opportunities to support sustainable food security.

Farouk made the remarks during a meeting with a high-level Uzbek government delegation to discuss cooperation in agriculture, food security, and mutual investment.

He highlighted Egypt’s recent advances in desert land reclamation, including the Future of Egypt project, as well as research efforts to develop high-yield, climate-resilient crops and water-saving farming technologies.

The Uzbek delegation expressed keenness to benefit from Egyptian expertise, particularly seed development and seed production.

The two sides agreed to expand cooperation to livestock, veterinary services and applied agricultural research, while supporting partnerships between government institutions, research centers and the private sector.

World.title: Iran war has cost $45.1 billion, Pentagon tells Congress
World.content:
The US war with Iran has cost $45.1 billion, the Pentagon informed Congress on Friday, according to two sources familiar with the matter.

The department told lawmakers that war costs were $43.6 billion as of September 3 plus an additional $1.5 billion for extra fuel, the sources added.

The estimate is not a full accounting of the war’s cost, however.

It does not include an assessment of the cost to repair damaged bases or buildings and did not provide Congress with detailed breakdowns of indirect costs of military operations as lawmakers have asked for, one source said.

The $45.1 billion cost estimate from the Pentagon surpasses the $38 billion price tag the Congressional Budget Office projected the war cost through August 1, and comes after the Pentagon estimated $37.5 billion as the bill for the war in July.

The estimate from the budget office also did not include the cost to repair US facilities damaged during the war, with most of the price tag coming from munitions expenditures, the office said. The CBO estimated the war will continue to cost the US approximately $2 billion to $3 billion per month past August 1, with higher costs estimated during periods of escalated fighting.

The office also told Congress that the war is expected to increase inflation for the first quarter of 2027, raising costs at a time Americans are growing more concerned about the economy.

World.title: Trump’s claim that ‘almost every item’ is getting cheaper comes up against a damning reality
World.content:
The Federal Reserve is raising interest rates to fight inflation that hurts Americans’ pocketbooks, but the move may also make voters feel the pinch in other ways heading into the November election.

There may not be a direct tie between the interest rates set by the Fed and mortgage and auto lending rates. But the Fed’s decision certainly won’t bring down the cost of housing, buying a car or paying off credit card debt. It won’t make it easier for American farmers already contending with record diesel prices and a surge in fertilizer costs to afford increased interest payments, all of which led the USDA this week to forecast a reduction in farm income for the year.

It is also designed to slow down the economy, something voters might not enjoy experiencing if it leads to jobs cuts.

While President Donald Trump opposed the rate hike, he’ll have to answer for any economic impact, even if his war on Iran and tariff policy helped create the inflation that led to it.

Trump has long groused about interest rates and elections.

He complained when rates were raised during his first term. And he complained when they were lowered before the 2024 presidential election. Earlier in his second term Trump publicly fantasized about firing the previous Fed Chair, Jerome Powell, but ultimately let his term as chairman expire and nominated Kevin Warsh, who Trump in January described as coming from “central casting” for the job.

Screens display a news conference held by Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange in New York, on Wednesday, September 16. Seth Wenig/AP

But while the unanimous decision by the Federal Open Markets Committee Wednesday to raise rates will keep Trump at odds with Fed policy, it also shows that Warsh lives in the reality where inflation and higher costs continue to be a problem for the economy as a whole, and not in Trump’s reality, where inflation does not exist.

And Warsh’s Fed is expected to raise interest rates again this year. The next opportunity is in late October, just before Election Day.

At a press conference Wednesday, Warsh acknowledged the reality that Americans feel every day.

“This summer’s inflation readings do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved,” he said, arguing inflation has been hurting the country for five years.

That is a clear break from Trump’s reality

During his convention speech to Republicans last week in Dallas, Trump said “almost every item” is getting cheaper.

After the Fed’s decision Wednesday to raise rates, Trump, without mentioning Warsh, painted a picture of his own reality. He said on social media that rates should be much lower because the US economy is “BOOMING.” And he seemed to reiterate that if rates don’t come down, he’ll try to cut off a large portion of US trade with the rest of the world.

Even Vice President JD Vance seemed to acknowledge in a podcast interview Wednesday that things aren’t exactly going to plan.

“Give us another chance,” Vance said, when asked for his message to voters before November.

Unintended consequences

The rate cut may be the Fed’s best, and really only, tool available to combat inflation, but it’s a blunt instrument, according to John W. Diamond, director of the Center for Public Finance at the Baker Institute at Rice University.

“That means the rate increase may further slow the weaker parts of the economy, such as housing, while barely affecting the strongest, namely the relentless investment in artificial intelligence,” he wrote for The Conversation.

Trump’s defense of AI development and data centers is another issue that puts him at odds with many voters.

Live by the economy, lose by the economy

Trump and Republicans harnessed anger over inflation and worries about the economy to send Democrats packing in the 2024 elections.

Now, they have to answer for the fact that the GOP’s two years in power haven’t solved the problem, at least not in the eyes of voters.

Democrats have a clear advantage to retake the House of Representatives, according to a recent New York Times / Siena poll.

Not surprisingly, the economy and inflation were among the top issues cited by registered voters in that poll. The problem for Trump is that he has lost their support on those issues.

Three-quarters of registered voters say the economy is only in fair or poor condition; 73% disapprove of his handling of cost-of-living issues, and 62% disapprove of his handling of the economy in general.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Democrat of New York, might as well have been reading from that New York Times poll when he opened a recent news conference arguing that Trump promised a “golden age,” but delivered a “rotten age.”

“The economy is not going in the right direction, it is failing everyday Americans. Gas prices are up, grocery prices are up, interest rates are up, housing costs are up, and health insurance premiums are up,” Jeffries said.

Democrats are on offense in red states

Those economy numbers have a lot to do with why Democrats feel competitive in Senate races that once seemed safe for Republicans, particularly in heartland states like Kansas and Iowa. Democratic candidates like Rev. Adam Hamilton in Kansas and Josh Turek in Iowa are making populist pledges to focus on housing and energy prices. In Iowa, the Republican candidate Rep. Ashley Hinson is talking in ads about working across the aisle, not a very Trump message.

Trump’s policies have not helped the cost of living

Trump made promises to bring down costs two years ago, but the policies he pursued as president probably aren’t helping inflation.

► Fighting AI regulation has given Big Tech room to spend. Enormous borrowing and spending by AI companies has fueled significant inflation in chip prices, electricity and building supplies.

► Tariffs he promised and defended have made things more expensive. But rather than pull back, Trump is launching a trade war with Canada.

And the actions he has taken to address inflation have often angered his supporters. The Republicans running for Senate in Iowa (Hinson) and Kansas (Sen. Roger Marshall) both channeled ranchers when they expressed frustration with Trump’s decision to import more beef as a way to bring down meat prices.

► His war on Iran has fuel costs rising again. Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen have attacked oil infrastructure in Saudi Arabia. The price of diesel is at a new record, hurting farmers, the trucking industry and ultimately consumers.

► High prices are expected to continue. The Congressional Budget Office set the cost of the war at $38 billion and counting in a report released this week. Perhaps more importantly to American consumers is that CBO expects the war to drive up inflation next year, a bet that fuel prices aren’t coming down any time soon, counter to Trump’s assurances.

► Trump also wants to cut $5,000 checks to every American. His administration is looking for ways to do it without Congress. People would appreciate the check, surely, but it would also drive up prices.

This is the dichotomy of “America First.” Trump wants lower rates. But his presidency is built around a list of policies that, at least on paper, drive up costs.

Trump has not yet turned on Warsh

Trump ultimately turned on his first-term pick for Fed Chair, who he later viewed as a “jerk” for not lowering rates on Trump’s timeline or bowing to Trump’s constant pressure.

Who knows if Trump continues to pressure Warsh to lower rates. In an angry social media post after the Fed’s announcement, Trump said rates should be at 1% rather than targeted between 3.75% and 4% as the Fed made clear.

Federal Reserve Board Chairman Kevin Warsh leaves after speaking at a news conference at the Federal Reserve in Washington, Wednesday, September 16. Mark Schiefelbein/AP

Trump said he did talk to Warsh before the Fed’s meeting.

“I talked to Kevin and I said, ‘you might as well vote with the board because it’s not going to matter.’”

Warsh, as chairman, is but one vote on the Fed board that set rates. But Warsh kept any counsel from Trump private.

“I’ve got nothing for you on a discussion with the president,” he told reporters.

Warsh may yet hold Trump’s trust because at heart he is thought to support rate cuts. It’s just that the economic reality, at the moment, is that prices are rising.

CNN’s David Goldman contributed to this report.

World.title: Trump says US reached Greenland security deal
World.content:
President Donald Trump said Friday that the United States has reached an agreement with Denmark and Greenland that gives the United States “permanent control” over Greenland’s security and bars any US adversary from having a military presence on the island.

“The United States of America has entered into an Agreement with The Kingdom of Denmark, and Greenland, that gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland, completely addressing ALL of our many U.S. concerns. There will be NO COST to the United States!” Trump wrote on Truth Social, going on to call the arrangement “an ‘Infinite Life’ Agreement.”

“Additionally, from now on, no U.S. adversary can EVER have a base in Greenland, have a military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval,” Trump said.

He added that the US would “immediately begin” building its own “large military presence” and work with the people in Greenland, a Danish territory, on “its development and construction.”

The United States, Greenland and Denmark are expected to sign an agreement on “strengthened security in the Arctic and North Atlantic Area” next week at the UN General Assembly, the Danish prime minister’s office said a statement.

“I am glad that we are about to make a great agreement for Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark, and the United States,” Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said, adding that the agreement would be “great for NATO and Europe as well.”

She also said the agreement “recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the Greenlandic people’s right to self-determination.”

Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said “the agreement recognizes Greenland’s interests and our place in the international cooperation,” adding, “It is to the benefit of us all.”

The signed agreement would still have to go through parliamentary procedures.

A US official said the agreement includes “permanent access, basing, and overflight rights” for the US on the island.

The agreement blocks non-NATO countries, including China and Russia, from having a base or sending troops to Greenland, the official said, adding that it guarantees “the necessary mechanisms are in place to prevent investment in sensitive sectors.”

Russia has expanded its military footprint in the Arctic for decades, and China has also deepened its presence there.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement the agreement “permanently and completely addresses our national security concerns in Greenland.”

Earlier this year, Trump repeatedly insisted on the importance of the United States obtaining Greenland for national security purposes, but discussion on the matter had largely faded from public view in recent months.

Trump’s repeated claims about seizing Greenland set off a diplomatic crisis within the NATO alliance and a scramble to try to defuse the threat.

In January, after a meeting between Danish and Greenlandic officials and Vice President JD Vance and Rubio, the United States, Denmark and Greenland formed a “high-level working group to explore if we can find a common way forward” amid ongoing disputes around the sovereignty of the island, in the words of Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen.

Later that month, at the World Economic Forum in Switzerland, Trump said he had secured the “framework of a future deal” on Greenland.

That framework, and the agreement described on Friday, bear strong similarities to an existing 1951 pact between the US and Denmark that allowed broad US military presence in Greenland.

The US official noted that “under the previous status quo, any country, including adversaries, could be allowed to build a military base in Greenland or send troops to Greenland.”

“By contrast, under this agreement, no non-NATO country may build a base in Greenland or maintain a troop presence in Greenland,” they said.

This story has been updated with additional details.

World.title: Frustration grows as Huthis widen Middle East conflict with US unwilling to intervene
World.content:
Dramatic recent advances by the Iran-backed Huthis, including the seizure of a strategically important island in the Red Sea, have dealt another blow to a region reeling from the US war with Iran and exacerbated an already severe global energy crisis. But neither the US nor its key ally Saudi Arabia has a clear plan to beat back the group, multiple sources told CNN, leading many in the region to ask where the counteroffensive will come from.

Although US officials acknowledge the Yemeni rebel group is advancing with the goal of ultimately asserting control over the critical Bab al Mandeb Strait, the Trump administration is signaling it has little interest in using the American military to stop them – relying instead on Saudi Arabia to do so.

But even with additional US intelligence and targeting support, Saudi Arabia has not been able to effectively stop the Huthis from taking key coastal towns in Yemen, frustrating Gulf and American officials. Sources who spoke with CNN expressed doubt that the Saudis would be able to stop the Huthis on their own.

The Huthis moves have not come as a surprise to sources in the region, as well as former diplomats, who said the weaknesses of the Saudi-backed Yemeni forces were well-known. For months US intelligence reports indicated the group would attempt to close another key waterway for commercial shipping as Iran did earlier this year, US officials said.

Still, the US believes it is currently providing Saudi Arabia with everything it needs to be successful against the Huthis, one American official told CNN, referring to the recent increase in sharing intelligence support and sharing of targeting data support with the Kingdom. And after about a decade of training the Yemen government’s military, the Kingdom had assured US officials that they were confident in their ability, two sources told CNN.

Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces started fighting the Huthis, who are supported and trained by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), more than a decade ago during Yemen’s brutal civil war. A 2022 UN-brokered truce had brought a period of relatively low levels of hostilities between the two sides.

However, the fighting has resumed and intensified in recent weeks. The Saudis accused the Huthis of targeting Mecca, Islam’s holiest city, and the Huthis claim to have shot down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet.

President Donald Trump has made clear that his current red line is direct US participation in kinetic strikes against the Huthis. To date, US military support has been strictly providing intel and targeting data for Saudi strikes.

“No offensive strikes,” said a US official.

‘The Huthis called us and they don’t want to fight’

Multiple Gulf and US sources say messaging from Trump signals to the Iranians he is unwilling to back US allies in the region.

“The Huthis called us and they don’t want to fight with us,” Trump said in remarks to reporters in Ireland last weekend. “They don’t want us to go after them and would much prefer not having us involved and they’re letting most ships go through.”

“It’s just one country they’re not too happy with,” Trump said, referring to Saudi Arabia, “and we’ll get that straightened out.”

Barbara Leaf, a former US diplomat who worked throughout the Middle East called Trump’s own comments about the Huthis “shocking.”

“It’s a pretty harsh way to treat your relationship with a close partner, to appear to privilege your agreement with a group you’ve designated as an (foreign terrorist organization) that attacked that partner,” she told CNN. The administration designated the Huthis as a Foreign Terrorist Organization in March 2025.

A view of a makeshift camp for people displaced by clashes between Iran-aligned Huthi fighters and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces, in Taiz province, Yemen September 13, 2026. Stringer/Reuters

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman spoke twice with Trump last week to ask for US strikes against the Huthis. That request, so far, has been rebuffed and sources said it is hard to tell if the administration policy will shift.

Amid this frustration over the Huthis advances, many Gulf sources believe the offensive represents a new front in the Iran war that could prolong the conflict. Despite some efforts to deal with the issues separately, sources increasingly believe there is unlikely to be progress on Iran without dealing with the Huthis.

“The Huthis’ Red Sea push is emboldening the IRGC. The Saudis have to get this fixed, otherwise they are negotiating with a gun on the table and they won’t do that,” said Joey Hood, a former US ambassador who spent much of his career working in the Middle East.

Hood, like other sources, noted that although the Huthis claim their fight is just with Saudis, there is a clear nexus to Iran.

“Iran is in an existential battle now and pulling on all of their proxies to fight. The Huthis are not remote-controlled by Iran but they need fuel from them. So, the Huthi statements of why they are carrying out this offensive now are not a complete reflection of reality,” said Hood.

The situation in Yemen has complicated the other negotiations, including those over the Strait of Hormuz.

A first meeting between Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries and Iran since the US-Iran war began was canceled earlier this week. Saudi Arabia decided not to attend amid concerns around the language of a potential agreement between Oman and Iran to open the Strait of Hormuz and other Gulf countries followed suit. Regional sources said it was a clear signal that the Kingdom sees no upside to engaging with the Iranians amid active Huthi attacks.

“Due to the Huthi attacks and the situation near the Bab-el-Mandeb corridor, it’s affecting the Strait of Hormuz deal,” a regional source told CNN. “The Saudis are demanding an all-or-nothing approach, which is understandable, but it delays the process.”

‘No one wants to fight alone’

For about a decade, the Saudis have been training Yemen’s military, and so far, those forces have been unable to effectively push back the Huthis. Saudi strikes, backed by US intelligence and precision targeting, have prevented the militia from exercising a firm command over some of the territory they have taken, but advances have not been wholly rebuffed.

The highest levels of the US government largely ignored the Huthi threat over the last decade despite lower-level US officials and regional players urging closer attention to the rebel group as it grew stronger, sources said. Last year’s US military campaign against the Huthis also laid bare the limits of American firepower – as months of bombing failed to effectively dislodge the group’s foothold inside Yemen and ended with an abrupt US-Huthi ceasefire.

The US “solidified the ceasefire” with the Huthis during a meeting in Oman this weekend, the US official said – a message that underscores the administration’s unwillingness to get involved.

“The Americans sent a message,” a senior Huthi official familiar with the matter told CNN Thursday, “that they don’t want to join the Saudis and be part of the conflict.”

“We received this message positively,” the source added.

There was a perception that Saudi Arabia’s own firepower coupled with its investment in Yemen’s military could counterbalance the Huthis’ offenses, some current and former US officials say. That expectation has not panned out.

Members of the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces fire a tank during what they say to be clashes with Yemen’s Iran-aligned Huthis in a location given as near Al-Hazm, Yemen, in this screen grab obtained from a handout video released September 9, 2026. Yemeni Armed Forces Media Center/Handout/Reuters

Others say the Huthi successes are hardly surprising, especially given unity of the militia and Iran’s support.

“The Huthis have the advantage of having this really deep and productive relationship with the (Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps) which has trained them and taken them up several notches from the hard-scrabble kind of cave fighters that they were 12 years ago to a force that can really be quite devastating,” said Leaf, who was a former Assistant Secretary of State for Near Eastern Affairs.

“The Huthi have spent a lot of time in the last months preparing their forces for just this kind of move,” she continued. “They punched through the Saudi-aligned and Yemeni government-aligned forces, not surprisingly, just punched through them – the forces just disintegrated.”

“No one wants to fight alone,” said a current Gulf official. “Either the Saudis fight or they cut a deal with the Huthis.”

But as it becomes clear that the Saudi-backed government will need more resources to take on the Huthis, the kingdom is also spread thin as they manage a wide array of challenges resulting from the ongoing war: a recent strike on their East-West pipeline, working with the US military on enabling tanker traffic through the strait, and keeping open a land-bridge to move critical resources through the region.

Saudi Arabia also cut oil exports to Europe for the month of September in recent days, triggering a recognition that the global energy crisis could deepen.

An effective pushback at the hands of Saudi-backed forces in Yemen is likely to require additional boots on the ground from Saudi Arabia or elsewhere, and a projection of commitment from the US, sources said. But neither of those inputs seem likely.

“At least the possibility of US involvement needs to hang over everyone to act as a deterrent, if you just unnecessarily wipe that away its demoralizing particularly to the Yemenis on the ground,” another regional source said.

Leaf said she has not heard exasperation with the Saudis from officials in the region, but rather questions of “What the hell is the US going to do here?”

Gulf and US sources have also expressed doubts about whether the Huthi escalation can actually be entirely resolved militarily.

“They have been trying for years” to defeat the Huthis, the regional source said, noting that military action “will weaken them, yes, but will not end them.”

CNN’s Nadeen Ebrahim contributed reporting.

World.title: Njapau Defends Invalidation Of IDs, Names HH’s Online Attackers
World.content:
Former Movement for Multiparty Democracy (MMD) Home Affairs deputy minister Grace Njapau said the Government should not be blamed for invalidating the national identity documents of people behind what she described as a vicious campaign to discredit it before the international community.

In a statement issued in Lusaka, Ms Njapau expressed sadness at what she called a continuing trend by politically disgruntled people of abusing cyberspace to target President Hakainde Hichilema. She named Emmanuel Mwamba, JJ Banda, Sishuwa Sishuwa and Lillian Mutambo, among others.

Ms Njapau said the perpetual use of vulgar language and hate speech, which she said had been consistently orchestrated by those individuals, was inimical to national unity and to the social cohesion that should bind Zambians regardless of ethnicity or political affiliation.

She described the behaviour as despicable and worrying, and said it reflected moral bankruptcy in people who, by virtue of their age and standing in society, were supposed to be role models for younger people.

“As a mother, I am concerned that our cultural values of respecting elders and those in authority are getting eroded. I’m deeply saddened that people who are politically disgruntled have resorted to relentlessly attacking President Hichilema through cyber space instead of promoting peace and national unity,” she said.

The former deputy minister went further. She said the Government should not be blamed for invalidating national identity documents for those behind a malicious campaign to discredit it in the eyes of the international community, saying necessary measures had to be taken in the national interest.

Ms Njapau said the gravity of the conduct of those whose national identity documents had been rendered invalid by the authorities called for drastic action. Their behaviour, she said, did not only border on dividing the nation but was also a serious threat to national security.

Her statement confirms that identity documents have been invalidated for people the Government accuses of discrediting it abroad. It does not say how many people are affected, which of those she named are among them, or under what legal process the documents were cancelled.

Ms Njapau said the opposition and President Hichilema’s opponents should accept that people from all parts of the country gave the United Party for National Development (UPND) a renewed mandate to govern for the next five years.

“As such, President Hichilema deserves to be respected and the decorum of his office protected from unnecessary attacks,” she said.

She urged Zambians to support the President and his administration, saying he had a clear vision to deliver development to all parts of the country. Mr Hichilema’s performance in his first term, she said, was self-explanatory, as shown by the milestones scored within a short time of assuming office.

Ms Njapau acknowledged that freedom of expression was a democratic right, but said it should be exercised with responsibility and only in the spirit of nation-building, not the opposite.

Her remarks come alongside a separate statement by the ruling party, in which UPND deputy media director Sikwindi Situla described Mr Mwamba as a renegade and “a wanted person in Zambia”, and accused Patriotic Front (PF) agents of feeding falsehoods to international election observers and journalists.

Ms Njapau maintained that the measures were taken in the national interest. Her statement did not set out how many people have had their documents invalidated or the procedure used.

World.title: Milenge targets 40,000 tonnes of maize by 2031
World.content:
Milenge District is targeting to produce more than 40,000 metric tonnes of maize by 2031, with over 4,600 farmers expected to benefit from the 2026/2027 Farmer Input Support Programme (FISP).

Milenge District Senior Agriculture Officer Baxter Musonda said achieving the production target would require farmers to adhere to recommended farming practices.

Mr Musonda said farmers should follow guidance provided by camp extension officers and other agricultural officials, particularly on improved farming practices.

He was speaking during the flag-off of the 2026/2027 FISP inputs.

Mr Musonda also cautioned FISP beneficiaries against selling their farming inputs after redemption, urging them to use the inputs for their intended purpose.

He said the district’s production target was in line with the Grow Zambia Agenda, which seeks to increase Zambia’s maize production to more than 10 million metric tonnes by 2031.

Government is supporting small-scale farmers through FISP to increase agricultural production, improve household incomes and contribute to national food security.

Meanwhile, Milenge Acting District Commissioner Chiluba Yamba said more than 4,600 farmers in the district would benefit from FISP during the 2026/2027 farming season.

Dr Yamba said FISP remained an important government intervention aimed at increasing agricultural productivity through the provision of subsidised farming inputs.

He said government remained committed to ensuring that farmers received farming inputs on time so that the programme continued to benefit intended beneficiaries, strengthen national food security and contribute to the broader objectives of the agricultural sector.

Mikula Ward Councillor Eric Kasongo urged FISP beneficiaries to safeguard their e-voucher codes to prevent unauthorised redemption.

Mr Kasongo also appealed to agro-dealers to stock a wider variety of approved agricultural inputs and other eligible items to give farmers more options when redeeming their e-vouchers, particularly when they have a balance after purchasing seed and fertiliser.

World.title: Mwense residents warned against politicising Govt programmes
World.content:
Mwense District Administrative Officer Philip Muonga has cautioned community members against politicising government programmes aimed at improving the livelihoods of citizens.

Mr Muonga said President Hakainde Hichilema had directed that all eligible beneficiaries of various government programmes should benefit regardless of their political affiliation.

He said this during the flag-off of the distribution of farming inputs under the 2026 Food Security Pack (FSP) in Mwense District.

Mr Muonga assured residents that all eligible beneficiaries would be considered under the programme, which he said was intended to benefit citizens across the district.

Under the social protection programme, 1,000 vulnerable but viable households in Mwense District are being targeted to improve household incomes and food security.

Mr Muonga also urged beneficiary households not to sell the farming inputs, saying his office had received reports of some beneficiaries engaging in the practice.

Meanwhile, FSP beneficiaries have commended government for promoting wetland farming in the district.

Kabelenga Katebe, who spoke on behalf of the beneficiaries, said the initiative had contributed significantly to improving household food security.

Mr Katebe said wetland farming had also helped improve household nutrition and contributed to efforts to address stunting.

He expressed gratitude to President Hichilema for the FSP inputs, saying they were helping households enhance food security.

“Wetland farming has also contributed towards improving nutritional status thereby helping in addressing stunting, we are grateful to the President for the FSP inputs, they really help in enhancing household food security,” Mr Kabelenga said.

Loading read count...

World.title: Kapasa Makasa students sensitised on GBV, economic empowerment
World.content:
The Gender Division in Muchinga Province has conducted a one-day sensitisation programme for students at Kapasa Makasa University in Chinsali District on economic empowerment and gender-based violence (GBV).

Muchinga Province Deputy Permanent Secretary Brian Sichande, who officially opened the engagement, said government remained committed to continuously engaging young people on issues critical to national development, including GBV and economic empowerment.

Mr Sichande said the programme had come at an opportune time when government was placing emphasis on human capital development, economic empowerment, skills development, gender equality and the prevention of GBV.

He said the participation of young people in such programmes was vital because they constituted a significant proportion of the country’s population and were an important resource for social and economic development.

Mr Sichande said economic empowerment was fundamental to enabling individuals and communities to become self-reliant and contribute meaningfully to national development.

He said economic and social development could not be fully attained while GBV continued to affect individuals, families and communities.

The Deputy Permanent Secretary stressed the need to equip young people, particularly students in higher learning institutions, with knowledge on GBV prevention, available reporting mechanisms, referral pathways and survivor support services.

Meanwhile, Kapasa Makasa University Deputy Registrar Lillian Mukuka, speaking on behalf of university management, commended the initiative to equip students with knowledge on economic empowerment, capacity building and GBV.

Ms Mukuka said the knowledge and skills were important not only to students but also to their roles as members of the wider community and society.

She said capacity-building skills were essential to the development of all people, particularly young people.

Ms Mukuka said the knowledge acquired through the programme would enable students to better understand and critically assess situations in their lives compared to those who had not benefited from similar sensitisation programmes.

Meanwhile, students at Kapasa Makasa University welcomed the programme, describing it as important to their well-being in a rapidly developing country such as Zambia.

Emmanuel Tembo, a fourth-year Animal Science student who delivered the vote of thanks, expressed gratitude to the Gender Division in Muchinga Province for organising what he described as a timely and impactful programme.

World.title: World Vision closes Pemba programme
World.content:
World Vision Zambia has closed its Moyo Area Development Programme in Pemba District after investing more than 12.9 million United States dollars in Moyo Chiefdom over the past 17 years.

The programme, which commenced in 2009, benefited more than 30,000 people through interventions in health, education, livelihoods and child protection.

Southern Province Acting Permanent Secretary Gift Monde said the investments had made a significant impact on the lives of people in the chiefdom.

Mr Monde said the construction of Moyo Mini Hospital and maternity annexes at health facilities across the chiefdom was in line with President Hakainde Hichilema’s vision of bringing health services closer to the people.

“Government appreciates the contribution that World Vision Zambia has made towards improving the lives of people in Moyo Chiefdom. The investments in health, education and livelihoods have left a significant impact on the community,” Mr Monde said.

He said government would continue working with development partners to complement its efforts in improving service delivery and creating opportunities for communities to become self-reliant.

World Vision Zambia Associate Director of Programmes Betty Mbewe said the organisation was pleased to leave behind an empowered community with skills to sustain the gains made under the programme.

Ms Mbewe said the community had acquired skills in livestock management, gardening and savings, which would help residents continue improving their livelihoods after the programme’s closure.

She said World Vision had distributed more than 11,000 goats during the programme, contributing to an increase in the goat population in the area from less than 5,000 at the beginning of the programme to about 55,000.

Ms Mbewe said 175 savings groups had also been established, providing community members with opportunities to save, access small loans and invest in income-generating activities.

She thanked government and the people of Moyo Chiefdom for supporting World Vision’s development initiatives over the years.

Meanwhile, Chief Moyo pledged to sustain the gains made under the programme and ensure that the infrastructure and skills transferred to the community continued to benefit residents.

The Chief said the community would take ownership of the projects and work together to protect the investments made in the chiefdom.

The traditional leadership also called on community members to maintain the spirit of self-reliance and ensure that the benefits of the programme were passed on to future generations.

World.title: Chifunabuli farmers start redeeming inputs
World.content:
Farmers in Chifunabuli District have begun redeeming their farming inputs under the 2026/2027 Farmer Input Support Programme (FISP).

Chifunabuli District Marketing Development Officer, Dolnald Sikazwe said 472 farmers have so far successfully redeemed their inputs through the E- voucher system.

Mr Sikazwe explained that a total of 2,375 farmers out of 3, 419 beneficiaries in the district have had their E-voucher codes activated in readiness to access inputs.

He explained that the 2, 375 farmers whose codes have been activated are those who supplied the required 10 by 50 kilogrammes of maize to the Food Reserve Agency (FRA) upon which they were automatically issued with E-voucher codes which will allow them to redeem their inputs.

Mr Sikazwe revealed that five agro-dealers have been engaged to supply inputs in the district and out of the five, four are already in the district with one in the process to finalise the movement of stock.

And Chifunabuli District Commissioner, Stanley Mukosa inspected the agro-dealers and expressed happiness with the service.

Mr Mukosa noted that timely redemption of inputs will allow farmers to plant their crops on time for a better crop yield.

He has called on agro-dealers not to supply farmers with underweight bags of fertilizer and seed.

“To our agro-dealers, I can see that you are equal to the task but as government, we will not allow you to supply underweight inputs to our farmers, if we receive such complaints, you will automatically be blacklisted and so to keep a good relationship between government and yourselves, ensure that you give farmers the quality and quantity that will allow them to give us even a better yield next year,” Mr Mukosa said.

World.title: CDF beneficiaries urged to use grants for intended projects
World.content:
Nchelenge Town Council Secretary Benson Malama has urged beneficiaries of Constituency Development Fund (CDF) grants to use the funds strictly for the purposes outlined in their respective project proposals.

Mr Malama said this when he addressed 70 beneficiaries and cautioned them against sharing the money among themselves immediately after receiving the grants.

He said such practices could undermine the objectives of the CDF programme and prevent beneficiaries from achieving the intended benefits.

“Stop the habit of sharing the money amongst yourselves immediately after receiving the grant. The money has been given to you for a specific purpose, and you should ensure that it is used for that purpose,” Mr Malama said.

He urged beneficiaries to remain committed to implementing the projects for which the grants were approved and avoid diverting the funds to activities that were not included in their proposals.

“Stick to your project proposals because that is what was assessed and approved. You must make sure that the money is put into the project so that it can benefit all the members of the group,” Mr Malama said.

Mr Malama explained that CDF grants were intended to improve the livelihoods of beneficiaries by supporting sustainable income-generating activities (IGAs) and promoting economic empowerment.

World.title: ZABS tests over 8,000 samples in eight months
World.content:
The Zambia Bureau of Standards (ZABS) recorded positive performance in its service delivery between January and August 2026, testing 8,571 samples at its laboratories in Chipata, Kitwe, Lusaka and Mongu.

ZABS Executive Director Nathan Sing’ambwa said the samples covered a wide range of products, including food and beverages, consumer goods, agricultural inputs and products, petroleum products, construction materials, medical consumables and infection prevention supplies.

Mr Sing’ambwa said water and environmental samples were also tested as part of ZABS’ mandate to protect consumer health and public safety.

According to a statement issued to the media Mr Sing’ambwa said the Bureau also developed and published 352 standards during the period under review, bringing the cumulative number of standards developed by ZABS to 8,351.

He said the standards covered various sectors of the economy and were aimed at strengthening the competitiveness of Zambian products and services on regional and international markets.

Mr Sing’ambwa said 297 products were certified during the period under review.

He said 169 products manufactured by large enterprises were certified under the Quality Mark, while 128 products manufactured by Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) were certified under the Certified Local Supplier Scheme (CLSS).

The ZABS Executive Director said the latest certifications had increased the cumulative number of products certified by the Bureau to 2,220.

Mr Sing’ambwa further disclosed that 733 industry personnel were trained between January and August 2026 to strengthen their capacity and knowledge in quality assurance, standards adherence and compliance.

He said ZABS had also intensified market surveillance activities to curb the illegal use of ZABS quality marks across the country.

Mr Sing’ambwa said the surveillance activities led to the identification of 27 products that were falsely displaying ZABS marks, adding that enforcement action had since been initiated and was ongoing.

He said ZABS remained committed to providing standardisation and quality assurance services to promote a competitive industry while safeguarding consumers in accordance with the Standards Act, Chapter 416 of the Laws of Zambia.

World.title: Nigeria: Tinubu Meets Macron for Private Dinner in Paris
World.content:
According to Mr Onanuga, the dinner reflected the longstanding relationship between Nigeria and France.

President Bola Tinubu met French President Emmanuel Macron on Thursday for a private dinner at the Élysée Palace in Paris.

It is the latest in the series of meetings and engagements between Nigeria and France since Mr Tinubu assumed office in 2023.

The president's Special Adviser on Information and Strategy, Bayo Onanuga, disclosed the meeting in a post on X on Friday. He also shared photographs of the two leaders at the French presidential palace.



PREMIUM TIMES reports that the meeting took place while Mr Tinubu was in France during the second leg of his three-week annual leave in Europe.

He arrived in Paris on Monday after spending the first part of his leave in London.

According to Mr Onanuga, the dinner reflected the longstanding relationship between Nigeria and France.

In the post, he wrote, "French President Emmanuel Macron received President Bola Ahmed Tinubu for a private dinner Thursday night at the Élysée Palace, reflecting the enduring relationship between Nigeria and France and their shared commitment to strengthening bilateral cooperation."

President Tinubu, in a separate post about the meeting, also said his conversation with Mr Macron reflects both countries' mutual interest in maintaining good relations and strengthening the existing partnership.

He also thanked the French president for his hospitality and friendship.

"It was a pleasure to share a private dinner with President Emmanuel Macron at the Élysée Palace in Paris. @EmmanuelMacron

"Our conversation reaffirmed the strong friendship between Nigeria and France, as well as our shared commitment to deepening cooperation and building a mutually beneficial partnership between our two nations," he wrote.

Photographs released from the dinner showed Mr Tinubu and Mr Macron together at the Élysée Palace, with another image showing Mr Tinubu, Mr Macron and France's First Lady, Brigitte Macron.

However, details of the interaction or any potential agreement between the two leaders were not provided.

World.title: Guinea: Guinea Bans France 24, Withdraws Jeune Afrique Correspondent's Accreditation
World.content:
Dakar — The Committee to Protect Journalists calls on Guinean authorities to reverse Thursday's ban on France 24 after a presenter called President Mamadi Doumbouya a "putschist president" and to reinstate the accreditation of the pan-African weekly Jeune Afrique's Guinea correspondent Diawo Barry.

"By prohibiting France 24 from broadcasting and Jeune Afrique's Diawo Barry from working, Guinean authorities have shown their ruthless determination to silence independent voices and to intimidate other media outlets into self-censorship," said Moussa Ngom, CPJ's Francophone Africa representative. "Authorities must immediately reverse these decisions and refrain from further actions that erode press freedom and the public's right to information."

In its September 17 decision, the regulatory High Authority of Communication (HAC) said it had banned France 24 because it had failed to comply with its order the previous day "to immediately cease using terms deemed derogatory to the dignity of the Head of State and to make the required editorial corrections." The HAC also withdrew press accreditation for all the French state-owned channel's correspondents, special correspondents, and contributors in Guinea.

On Monday, a France 24 presenter used the word "putschist" while commenting on Doumbouya's visit to Ivory Coast.



Hours after the HAC's September 16 notice, France 24 added an online correction to the video's description, saying that Doumbouya had been "mistakenly labeled a coup leader."

"Having seized power in a coup on September 5, 2021, which overthrew President Alpha Condé, he was subsequently elected President of the Republic following the presidential election of December 28, 2025," the correction said.

France 24 told Agence France-Presse news agency that it had also apologized and corrected the error on air.

Also on September 16, the HAC revoked Barry's accreditation as Jeune Afrique's correspondent on the grounds that his coverage of news in Guinea did not meet the requirements of objective, neutral, balanced reporting.

The Guinean satirical newspaper Le Lynx, where Barry is publishing director, suggested that Jeune Afrique's September special report on Guinea, "Democracy under surveillance," had "ruffled feathers."

Jeune Afrique said that the HAC's decision had been handed down "without prior consultation" and was "not based on any specific allegation" to support its "vague" accusations.

Since Doumbouya took power, the HAC has introduced long-term and indefinite bans on numerous critical outlets and reporters. The whereabouts of journalist Habib Marouane Camara, who was seized by uniformed men in 2024, and of exiled journalist Mamoudou Babila Keita's elderly father, Elhadj Adama Keita, who was kidnapped in 2025, remain unknown.

Close 

CPJ's calls to request comment from the HAC went unanswered.

World.title: Nigeria: Niger State Imposes 24-Hour Curfew After Suspects Die in Custody
World.content:
The Niger State Government has imposed a 24-hour curfew across Minna, the state capital, as tension rises over the deaths of about 37 suspected illegal miners in the custody of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC).

The curfew takes effect immediately after Juma'at prayers on Friday, the government announced.

The government has also ordered the suspension of all mining activities in the state until further notice.

The directives are part of the state government's measures to address the prevailing security situation and restore safety across the state.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The government advised residents to remain indoors and comply fully with the curfew and other security directives until further notice.

The government also cancelled an All Progressives Congress (APC) rally scheduled for Minna on Saturday and suspended the NSCDC State Commandant, Suberu Aniviye, and his team.

Governor Mohammed Bago announced the measures during a press briefing in Minna on Friday.

He said the curfew was necessary to prevent a breakdown of law and order and to allow the government to manage the situation while investigations continue.

Background to the curfew

The deaths occurred after the NSCDC detained suspects arrested in connection with mining activities in the Ema Ushishi area of Niger State.

More than 37 detainees reportedly died while in custody, although the exact number and cause of the deaths have not been officially established.

The bodies were later moved to a mortuary, a development that heightened tension among youths and residents in Minna.

The incident triggered public concern and fears of possible protests or violence, prompting the state government to cancel the APC rally and impose the curfew.

Mr Bago described the deaths as tragic and unacceptable and said the government had begun steps to establish what happened.

He announced the constitution of a committee of inquiry to investigate the incident and determine the cause of the deaths.

Cause of death not established

The governor cautioned against concluding the forensic examinations, medical assessments, and autopsies.

He said possible causes being considered included suffocation caused by overcrowding in the detention facility and exposure to hazardous substances allegedly linked to illegal mining.

"There is no official root cause of these deaths yet. It is too early for anybody to conclude the root causes," Mr Bago said.

He said the state government was compiling a register of the deceased to identify and contact their families.

Mr Bago assured the victims' relatives that the government would engage with them and provide the necessary support during the investigation.

NSCDC commandant suspended

The governor announced the immediate suspension of Mr Aniviye and his team to allow for an impartial investigation.

He said the suspension was not a declaration of guilt but a measure to ensure that the investigation was conducted without interference.

The governor said the Director-General of the NSCDC, who is currently outside the country, had delegated his deputy to represent him in engagements concerning the incident.

He added that the state government had already met with the senior NSCDC official.

'We will probe deeply'

Mr Bago pledged that the government would investigate the incident thoroughly and ensure that those responsible for any wrongdoing were held accountable.

"Lives of human beings are lives of human beings. Such an unjust government will not tolerate any injustice, and we are going to make sure that we probe this thing deeply until we get to the root of this," he said.

He urged residents, particularly youths, to remain calm and obey the curfew.

Close 

"We are calling on all the youth to please stay away from violence. It is not going to bring about those who have died. It will rather cost us a lot at the end of the day," he said.

Mining suspended

The governor also ordered the closure of activities at the illegal mining site in Ema Ushishi.

He expressed concern over mining operations conducted without adequate technology, safety equipment and protective gear.

According to him, such practices expose miners to dangerous conditions and may have contributed to the incident.

The state government said it would continue to work with the NSCDC, the police, the State Security Service and other relevant agencies to establish the facts.

Mr Bago commiserated with the families of the deceased and declared three days of mourning in the state.

He said the cancellation of the APC rally was intended to allow the state to mourn the victims and focus on restoring calm and completing the investigation.

World.title: Algeria: Algeria Shifts Towards English As French Loses Ground in Schools
World.content:
Primary school pupils in Algeria are in for a change this year when, for the first time, the national curriculum will focus on English over French. The move follows a general trend across former French colonies in North Africa that are now prioritising English.

Algeria's 2026-27 school year kicks off next week with a change: a shift away from its usual focus on French as a second language.

Introduced in primary schools alongside French in 2022, from now on English will be the first foreign language children study.

Algerian education minister Mohamed Seghir Saadaoui announced in July that English classes would begin in the third year of primary school, when children are around 8. French lessons will follow a year later.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"In third year, only English will be taught," Saadaoui said.

Colonial baggage

The reform is part of a broader shift towards English in Algeria, where French remains closely tied to the country's colonial history.

In a paper published earlier this year, Algerian linguist Fadhila Leroul of the Mouloud Mammeri University of Tizi-Ouzou says the change can be explained not only by English's status as a global lingua franca, but because in the political context of former French colonies cutting ties from France, it steers Algeria "beyond the colonial legacy attached to French".

Algeria's history with France is long and tightly knit. Algeria was under French rule from 1830 to 1962, and was formally incorporated into France in 1848.

The French language was imposed everywhere from administration to formal education, but French was not accessible to just anyone. Arabic remained the language of the majority, while French was for Europeans and those with access to education.

According to Abu Bakr Khaled Saad Allah, an Algerian professor and researcher on higher education, this division made language deeply bound up with questions of national identity. Algerian writer Kateb Yacine, who wrote in French, once described the language as a "war trophy" taken from the former colonial power.

How a Nigerian town came to speak 'street French'

Following its independence, Algeria pursued policies to make Arabic the official national language. Arabic has been the country's primary language ever since, but for decades French remained prevalent in academia.

Algiers began toying with the idea of pushing English in the early 1990s, when primary school students were given the choice between English and French as a second language.

The plan was shut down and English was taken off the syllabus until 2019, when the minister of education put forward a plan to promote the use of English in universities. In 2022, President Abdelmadjid Tebboune announced that English would be introduced in primary schools.

The move coincided with a weakening of Algeria's relations with France. The relationship between the two countries has been tense since 2021 and, despite a period of rapprochement in 2023, worsened in 2024 after France declared its support for Morocco's sovereignty over the disputed Western Sahara.

The last word: why half of the world's languages could vanish this century

Regional shift

Both Morocco and Tunisia also took pains post-independence to cut ties to their former colonial power.

Morocco was a French protectorate from 1912 to 1956. Under Paris, French was the only language used for instruction. When Morocco got its independence, it steered the country towards policies of Arabisation to ensure Arabic once again took a central place.

The Moroccan government progressively introduced Arabic into primary education, but French remained the language of higher study, particularly in mathematics and science.

In the 2000s, the kingdom began to move towards a more multilingual model that supported both Arabic and French. At the same time, English was cementing its dominance as a global language - particular with younger generations.

One 2021 survey of 15-25-year-olds, commissioned by the British Council, found 40 percent of respondents believed English was the most important language to learn, compared to only 10 percent for French. As one participant said: "Everyone is turning to the English language because of its dominance on the internet."

By 2023, the Moroccan government began introducing English in public schools, where before it had been limited mainly to private institutions.

Close 

French overtakes Arabic to become world's fourth most spoken language

Tunisia was also a French protectorate from 1881 to 1956. The colonial rulers soon established a public education system that prioritised French, and it became the language of administration and economy. Those seeking access to higher opportunities therefore became bilingual in both French and Arabic.

After its independence, unlike Morocco and Algeria, Tunisia did not seek to cut out French from education and daily life. While it also pursued a policy of Arabisation, it maintained strong links with French education. The language of its former colonisers remained important in science, medicine, higher education, business and government.

But in contrast to its neighbours, Tunisia introduced English early on after independence as a foreign-language option in schools. Decades on, young people are increasingly choosing it.

In a 2020 Afrobarometer survey, around 68 percent of Tunisian respondents said English was the most important language for young people to learn. Only some 13 percent chose French.

World.title: Africa: Can Africa Turn Red Sea Rivalries to Its Advantage?
World.content:
A map of ports in the Horn of Africa.

analysis

Growing competition for African ports and security partnerships offers new leverage - if countries can avoid deeper geopolitical fragmentation.

Ongoing conflict in the Middle East exposes shifting regional geopolitical fault lines that are pulling African states into an emerging macro-conflict system anchored along the Red Sea.

This stems from several overlapping crises arising from US and Israeli military offensives against Iran and renewed Houthi attacks on shipping lanes, Saudi-Emirati competition across the Horn of Africa, and disputes amongst African states over sovereignty and regional influence.

Should these crises deepen and become self-reinforcing, the implications for African states across much of the Red Sea littoral could be dire.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The most recent US and Israeli offensive against Iran has added to these dynamics. Iran's retaliatory offensives against Gulf actors have called into question longstanding presumptions about the US' reliability in providing security for its traditional Gulf allies.

That in turn has precipitated more overt hedging strategies among regional powers, most notably the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and Saudi Arabia. Their prior security coordination to counter Iranian influence has buckled under the weight of opposing conceptions of regional order and claims to regional leadership.

Abu Dhabi projects power through expansive investments in ports and infrastructure, and through ties to non-state armed actors and secessionist movements in Yemen, Sudan, Libya and Somalia. It has also deepened engagement with Israel since normalising relations with Jerusalem under the 2020 Abraham Accords.

Riyadh has sought to undercut Abu Dhabi's efforts by backing recognised central state authorities and building countervailing partnerships with like-minded regional actors. Its closer coordination with Egypt, Pakistan and Turkey points to its growing efforts to reinforce state-centric alliances, constrain the UAE and hedge against Abu Dhabi's close ties with Israel.

This fluid security environment raises the stakes for African states along the Red Sea, which can offer access to ports, airfields, intelligence and security partnerships.

Landlocked Ethiopia seeks sea access to reduce its heavy dependence on Djibouti. Somaliland's Berbera port appealed because the Emirati-owned logistics company DP World had already developed the port, an economic zone and a transport corridor to Ethiopia.

But since the controversial 2024 Ethiopia-Somaliland cooperation memorandum, Ethiopia and Somalia recommitted to each other's territorial integrity in the Turkish-brokered Ankara Declaration, agreeing to negotiate Ethiopian commercial sea access under Somalia's sovereign authority.

This has not, however, removed Ethiopia from Gulf competition. Turkey has become an important mediator between Ethiopia and Somalia, while the UAE retains deep commercial and political ties with Ethiopia and Somaliland.

Meanwhile, 2026 reports of UAE-linked training and logistics networks supporting Sudan's Rapid Support Forces (RSF) from Ethiopian territory (which both Ethiopia and the UAE deny) have heightened regional tensions.

Africa's Red Sea States

Egypt, by contrast, controls the Suez Canal, has substantial military and naval capabilities and is strategically positioned at the Red Sea's northern end. Disruption around the Bab al-Mandab Strait directly hits Suez traffic and Egyptian revenues, while instability in Sudan and Somalia weighs heavily on Cairo's security interests.

Egypt's long-standing rivalry with Ethiopia has drawn Cairo into closer alignment with Saudi Arabia. Tensions have escalated since the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam was inaugurated in September 2025 and Ethiopia revived plans for three more dams on the Blue Nile.

Cairo has responded by working to undercut Addis Ababa, opposing Ethiopia's sea-access claims and unilateral control over Blue Nile waters, and bolstering ties with Eritrea.

Sudan's value to Gulf actors lies in both its war and its geography. Port Sudan is a crucial gateway for the weapons, logistics and personnel inflows sustaining the conflict. The UAE faces persistent allegations of backing the RSF, which it denies, while Egypt and Saudi Arabia have generally kept closer ties with the Sudanese Armed Forces.

Somalia's federal government decision in January 2026 to cut ties with the UAE was rejected by breakaway Somaliland and autonomous Puntland (and Jubaland), all of which have their own Emirati relationships. Turkey, Qatar and Saudi Arabia, however, have deepened engagement with the federal government.

Europe also has a role in this complex security landscape. The European Union (EU) maintains a substantial maritime presence through Operation ASPIDES, which protects commercial shipping in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, and Operation ATALANTA, which covers the Western Indian Ocean and parts of the Red Sea.

A July 2026 EU-Djibouti agreement on ASPIDES underlines European navies' reliance on African partners for access, logistics and onshore support.

In Somalia, the EU runs a civilian capacity-building mission and a military training mission, alongside anti-piracy initiatives. It is building maritime law enforcement and coast-guard capacity in Mogadishu, Somaliland and Puntland, with an emphasis on accountable security institutions and maritime governance.

This is a very different model of influence from the Gulf powers, who attach their support to greater access to ports, political patronage and strategic infrastructure in the Horn.

As African states along the Red Sea are pulled into the geopolitical orbit of rival Gulf powers, how sustainable are these partnerships and how might they change?

Gulf investment in ports, logistics, energy and other strategic infrastructure will probably continue, spurring deeper defence and security coordination. Commercial deals may become increasingly bundled with defence, security and intelligence commitments - a more compelling offer than anything Europe can provide.

The risk, however, is that African states become entrenched in rival security architectures and geopolitical alignments that narrow their room for manoeuvre.

Close 

This leaves Africa's Red Sea countries facing a policy dilemma. They could engage Middle Eastern powers through a coordinated approach that channels external competition towards a common development agenda. Or they could continue the current fragmented bilateral engagements that provide immediate investment, diplomatic backing and help with pressing security-related concerns.

But the short-term gains of bilateralism come at the expense of longer-term shared development and stability.

The African Union could help by assigning North and East African states a leading role in shaping the continent's engagement with Middle Eastern powers. Their proximity to the Red Sea and growing value to external players give them outsized access and influence that could be exercised on the continent's behalf.

The central question is whether Africa will harness this new value to advance shared development or allow it to deepen the continent's fragmentation.
