We cannot do what we do without your support. Moody’s, one of the big three global credit rating agencies, has lowered Poland’s rating from A2 to A3. The last time the agency had Poland at such a low level of creditworthiness was in 2002. The decision is likely to push up borrowing costs for Poland and reduce investor confidence. It is the first time any of the big three agencies has downgraded Poland’s rating since 2016, when Standard & Poor’s shifted it from A- to BBB+ on its scale. However, it restored Poland to A- two years later Moody’s obniżył dziś rating Polski z A2 do A3. To pierwsza obniżka ratingu Polski przez Moody’s od 2002 r. Przez lata agencja utrzymywała A2, nawet gdy zmieniała perspektywę na negatywną. Trwałe wysokie deficyty i rosnące koszty obsługi oznaczają pogorszenie perspektyw dla Polski pic.twitter.com/iGeuBb5hih — Piotr Arak (@piotrarak) September 18, 2026 “The downgrade of Poland’s ratings to A3 reflects our expectations of a sustained deterioration in Poland’s fiscal strength,” said Moody’s in an announcement late on Friday, quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP). The agency noted that “large fiscal deficits” had led to a growing level of public debt that, together with rising costs, has “weakened debt affordability metrics”. It pointed to a “limited willingness or ability on the part of the Polish authorities to rebuild fiscal buffers during favourable economic conditions”, and noted that high spending on social policies and defence limits the scope for deficit reduction. In response to the announcement, Poland’s finance minister, Andrzej Domański, noted that Moody’s had previously “had the highest rating for Poland among the three major agencies”. After the downgrade, it is now aligned with Standard & Poor’s and Fitch, the other two agencies, he added. “We take this decision seriously, but calmly,” continued Domański. “The Polish economy is growing rapidly, and its fundamentals remain strong. We will consistently strengthen public finances, but this requires cooperation from all state institutions, including the president.” The latter comment was directed at President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition and has blocked many of the government’s initiatives, including some of its fiscal policies. Moody’s pointed to this gridlock in its announcement on Friday. However, Przemysław Czarnek, deputy leader of the opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, said that Moody’s downgrade undermines Prime Minister “Donald Tusk’s claim that Poland is Europe’s financial tiger”. In fact, “that tiger is living on credit”, wrote Czarnek. Dziś agencja ratingowa Moody’s obniżyła rating Polski do poziomu A3, jednocześnie podnosząc perspektywę ratingu z negatywnej do stabilnej. Dotąd Moody’s miała najwyższą ocenę Polski spośród trzech głównych agencji – po obniżce dostosowała ją do poziomu agencji Fitch i S&P.… — Andrzej Domański (@Domanski_Andrz) September 18, 2026 Poland’s worsening fiscal situation has been drawing the attention of the rating agencies for some time. The government’s budget deficit has ballooned, reaching 7.3% of GDP in 2025, the second-highest figure in the European Union. That was despite Poland being placed under the EU’s excessive deficit procedure in 2024, at which time it set out a plan to reduce the deficit. Instead, the deficit has risen. The draft budget for 2027 puts the deficit at 7.1%, almost double the 3.7% the government had previously committed to reach by that year. As a result, Poland’s level of debt has risen rapidly. In the first quarter of this year, it went above 60% of GDP for the first time on record, thereby exceeding the limit enshrined in EU law. Poland's government has approved a draft budget for 2027 that keeps defence and healthcare as spending priorities, while continuing heavy borrowing The deficit, at 7.1% of GDP, remains well above the EU limit of 3% that the government has pledged to reach https://t.co/gxLdsHjYPz — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 28, 2026 Meanwhile, the ability to introduce measures to better balance the budget has been hindered by hostility between the government – a coalition ranging from left to centre right – and Nawrocki. Since coming to power just over a year ago, Nawrocki has vetoed a record number of bills, including a proposed tax increase on alcoholic and sweet drinks. He also recently blocked a windfall tax on fuel companies. The situation led two of the big three rating agencies, Fitch and Moody’s, to shift their outlook for Poland from stable to negative last year, indicating that they may lower the country’s score. Moody’s has now done so, although in Friday’s downgrade announcement it also shifted Poland’s outlook back to stable, saying that it forecasts strong economic growth in the coming years and government debt stabilising around 70-75% of GDP by the late 2020s. Ratings agency Fitch has again warned that the "political gridlock" between Poland's government president – such as the current clash over EU defence loans – is hindering efforts to tackle "large fiscal deficits and rapidly rising debt" https://t.co/JSqwwayTdm — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 18, 2026 Fitch has so far maintained its credit rating for Poland at A-, where it has been since 2007. However, in March this year, the agency warned that the “political gridlock” between the government and president is hindering efforts to tackle Poland’s “large fiscal deficits and rapidly rising debt”. The third of the main agencies, Standard & Poor’s, has so far maintained both Poland’s credit rating at A-, where it has been since 2018, and its outlook at neutral. In a comment on Moody’s decision on Friday, Ignacy Morawski, editor-in-chief of Polish business daily Puls Biznesu, wrote that the downgrade had “happened faster than most market participants had predicted”. He cited “uncontrolled political inertia” in tackling public finances as the primary reason behind the downgrade, which he said should provide “even more reason for the government and president to start seeking agreement”. Prime Minister Donald Tusk has announced during a visit to Ukraine that Poland has joined the Anti-Ballistic Missile Coalition, a group of European countries that are jointly developing an integrated air defence system for the continent. “Yes, Poland is now part of this great project,” said Tusk, “a group of countries and companies that will work together to protect against ballistic missiles…mean[ing] much safer European, and therefore also Polish, skies.” He added that he had “established the form and framework for this cooperation” during talks today with President Volodymyr Zelensky, who was hosting a summit of eight countries from around the Carpathian Mountains: Ukraine, Romania, Serbia, Poland, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Austria and Hungary. Speaking at a press conference alongside Tusk, Zelensky also confirmed that “we will be partners” in the missile coalition and Poland “is welcome there”, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Jesteśmy w Koalicji Antybalistycznej. pic.twitter.com/prtqKznHnB — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) September 18, 2026 The Anti-Ballistic Missile Coalition was established in mid-July this year during a meeting in Paris of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, a group of countries that are supporting Ukraine in its defence against Russian aggression. Alongside Ukraine, the coalition also included Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Spain, Sweden and the United Kingdom. In late July, Kyiv announced that it wants a prototype anti-ballistic system, which has been codenamed Freyja, ready in the first half of next year. Ukrainian arms manufacturer Fire Point is the lead industrial partner in the project. At the time, there was some confusion and criticism in Poland regarding the fact that the country had not been included in the coalition. Speaking today, Tusk admitted that there had been “a certain misunderstanding” at the time, but it is “now clear that Poland is also part of this initiative”. The alliance is hoping to develop a cheaper complement to the US-made Patriot air-defence systems, which Ukraine and many other European countries use but which rely on American supplies. Zelensky has recently called on Ukraine’s allies to provide it with Patriot missiles. However, that issue caused political controversy in Poland earlier this year, when the right-wing opposition criticised the government for handing over some of its missiles to Kyiv, arguing that it would weaken Poland’s own defences. Speaking today alongside Tusk, Zelensky said that the new missile coalition would bring Poland and Ukraine “even closer to each other” and provide benefits to both countries, reports PAP. “Ukraine possesses unique technologies developed during the war, and we are ready to share them with Donald [Tusk] and our Polish partners,” said Zelensky. The Polish government has confirmed that it has transferred Patriot missiles to Ukraine following opposition criticism It also released a list of all military donations to Ukraine since 2022, showing that the former PiS government gave much more equipment https://t.co/8BmDy5BjiB — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 7, 2026 Both leaders made reference to recent tensions between their countries, in particular over the Volhynia massacres during World War Two, in which Ukrainian nationalists killed around 100,000 Polish civilians. “We may sometimes speak very directly, but if we are friends, we must openly discuss topics that are sensitive to both sides,” said Zelensky, quoted by PAP. “We are friends, and Russia is the enemy. If we begin a dialogue based on common understanding, we will manage everything.” Tusk, meanwhile, thanked Zelensky “for your willingness to at least try to understand our Polish sensitivities” regarding “difficult, painful issues from the past”. He pledged to “always support Ukraine in your fight against aggression”, regardless of “adversities and negative trends”. Meanwhile, Tusk expressed hope that the newly formed Carpathian Eight group of countries, which met today in that format for the first time, would help provide further impetus for Ukraine on its path towards European Union membership. Today, for the first time, here in Ukraine, in our part of the Carpathians, we hold a Summit that brings together all the Carpathian states, the regions and communities of our countries. World.title: American Nobel laureate receives Polish citizenship
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. American Nobel laureate Victor Ambros, whose father emigrated from Poland after World War Two, has received Polish citizenship. Prime Minister Donald Tusk called him to give him the good news personally. Ambros, who won the 2024 Nobel Prize in Medicine for his research on microRNA, revealed earlier this year during a visit to Warsaw that he was seeking Polish citizenship and hoped to help strengthen Poland’s scientific standing worldwide. Jesteś obywatelem najlepszego państwa na świecie!🇵🇱❤️ pic.twitter.com/cBDfMDS3Ax — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) September 16, 2026 “I have great news for you: you are a Pole, you have a Polish passport,” Tusk told Ambros during the call. “You are a citizen of the country that is the best place on Earth – at least I believe that.” Ambros told Tusk that he was “honoured” to receive the news. Speaking later to the Polish Press Agency (PAP), the scientist said that he was “very grateful to Prime Minister Tusk and to Poles for awarding me Polish citizenship”. “I hope that my having dual citizenship – American and Polish – will honour both my father’s Polish roots and the opportunities that America created for him and me.” Ambros, who is already chair of the scientific council of the International Institute of Molecular Mechanisms and Machines of the Polish Academy of Sciences, also expressed hope that there would be “additional opportunities to help improve the international position of Polish science, especially in the field of biomedical research”. Ambros’s father, Longin, was born in 1923 in what was then the village of Dordziszki in Poland but which, after postwar border changes, is now Dordishki in Belarus. He later attended high school in the city then known as Wilno, and which was part of Poland, but is now Vilnius, the capital of Lithuania. During World War Two, Longin Ambros was deported to Nazi Germany and used as forced labour, before being liberated at the end of the war by American forces, who then employed him as an interpreter. In 1946, Longin emigrated to the United States, where he settled on a farm and raised a family. Victor was one of eight children and the first scientist in the family. American Nobel laureate Victor Ambros has announced that he is seeking Polish citizenship in order to honour his family “and all those who fought and survived so that I could exist today” He also wants to contribute to the development of science in Poland https://t.co/70uXhh1fj6 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 10, 2026 There has been a growing trend in recent years for foreigners to seek Polish citizenship. There are three paths for those wishing to obtain it. The first is through Polish ancestry. People with a Polish parent, grandparent or great-grandparent who lived in Poland after 1920 and never lost their citizenship can apply to have their status as a Polish citizen officially confirmed. Last year, Hollywood star Jesse Eisenberg, whose ancestors were Jews from Poland, received Polish citizenship, describing it as the “honour of a lifetime”. His Oscar-nominated 2024 film A Real Pain was set entirely in Poland. Eisenberg is currently starring in a new state campaign promoting Poland abroad, along with football star Robert Lewandowski and supermodel Anja Rubik. Poland has launched a new advertising campaign to attract tourists from Europe and the US. The first video, under the slogan "Poland. More than you expected", features footballer Robert Lewandowski, Hollywood star Jesse Eisenberg and supermodel Anja Rubik https://t.co/3jtqyUWQyy — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 19, 2026 The second route is for foreign residents in Poland who meet requirements relating to their length of residency, language skills and personal situation to apply to the governor of the province where they live. The third is by applying directly to the president, who has discretion to grant citizenship without any specific legal requirements being met. Applicants are expected to show personal ties to Poland and explain their reasons for seeking citizenship. One recent example was Russian-born speed skater Vladimir Semirunniy, who fled to Poland and was granted citizenship last year by President Karol Nawrocki. This allowed him to win a medal for Poland at the recent Winter Olympics. Poland granted citizenship to a record 19,135 foreigners in 2025, up 17% from the previous year and almost five times higher than a decade ago. Over half of recipients were Ukrainians, followed by Belarusians, Russians, Vietnamese and Turks https://t.co/FoyWd5UPJx — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 15, 2026 Last year, Poland granted citizenship – either through provincial governors or directly from the president – to a record 19,135 people. Over half of the recipients were Ukrainians, who constuitute by far Poland’s largest immigrant group. In 2024, the figure stood at 16,342. However, the Polish government is currently working on measures to make it tougher for foreigners to obtain citizenship, including increasing the minimum residency period and requiring applicants to take a test proving they are integrated. They would also have to sign a declaration of loyalty. Applications to confirm citizenship through descent have also risen sharply, in particular among Israelis, many of whom have roots in Poland. Last month, rising US sprint star Sam Blaskowski announced that he was also applying for Polish citizenship with a view to representing and winning medals for the land of his ancestors on the international stage. Rising US sprint star Sam Blaskowski has announced he wants to represent Poland, the country of his ancestors. His best 100m time of 9.89 seconds is the 9th fastest in the world this year and over a tenth of a second faster than Poland's national record https://t.co/S2tZsiSAhh — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 24, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Polish ruling party MP stripped of immunity and detained at request of EU prosecutors
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! An MP from Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s party, the centrist Civic Coalition (KO), has been detained by anti-corruption officers after parliament approved a request from the European Public Prosecutor’s Office to lift his legal immunity. It is the first time in history that the EPPO, which Tusk’s government signed Poland up to in one of its first actions after taking power in 2023, has taken action against a sitting Polish member of parliament. Poseł Wojciech Król został doprowadzony do biura Prokuratury Europejskiej w Katowicach. Śledczy zamierzają przedstawić mu zarzuty dotyczące przestępstw korupcyjnych i przesłuchać.https://t.co/AknEyHwIHL — PolsatNews.pl (@PolsatNewsPL) September 18, 2026 The MP in question, Wojciech Król, is accused of trading in influence in relation to the EU-funded modernisation of tram infrastructure in the Upper Silesian-Zagłębie Metropolis, an agglomeration of municipalities in southern Poland that includes Katowice, a major city. The EPPO says it has found evidence of “a system of corruption” that involved inflated costs and fictitious work on the project, for which 1.9 billion zloty (€435 million) of EU funds were designated. Its investigation found that, as part of this system, a member of parliament – not named directly by the EPPO but who is known to be Król – had “accepted financial benefits in exchange for arranging favourable outcomes for several companies”. Polish news website Interia reports that the EPPO suspects Król of accepting over 1.4 million zloty in bribes. The MP has publicly denied the accusation. Eleven other people have already been charged in relation to the alleged corruption scheme, reports broadcaster TVN. They include senior executives from a municipal tram operator. In May, the EPPO submitted a first request to Poland’s parliament to lift the immunity that Król enjoys as an MP and bring him into detention. At the time, Król was deputy head of KO’s caucus in the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, but he has since lost that position and been suspended from the caucus entirely. In late July, a majority of MPs in the Sejm approved the lifting of Król’s immunity to face prosecution. However, at the same time, they rejected the EPPO’s request for Król to be taken into detention, after MPs from the ruling coalition voted against it. The same week those votes took place, the EPPO issued a second request, outlining additional evidence and suspicions regarding Król’s alleged involvement in corruption. On Thursday this week, the Sejm voted almost unanimously in favour of that second request, again lifting Król’s immunity to face further charges but this time also approving his detention. A few hours later, officers from Poland’s Central Anti-Corruption Bureau (CBA) arrested Król in Warsaw. Po południu decyzja Sejmu, wieczorem działanie służb. Tak działa państwo prawa, w którym legitymacja poselska i barwy partyjne nie dają żadnego immunitetu od odpowiedzialności karnej. Nie ma świętych krów! https://t.co/7DpmV7q4RF — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) September 17, 2026 “This is how a state of law operates, in which parliamentary credentials and party colors offer no immunity from criminal liability,” wrote justice minister Waldemar Żurek on social media. “There are no sacred cows.” A Polish prosecutor delegated to the EPPO, Agnieszka Marcińczyk, told the Sejm this week that bringing Król into detention was necessary to prevent potential obstruction of the proceedings against him. She also said that Król had not complied with some of the preventative measures imposed on him after his immunity was previously stripped, including failing to post the required bail and to appear at a police station as part of his supervision order, reports news website Wirtualna Polska. Oświadczenie ws. drugiego wniosku o uchylenie immunitetu Uprzejmie informuję, że zapał do mojego aresztowania skończy się w grudniu. Do tego czasu będą składane kolejne wnioski o uchylenie immunitetu oraz zgodę na zatrzymanie i aresztowanie. Przypomnę, że pierwszy wniosek o… — Wojciech Król (@wojciech_krol) September 11, 2026 The EPPO was established in 2021 in order to investigate and prosecute crimes against the financial interests of the EU. However, under Poland’s former national-conservative, eurosceptic Law and Justice (PiS) government, the country initially did not join the body. After Tusk’s more liberal, pro-EU coalition replaced PiS in December 2023, one of its very first actions was to begin the process of joining the EPPO, which was completed in March 2024. World.title: Russia planning “accidental” strikes on eastern NATO states, warns Poland

Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, has warned that, according to intelligence sources, Russia is planning drone and missile strikes on eastern NATO countries, which it would present as accidental. Addressing parliament on Thursday, the prime minister said that “citizens absolutely have the right to know what scenario can be expected based on the information available today”. Intelligence from allies, including the United States and Ukraine, indicates that various scenarios are possible, but one is most likely, said Tusk. Over the next few months, Russia’s recent tactic of using jet-powered drones to strike targets in Ukraine near the Polish border will likely continue, said Tusk, as well as attacks on Ukrainian economic and logistics infrastructure, such as railways. “Russia’s plan, according to intelligence, also includes hybrid drone and missile strikes against countries supporting Ukraine, including Poland,” continued Tusk. “These possibilities have been discussed for some time. This information is now very consistent and, unfortunately, convincing.” 💬 Premier @donaldtusk ⤵️ Istnieje realne ryzyko, że na teren któregoś z państw NATO mogą wlatywać drony, dokonywać zniszczeń. I te „przypadkowe” według Rosji uderzenia mogą się powtarzać. pic.twitter.com/bScJBjQQF1 — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) September 17, 2026 The aim, said Tusk, would be to “weaken NATO member states’ motivation to apply appropriate NATO regulations in the event of aggression against any member state”. Russia’s “official narrative will be that this is an accident and there’s no reason for anyone to consider any kind of NATO response”. The prime minister said that the incidents could be similar in nature to the night one year ago when around 20 Russian drones entered Polish airspace across its eastern border. “These ‘random’ attacks could repeat themselves, becoming an increasingly glaring illustration of NATO’s helplessness, as conceived by the Russians,” said Tusk. In response to last year’s drone incursions, Polish and allied NATO jets shot down some of the drones. Poland then invoked article 4 of the NATO treaty and received increased air-defence support from a number of NATO allies. Russia has recently stepped up its attacks on western Ukraine, including a number of strikes close to the Polish border. Tusk noted that, in response, Poland has begun reinforcing security at border crossings, including installing 28 new bomb shelters and expanding air-defence systems The prime minister also confirmed that he would be travelling to Kyiv later on Thursday. He planned, among other things, to discuss with President Volodymy Zelensky how they would cooperate on air defence and utilise Ukraine’s experience and capabilities in this area. On the night of Thursday to Friday, the latest round of Russia attacks on Ukraine prompted Poland to scramble aircraft, activate air-defence systems, and close parts of its eastern airspace – actions that have recently become increasingly common. A drone has struck a passenger train travelling between Kyiv and Warsaw, around 2 km from the Polish border, amid the latest mass Russian attacks on Ukraine. Separately, a truck around 800 metres from a border crossing with Poland was also hit last night https://t.co/ZbfE2iDLOk — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 13, 2026 In his remarks to parliament, Tusk also noted that “announcements by some global leaders that Russia is ready for a kind of ceasefire…have not come true”. He then mentioned President Donald Trump directly. “Since the president of the United States announced that Russia had assured him it was ready to honour such a partial ceasefire with Ukraine, numerous attacks have occurred, including on energy infrastructure in Ukraine,” said Tusk. “The information we have received regarding the course of consultations and talks at various levels between the US and Russia is quite clear: Russia is not ready for any serious talks on a ceasefire, let alone peace, without Ukraine’s de facto surrender.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. Warsaw has launched special joint patrols by its municipal police and roads authority to check whether electric scooters are being parked legally and in keeping with rules introduced under a recent agreement with rental firms. According to the city’s mayor, Rafał Trzaskowski, more than 140 improperly parked scooters have been towed away within just a few days. Under the agreement, their operators now face potential fines. Nie ma miejsca dla hulajnóg tam, gdzie nie ich miejsce. Zdecydowałem o uruchomieniu specjalnych patroli Straży Miejskiej i ZDM. W ciągu ostatnich kliku dni dzięki ich pracy odholowanych zostało ponad 140 nieprawidłowo zaparkowanych hulajnóg elektrycznych. Taką możliwość daje… pic.twitter.com/U5fd7YDN8U — Rafał Trzaskowski (@trzaskowski_) September 16, 2026 “There’s no place for scooters where they don’t belong,” Trzaskowski said in a social media post announcing the patrols. “There are specific provisions, agreements and legal regulations – and action is being taken. No leniency.” An agreement reached between the city and three scooter operators – Bolt, Dott and Lime – in May expanded the number of streets where the vehicles are subject to a maximum speed of 12 km/h (7.5 mph) and increased the areas where their use is entirely prohibited. It also introduced measures to prevent scooters from being left in places where parking is illegal. Riding and parking electric scooters was banned in several areas of Warsaw, including popular tourist attractions such as the Old Town, Krasiński Garden and Łazienki Park. Trzaskowski added that the city has now expanded the list of areas covered by the ban, as permitted under the agreement. He did not, however, provide the new list. The agreement requires operators to programme their scooters so they cannot enter areas where riding is prohibited or be parked in places where parking is illegal, including on bridges, in tunnels, in residential areas and on streets where the pavement is too narrow to allow legal parking. Operators can be fined when scooters are left in violation of the rules. The city says that, despite electric scooters accounting for just under 8% of all traffic on cycle lanes, their riders were found to be responsible for 39 of the 66 accidents recorded on cycle lanes last year. Those accidents resulted in 73 injuries. Concerns over the safety of electric scooters have also prompted the national government to introduce stricter rules, including a nationwide requirement for children under 16 to wear a bicycle helmet when riding bicycles and electric scooters, which took effect in early June. Poland first introduced regulations governing electric scooters in 2021, formally setting out rules for their use. Under those rules, scooters are generally required to use cycle lanes where available, with their maximum speed capped at 20 km/h. The Polish government has moved to introduce new rules on the use of electric scooters. E-scooters, which are currently unregulated in Poland, have been blamed for hundreds of accidents annually, with half of victims being pedestrians hit by riders https://t.co/TcrfPQocfr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 3, 2021 Under the nationwide legislation, electric scooters must be parked parallel to the outer edge of the pavement, and municipal authorities have the power to penalise those responsible for improper parking – a provision that primarily affects rental companies. A year after the legislation was introduced, after the first report on e-scooter-related accidents showed that they had caused hundreds of injuries and three deaths in 2021, Poland’s police launched a campaign publicising the new rules. At national level, infrastructure minister Dariusz Klimczak has announced further restrictions the government is working on, including a new law requiring scooters to be collected and left only in specially designated zones. The police have launched a campaign on the legal requirements for using e-scooters, including a warning that riding or parking them on pavements can be illegal. In 2022, accidents involving e-scooters in Poland resulted in 421 injuries and three deaths https://t.co/dMOBiNUBNG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 15, 2023 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Polish right-wing opposition MPs call for Independence Day march in Ukrainian city of Lviv

A group of MPs from Poland’s main right-wing and far-right opposition parties have jointly called on the government to organise a march on Polish Independence Day in the Ukrainian city of Lviv, which was historically part of Poland. The idea has been firmly rejected by figures from the ruling coalition, who have called it “gross stupidity” and “madness”. It is also unclear to what extent the leadership of the opposition parties support the proposal. Pomysł zorganizowania "polskiego Marszu Niepodległości ulicami Lwowa" połączył polityków całej prawicy: PiS, Konfederacji, Rozwoju Plus i Konfederacji Korony Polskiej. Odsłaniamy kulisy. Pisze @patrykmichalski, autor programu #NewsMichalskiego ⤵️ 🔵 https://t.co/9L0M5lN0zY pic.twitter.com/1W3YxHdXHT — TVN24+ (@tvn24plus) September 15, 2026 The suggestion was made in a so-called parliamentary interpellation – through which MPs can ask questions and make suggestions to the government – submitted this month and signed by a group of 21 opposition MPs. They called on the government to do more to support the ethnic Polish community that still lives in Lviv, arguing that neither the Polish nor the Ukrainian state does enough to help them preserve and celebrate their identity. By contrast, argued the signatories, Polish state entities provide funding for Ukrainian organisations and events in Poland, including celebrations of Ukrainian Independence Day on 24 August. As such, they called upon the government to “organise official celebrations of [Polish] Independence Day in Lviv, including a Polish Independence March through the streets of the city” on 11 November. This would be “a concrete sign of remembrance and solidarity with Poles living in Ukraine”. Among the 21 signatories, 14 are from the caucus of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s ruling party between 2015 and 2023 and now the largest opposition group. A further three are from Confederation (Konfederacja), a far-right opposition group. One is from Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), a group that broke away from PiS earlier this year; another is from Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), a radical-right, pro-Russian party led by Grzegorz Braun. The final two are an independent, Janusz Kowalski, who recently quit PiS; and Jarosław Sachajko, who was elected in 2023 on the PiS party list but is part of the small Direct Democracy (Demokracja Bezpośrednia) group associated with Paweł Kukiz, a right-wing, anti-establishment figure. Interpelacja do Prezesa Rady Ministrów w sprawie zorganizowania 11 listopada polskiego Marszu Niepodległości ulicami Lwowa 11 listopada Rzeczpospolita Polska obchodzi Narodowe Święto Niepodległości. Jest to święto wszystkich Polaków, również tych, którzy mieszkają poza granicami… pic.twitter.com/7m6yUg1iKZ — Dariusz Matecki (@DariuszMatecki) August 25, 2026 It remains unclear to what extent the MPs have the backing of their parties in calling for the government to organise an Independence Day march in Lviv. Indeed, when Krzysztof Bosak, one of the leaders of Confederation, was asked about the idea on Wednesday, he appeared to know very little about it. Speaking to broadcaster RMF, Bosak said that he had first heard about the proposal on Tuesday and that, after looking into it, he said it appeared to be a “stunt”, and one that he felt was “unnecessary”. “I think the point is to draw attention to the fact that Polish institutions are participating in the celebration of Ukraine’s Independence Day in Warsaw, and that there should be some symmetry,” said Bosak. However, he added that he felt many people would not understand this intention. “The appeal should be directed at Ukrainian institutions, not the Polish foreign ministry,” he said, adding that the MPs who came up with the idea should better explain it. “Frankly, I have more serious matters to attend to.” Czy przemarsz Polaków ulicami Lwowa z okazji Dnia Niepodległości to dobry pomysł? Zdaniem @krzysztofbosak niepotrzebny, a traktować go należy w kategorii happeningu. Ale jeśli się trzymać zasady wzajemności, to już lepiej organizować coś podobnego… w Kijowie. pic.twitter.com/PxdqNKBlCC — Ekonomat (@ekonomat_pl) September 16, 2026 Throughout much of history, Lviv (known in Polish as Lwów) was part of the Polish state, most recently during the period between the First and Second World Wars. However, amid postwar border movements, it became part of Ukraine along with some other former Polish territories. Many in Poland still feel a sense of attachment to the former Polish “borderlands” (kresy) that are now located in Ukraine, Lithuania and Belarus, and which are still home to at least hundreds of thousands of ethnic Poles (though the exact number is a matter of dispute). In Lviv itself, the most recent Ukrainian national census, taken in 2001, showed just under 10,000 people declaring Polish ethnicity in the city (around 1% of the population), though some estimates put the figure higher. Poland's culture minister has condemned Russia's attacks on the historic centre of Lviv in Ukraine, a UNESCO World Heritage site. She noted that Lviv, which was once part of Poland, represents the "shared history of Ukraine, Poland and all of Europe" https://t.co/qPhqXMAZ9r — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 25, 2026 Last year, Confederation’s other main leader, Sławomir Mentzen, clashed with the mayor of Lviv, Andriy Sadovyi, after visiting the city and criticising a monument commemorating nationalist leader Stepan Bandera, a figure seen as a hero by many in Ukraine but regarded as a war criminal in Poland. Followers of Bandera were responsible for the so-called Volhynia massacres during World War Two, in which Ukrainian nationalists massacred around 100,000 ethnic Polish civilians. Poland regards the killings as a genocide but Ukraine rejects that label. The issue has caused renewed tension this year after President Volodymyr Zelensky named a Ukrainian military unit after the “heroes of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army”, which led the massacres. Any Polish attempt at a state-backed Independence Day march in Ukraine would likely stir further controversy. A leading candidate in Poland’s presidential election has clashed with a Ukrainian mayor after visiting his city and criticising the presence of a monument to Stepan Bandera, who is seen as a hero by many in Ukraine but regarded as a war criminal in Poland https://t.co/nA9JzMmBcg — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 26, 2025 Although the Polish government has not yet officially responded to the opposition MPs’ interpellation, a number of figures from the ruling coalition – which ranges from left to centre right – criticised the idea on Wednesday. Deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk called it “gross stupidity” to think of organising such a march in Ukraine, especially at a time of war. He asked how Poles would feel if Germany tried to organise a similar march in Poland (some of whose current territory was part of Germany before World War Two). Both Dariusz Wieczorek, an MP from The Left (Lewica), and Marek Biernacki from the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL) told broadcaster TVN that the idea was “madness”. Próba zorganizowania we Lwowie prawicowej prowokacji z udziałem PiS-u, Rozwój Plus i Brauna to jednoznaczne działanie na rzecz Rosji i przeciwko polskiej racji stanu. — Witold Zembaczyński🇵🇱 (@WZembaczynski) September 16, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: European Parliament strips Polish far-right leader of immunity to face Holocaust denial charge
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The European Parliament has again stripped Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun of legal immunity to face charges in his homeland of denying Nazi crimes, an offence that carries a potential prison sentence of up to three years. The decision marks the sixth time that the European Parliament has lifted Braun’s immunity, and the second time for charges of Holocaust denial. Braun is already on trial in Poland for an attack on a Jewish religious celebration in parliament and is facing a number of other legal cases. Parlament Europejski w głosowaniu w Strasburgu uchylił immunitet europosła Grzegorza Brauna. Sprawa dotyczy negowania przez niego Holokaustu. Więcej: https://t.co/rB3UPUiS8o pic.twitter.com/icRLEqsWmF — Gazeta.pl (@gazetapl_news) September 15, 2026 In a vote on Tuesday, a majority of MEPs voted in favour of a request, submitted in February by Poland’s justice minister, Waldemar Żurek, to lift the immunity enjoyed by Braun as an MEP. He has sat in the European Parliament since being elected in 2024. In his request, Żurek said that Polish prosecutors wish to charge Braun in relation to “denial of genocide crimes committed by functionaries of the Third Reich in the Auschwitz-Birkenau concentration camp and the Lublin concentration camp (Majdanek)”. Poland’s Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), a state historical body that has prosecutorial power, also revealed that the accusation relates to the use of gas chambers at those two camps. Neither the IPN nor Żurek confirmed at the time what specific words Braun had said that prompted the planned charges against him. However, the IPN noted that they had come at a live event broadcast online on 27 September 2025. On that date, Braun took part in a discussion with Jan Żaryn, a right-wing historian and former senator for the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party, titled “The Polish Underground State and the Jewish Issue”. A recording of the event is still available online. During his remarks, Braun referred to the “fake gas chambers of Majdanek and Auschwitz”, calling them “a dark, monstrous fantasy that has no satisfactory historical or academic support”. He suggested that the idea of the gas chambers had been invented as part of “propaganda and black PR operations conducted by the Soviet and Anglo-Saxon security services during World War Two”, and that the false claim continues to be exploited by Jews today. The European Parliament has again voted to strip Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun of immunity to face further charges for Holocaust denial as well as various antisemitic, anti-Ukrainian and anti-LGBT incidents during last year's presidential campaign https://t.co/4EHVEuSDnM — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 26, 2026 In actual fact, historians estimate that around 900,000 people were killed in the gas chambers at Auschwitz. The vast majority were Jews, but victims also included Roma, Soviet prisoners of war, and ethnic Poles. Meanwhile, gas chambers at Majdanek were used to kill tens of thousands, again mainly Jews. Today, the ashes of the camp’s cremated victims are preserved in a memorial at the site of the former camp. Braun, who has a long history of promoting antisemitic conspiracy theories, has repeatedly sought to cast doubt on the veracity of Nazi crimes against Jews. Last month, he was charged with denying Nazi crimes in a separate case over earlier comments in which he called Auschwitz’s gas chambers “fake”. Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun has been charged with denying Nazi crimes, a criminal offence in Poland that carries a prison sentence of up to three years, for statements he made suggesting that the gas chambers at Auschwitz are "fake" https://t.co/PCssZt5eXD — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 25, 2026 In December, Braun went on trial over a separate set of charges relating to four other incidents, including his attack on a celebration of the Jewish festival of Hanukkah in parliament in December 2023 and his disruption of a lecture by a Holocaust scholar. “I am standing before this court because I dared to defend myself against oppression and the ritual manifestation of Jewish supremacy,” declared Braun at the start of the trial, which remains ongoing. Braun is also facing various legal cases relating to his anti-Ukrainian and anti-LGBT actions. World.title: Prague Unveils Future Metro Stations in Nusle and Náměstí Míru
World.content:
Prague’s future Metro Line D has taken another step toward becoming a reality, with new preliminary designs released for two stations planned along the route.

The Prague Public Transit Company (DPP) has presented renderings of the future Náměstí Míru interchange and Nusle station, offering an early look at how the new metro line could change the city’s underground transport network.

The images do not represent the final appearance of either station. DPP plans to select the architectural solutions through a two-stage competition, which will focus on the design of the interiors and the public spaces around the stations.

DPP intends to organise the competition in two stages, using a workshop format. The winning designs are expected to be selected within 18 months of signing the contract with the competition organiser. Preparations for that contract are currently underway.

Náměstí Míru station will connect Metro Lines A and D

The future Náměstí Míru station is planned beneath Sázavská Street, approximately 40 metres underground. It will be built using underground mining methods and will feature a single-vault design with an island platform.

The new station will be located above the existing Line A station, creating a new interchange between the two metro lines.

The design includes two vestibules equipped with escalators and a third access point with an elevator. The renderings show the planned exits towards Vinohradská, Francouzská, and Sázavská streets, as well as an elevator entrance on Korunní Street.

Metroprojekt has also presented a possible design for the outlet of a ventilation shaft in Riegrovy Sady. The structure will form part of the station’s technical infrastructure, although its final appearance may change following the architectural competition.

New Nusle station will serve Náměstí Bratří Synků

The second station featured in the new designs is the future Nusle station, which was previously known as Náměstí Bratří Synků.

The station will be built using cut-and-cover construction methods, with its island platform located approximately 13 metres below ground level. It is planned between Náměstí Bratří Synků and Otakarova Street.

Plans also include an underground parking garage for local residents above the station.

The new renderings show the proposed station entrances on Náměstí Bratří Synků, the northern vestibule beneath Otakarova Street, and the planned completion of the existing urban block.

When will Prague’s Metro Line D open?

Construction of Metro Line D began in 2022 with the section between Pankrác and Ryšánka. Work on the following section, extending towards Nové Dvory, began in June 2026.

The Pankrác–Nové Dvory section is planned to be the first part of the new metro line to open to passengers. DPP currently expects the section to enter service in the second half of 2032.

World.title: Two New Squares and a Tower Planned Around Holešovice Station
World.content:
The area around Prague’s Nádraží Holešovice station is set for a major redevelopment after the international architectural competition for the site was won by Czech studio Chybík + Krištof.

The winning proposal envisions turning the current transport hub and surrounding brownfield into a new urban district, with two public squares, improved connections between public transport services and a new high-rise building designed to become a landmark.



The redevelopment covers roughly eight hectares around the station. Its aim is not only to add new buildings, but also to reorganise one of Prague’s important transport nodes and connect it more closely with the surrounding neighbourhood.

The competition jury selected the proposal by Chybík + Krištof as the winning design.

From transport hub to urban district

Nádraží Holešovice is currently one of Prague’s major transport interchanges, but much of the surrounding area has traditionally been used primarily for transport and other infrastructure.

The redevelopment is intended to change that. Alongside new construction, the project places emphasis on making transfers between different modes of public transport easier and fully accessible.

The project forms part of the wider Nové Holešovice development, which brings together the Prague Public Transit Company and private investors.

CPI Property, EP Real Estate, Penta Real Estate and AKIPIA are among the companies involved. The City of Prague and Prague 7 municipal district are also participating in the project.

World.title: ČokoFest to Bring Three Days of Chocolate to Galerie Harfa
World.content:
Chocolate lovers will have plenty to discover in Prague this October as ČokoFest 2026 returns to Galerie Harfa for three days of tastings, workshops, competitions and sweet treats.

The festival will take place from October 16 to 18, 2026, at the shopping center in Prague 9. Admission is free.



Now in its 14th year, ČokoFest brings together Czech and international producers, including established chocolatiers and smaller makers.

Visitors will be able to sample and buy a wide selection of chocolates and confectionery, including handmade and bean-to-bar products, pralines, cakes, cookies and macarons.

The festival will also feature a range of less conventional chocolate and sweet specialties. Among the offerings will be a chocolate fountain, chocolate kebabs, chocolate-covered fruit, as well as chocolate-infused wine and beer. Other products on sale will include jams, liqueurs, syrups, dried fruits, honey products, coffee and tea.

Exhibitors from several European countries will join Czech producers, giving visitors the opportunity to discover different chocolate styles and specialties while shopping at international sales stalls.

ČokoFest will also feature a program of activities for both adults and children. Visitors can take part in tastings, competitions and creative workshops, while children can enjoy a dedicated zone and entertainment from performers dressed as popular children’s characters.

Cooking demonstrations will be another part of the program, with chefs from local restaurants sharing their experience and showing visitors how to prepare various sweet treats. Some workshops will also focus on chocolate-making techniques that can be tried at home.

The festival is designed as a family-friendly event, with activities taking place throughout the three days. In addition to tasting and shopping, visitors can watch pastry chefs at work, take part in competitions and learn more about the production and preparation of chocolate and other confectionery.

Opening hours:

Friday, October 16: 2:00–6:00 p.m.

Saturday, October 17: 10:00 a.m.–6:30 p.m.

Sunday, October 18: 10:00 a.m.–5:00 p.m.

World.title: Poznej Vltavu Festival Returns to Prague on September 28
World.content:
The second edition of the Poznej Vltavu (Get to Know the Vltava) festival will take place across Prague on September 28, 2026.

For one day, the banks of the Vltava will host a programme exploring the river from a variety of perspectives.

The festival will feature workshops, exhibitions, sports activities, boat trips, and tours of places that are not normally open to the public.



Prague’s riverfront embankments and other locations along the Vltava will offer activities for children, adults, and seniors.

The festival aims to highlight the Vltava as a natural part of Prague’s urban environment and an important ecological feature, while giving visitors the opportunity to spend a day exploring the river and its surroundings.

Experts from a range of fields will discuss the Vltava in its broader context and offer insights into lesser-known aspects of the river.

This year’s programme will involve organisations including the Prague Institute of Planning and Development, Prague City Tourism, the Prague City Gallery, the Vltava River Authority, Prague Waterworks and Sewerage Company, the Prague Water Management Company, ROPID, Prague City Forests, the Nature Conservation Agency of the Czech Republic, and many others.

The festival area will extend farther along the Vltava this year, reaching Žluté lázně and the new Dvorecký Bridge, which has quickly become a popular destination for Prague residents since opening.

Most events will be free to attend, although some activities will require advance registration due to limited capacity.

More information is available on the festival’s Facebook event.

World.title: Red Arrows to Fly Over Charles Bridge This Friday
World.content:
Prague will hear the roar of Royal Air Force jets on Friday, September 18, when the Red Arrows aerobatic team stages a flypast over the city.

Ten BAE Hawk T1 aircraft from the British RAF team are scheduled to pass over the Charles Bridge at around 2:00 PM. The jets will leave smoke trails in the colours of the Czech flag during the display.



The formation is expected to approach Prague from the north before reaching the area around Václav Havel Airport. The aircraft will then form an arrow-shaped formation and fly around the western and southern parts of the capital before turning north along the Vltava.

The jets are expected to fly at an altitude of roughly 300 metres above the ground. The engines will be clearly audible across parts of the city, although the flypast itself will last only a short time.

After passing through central Prague, the formation will turn northeast and continue toward Ostrava. The city is hosting NATO Days, one of the Czech Republic’s largest military and security events, this weekend.

The timetable and route could still change because of weather or other air traffic in the Prague area. A similar Red Arrows flypast was held in Prague last September, but poor weather delayed the aircraft by more than an hour.

The flypast is being held in connection with Czech Air Force Day, which is observed on September 15.

The Red Arrows are the official aerobatic display team of the Royal Air Force and regularly perform at air shows and military events in Britain and abroad.

World.title: Groovy Market Fest Returns to Riegrovy Sady on October 3
World.content:
Prague’s Groovy Market Fest will return to Riegrovy Sady on Saturday, October 3, bringing together food, independent brands, design and live music for its third edition.

The one-day event will take place at Energy Pub from noon until 10 p.m.

Following two editions held during the summer, the organizers are extending the concept into the autumn, with visitors able to browse local products, eat street food and listen to live music and DJs throughout the day.



The market is organised around three main areas. The Food Garden will focus on gastronomy and street food from local businesses, while Palm Street will feature bakeries, artisanal products and other local goods. The Design Zone will bring together fashion, design and products from independent Czech brands.

Live performances and DJ sets will run from the afternoon into the evening, providing the musical programme alongside the market stalls.

Marek Novák, founder of Groovy Market Fest, said the first two editions helped the team establish the format and identify what visitors respond to.

“After two editions, we know exactly what works at Groovy Market Fest: high-quality local brands, good food, and an atmosphere that keeps people coming back,” Novák said. “This third edition is an opportunity for us to show that Groovy isn’t just a summer event, but a festival that holds a firm place in Prague all year round.”

Visitors can buy tickets for either of the two five-hour sessions. The first runs from 12 p.m. to 5 p.m., followed by a second session from 5:30 p.m. to 10 p.m.

A ticket for one session costs 100 CZK, while an all-day ticket covering both sessions is available for 190 CZK. Tickets are sold through GoOut.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Groovy Market Fest (@groovymarketfest)

From Barcelona street food to a Prague market

Groovy Market Fest was founded by Marek Novák and Veronika Kracíková, a couple with experience in Prague’s food scene and Barcelona’s street-food sector.

One of their main inspirations was Barcelona’s Palo Alto Market, an urban market known for combining food, design, music and independent creative businesses.

World.title: Prague Run Day to Bring Six Races to Riegrovy Sady on September 19
World.content:
On September 19, runners of all levels can take part in a new running event combining track and park races in one of Prague’s best-known green spaces.

There are six different races to choose from, so whether you’re looking for a serious challenge or just want to get out and run, there’s an option for you.



Six races to choose from

The programme includes six races, ranging from a short family run to a one-hour challenge.

The day will begin with the 800m Family Run, designed for young runners and their accompanying adults. There will also be an 800m race on the athletic track, offering participants the opportunity to compete over a short distance in a traditional track setting.

For those looking for a longer challenge, the 1 Mile race will take place on the athletic oval. The organisers describe it as a special opportunity to race over the classic distance, with participation limited to a maximum of 30 runners.

The 5km Solo Run will offer a more familiar challenge for runners of different experience levels. It is followed by the 4x3km Relay, a team race in which four runners each complete two 1.5km laps.

The final event of the day will be the Golden Hour Race, a one-hour running challenge taking place during the golden hour.

The event will be based at the Sokol Vinohrady athletic oval, which will serve as the main hub for the day.

Find all race distances, times and registration details at praguerunday.cz

📍 Riegrovy Sady Athletic Oval

📅 Saturday, September 19

🏃 6 races for different levels

🏅 Medal for every participant

World.title: Prague Is Turning a Historic Factory Chimney Into an Observation Deck
World.content:
A glass elevator will carry visitors through the preserved chimney of a former distillery before emerging above its rim to reveal views of the city.

Inside the developing Lihovar district in Smíchov, a historic factory chimney is being transformed into a viewing platform, with visitors set to travel through the structure in a panoramic glass elevator.



The chimney, which stands approximately 50 meters tall, is part of the former Zlíchov distillery. Rather than demolishing the industrial landmark, developers have incorporated it into the redevelopment of the site.

The project is being developed by Trigema, which is building the new Lihovar district on the former distillery grounds.

The elevator itself is one of the project’s most unusual features. Once it reaches the top of the chimney, the cabin will lift a special cap weighing approximately 500 kilograms, allowing it to rise above the chimney’s opening.

The glass cabin will then serve as an observation deck, offering a 360-degree view of Prague.

From industrial site to new Prague district

The Lihovar development is being built on the site of the former Zlíchov distillery in Prague 5. The redevelopment includes new buildings alongside the preservation of selected elements of the original industrial complex.

The factory chimney is among the structures being retained. Another is the historic former brewhouse, which is planned for cultural use.

The opening date for the observation deck has not been announced.

World.title: Hungary reveals new diesel subsidy details: Who gets HUF 20,000 and when will payments begin?
World.content:
Hungary has published the detailed rules for its HUF 20,000 diesel fuel subsidy, clarifying who qualifies, how payments will be made and when motorists can expect their money. The new regulation also sets out the conditions for people who acquired eligible vehicles during the year.

As we previously reported , Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced the diesel support scheme earlier this month to help motorists cope with rising fuel prices. The detailed rules, published in the Hungarian Official Gazette on Friday evening, now confirm the exact payment dates, eligibility criteria and how the money will be distributed.

The Hungarian State Treasury will distribute the subsidy in instalments, with payments continuing until December. The measure is intended to ease the financial burden on diesel motorists following a significant rise in fuel prices this year.

When will the diesel subsidy arrive?

Under the newly published rules, the HUF 20,000 subsidy will generally be paid in four instalments.

The government has set the following payment dates:

30 September 2026

30 October 2026

13 November 2026

7 December 2026

Motorists who already met the ownership or registered keeper requirements on 1 January 2026 are scheduled to receive their first HUF 5,000 payment on 30 September.

However, those who acquired a qualifying vehicle or became its registered keeper after the beginning of the year will receive their first payment on 30 October. The scheme provides for a total of HUF 20,000 in support per eligible person in 2026.

The new schedule brings forward the first payment for existing eligible motorists compared with the October start initially announced by the government.

If you missed it: Social workers protest for pay rise in Budapest, Péter Magyar meets the demonstrators

Who is eligible for the HUF 20,000 support?

The subsidy is available to private individuals who operate or own a passenger car powered exclusively by diesel, with a maximum engine output of 110 kilowatts, approximately 150 horsepower.

Eligibility is generally determined using vehicle registration records from 1 January 2026. However, the new decree also covers motorists who acquired a qualifying vehicle later in the year, provided they meet the requirements when the regulation enters into force.

Importantly, the HUF 20,000 subsidy is available per person, not per vehicle. Someone who owns or operates several eligible diesel cars can receive support for only one of them.

Where a vehicle has multiple owners or registered keepers, the payment goes to the person named on its registration certificate.

Do motorists need to apply for the subsidy?

Eligible drivers will not normally have to submit a separate application. Hungary’s National Tax and Customs Administration (NAV) will determine eligibility using vehicle registration records. The Hungarian State Treasury will then distribute the funds automatically.

Payments will primarily be transferred to the bank account recorded by the tax authority. Motorists without a suitable bank account will receive the subsidy by post, using the correspondence address held by NAV. The support is tax-free and will be financed from the central budget.

Why is Hungary providing diesel support?

The government originally announced the scheme on 11 September, saying that it could benefit nearly one million motorists.

Rather than reintroducing the previous regulated fuel price, the government opted for direct financial assistance. Magyar argued that the measure should target drivers particularly affected by rising diesel prices, rather than subsidising the fuel costs of owners of expensive, high-performance vehicles.

The prime minister previously said that restoring Hungary’s former protected fuel prices could cost the state budget between HUF 50 billion and HUF 100 billion per month. Hungarian oil and gas company MOL has also warned that reintroducing a price cap could discourage fuel imports and lead to supply shortages.

World.title: PM Magyar responds after callers suggest sniper attack and chaining him up on Hungarian TV
World.content:
Prime Minister Péter Magyar has condemned violent remarks made about him during a phone-in programme on a privately owned television channel.

The controversy centres on Paláver, a political phone-in programme broadcast by Hír TV, a Hungarian commercial television channel owned by Mediaworks company. In his post, Magyar shared recordings of two callers making violent remarks about him and suggested that the situation had at least improved since the beginning of the week.

One caller suggested that a sniper should eliminate him, while another proposed chaining him to a railing. Magyar responded with a sarcastic Facebook post, criticising the broadcaster for giving airtime to such statements.

“At least there is progress. Earlier this week they wanted to eliminate me with a sniper on Hír TV; yesterday they only wanted to chain me up,” the prime minister wrote.

His comments came after the broadcaster dismissed one of its presenters over her handling of the earlier incident.

What did the callers exactly said about the Hungarian prime minister?

The first incident occurred on Tuesday, 15 September, when an angry female caller questioned why there was no sniper or skilled marksman in Hungary who could eliminate Magyar.

Illustration: Hír TV’s Paláver programme. Source: Hír FM / YouTube

The woman subsequently claimed that she was not inclined towards murder and did not like violence. During a later broadcast, a male caller suggested putting a strap around the prime minister’s hand and chaining him to a railing.

TV presenter fired following sniper remarks

The first incident had already resulted in disciplinary action at Hír TV. On Wednesday, 16 September, the broadcaster’s owner, Mediaworks, announced that presenter Nóra Palányi had been dismissed for failing to interrupt the female caller immediately.

According to a statement published by Media1 , the company considered her response a serious professional error. The presenter had only distanced herself from the remarks after a delay, contrary to the broadcaster’s established protocol.

Mediaworks apologised to viewers, listeners and those affected by the incident. It also launched an internal investigation to prevent similar situations in the future.

If you missed it: Fidesz announces protest and 23 October commemorations at Budapest’s House of Terror

Magyar speaks out against aggressive political rhetoric

In his Saturday statement, Magyar said he did not hold the individual callers personally responsible for their aggressive remarks, arguing that they had been influenced by Hungary’s previous political leadership.

However, he criticised the television channel for providing a platform for such comments and accused it of encouraging hostility. The prime minister described Hír TV as a propaganda outlet and argued that its continued promotion of what he called hatred and aggression should not have to be tolerated.

Magyar ended his post with a reference to the planned Békemenet, or Peace March, a demonstration traditionally associated with Viktor Orbán’s Fidesz party.

The Civil Cooperation Forum (CÖF), which has traditionally organised the event, announced on Friday that it considered holding the proposed 23 October march premature. The organisation said another march could take place at a later date.

Magyar also commented on the cancellation of the planned 23 October Peace March (Békemenet), a demonstration traditionally associated with former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán’s Fidesz party.

“Two days ago, the weary warriors announced that the Peace March would return on 23 October. Today, they said it would not take place after all because it was ‘premature’,” Magyar wrote.

He added sarcastically: “In other words, it has been cancelled due to a lack of interest and public money.”

World.title: Budapest and Kyiv face sharp criticism from the Russian Embassy over alleged secrecy and unfulfilled promises
World.content:
Russia’s embassy in Budapest has sharply criticised both Hungary and Ukraine over their handling of minority rights in Transcarpathia. The diplomatic mission questioned the transparency of recent agreements between Budapest and Kyiv, arguing that the Hungarian minority’s concerns remain unresolved despite signs of improving bilateral relations.

According to Index , the Russian Embassy published a statement on Facebook addressing Kyiv’s obligations towards the ethnic Hungarian community in western Ukraine.

The embassy argued that, following the change of government in Hungary, Ukrainian authorities have sought to portray relations with Budapest as improving. However, it claimed that the underlying disagreements over minority rights have yet to be resolved.

The statement also criticised Ukrainian references to the two countries’ shared historical resistance to imperial Russia and Soviet rule, describing this narrative as an attempt to divert attention from unresolved bilateral issues.

Russian embassy questions the transparency of Hungary–Ukraine agreements

The Russian statement comes more than three months after Hungary and Ukraine announced an agreement intended to address their longstanding disagreements over minority rights.

Now, the Russian embassy argued that the lack of publicly available documentation makes it difficult to assess what has actually been agreed and whether the commitments are being fulfilled. It also accused Kyiv of relying on promises rather than implementing substantial changes to minority legislation.

“They have so far gone no further than words, promises or symbolic concessions,” the Russian Embassy in Budapest wrote in its Facebook post.

It also pointed to a Ukrainian diplomatic note reportedly outlining Kyiv’s commitments regarding 11 demands raised by Hungary’s previous government, as well as Hungarian amendments to Ukraine’s action plan on protecting national minorities.

If you missed it: Zelensky launches new Carpathian Eight alliance with Hungary on board

What have Hungary and Ukraine agreed on?

According to the Hungarian government’s official announcement , Ukraine agreed to restore the system of minority schools, expand the use of Hungarian in educational institutions and permit the display of Hungarian national symbols in municipalities where the community accounts for more than 10% of the population.

Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced that Kyiv had committed to incorporating the agreed measures into Ukrainian law. The arrangements included restoring minority education provisions, allowing greater use of Hungarian in schools and protecting the community’s cultural rights.

At the same time, Hungary has maintained its position on Ukraine’s EU accession. In September, Budapest again blocked progress on additional negotiating clusters, making further advancement conditional on Kyiv taking concrete steps to implement the minority rights agreement. Legislative guarantees remain a prerequisite for Hungary’s support.

The Russian embassy’s statement also referred to Ukrainian legislative proposals expected in September, questioning whether they would introduce meaningful changes to laws governing education, the state language and national minorities.

Zelenskyy sees no major obstacle between Budapest and Kyiv

The latest Russian criticism comes as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has sought to play down the disagreements with Hungary. Speaking at the Carpathian Eight summit in western Ukraine on Friday, 18 September, Zelenskyy said he did not see a major problem between Kyiv and Budapest regarding minority rights.

He acknowledged that Hungary was waiting for the Ukrainian parliament to adopt the relevant legislation, but expressed hope that Budapest would subsequently allow Ukraine’s EU accession negotiations to move forward.

According to Interfax-Ukraine , Zelenskyy said Kyiv hoped to open two additional negotiating clusters in September or October, with another two potentially unblocked by the end of 2026.

The Ukrainian government is preparing a draft law addressing the issues raised by Hungary, although the timetable for its introduction and adoption remains unclear.

World.title: Fidesz announces protest and 23 October commemorations at Budapest’s House of Terror
World.content:
Hungary’s Fidesz party will hold both a protest on Sunday and its 23 October commemoration outside Budapest’s House of Terror Museum, the party announced on Friday.

Party chooses museum as venue amid dispute over its leadership and future

In a statement sent to MTI, Fidesz called on supporters to “protest together against the new communist authoritarianism”. The announcement comes amid a political dispute over the museum following the termination of the mandate of its long-serving director, Mária Schmidt, and a review of the institution’s exhibition and operations.

23 October this year marks the 70th anniversary of Hungary’s 1956 Revolution and Freedom Fight, making the House of Terror a particularly prominent location for political events connected with the anniversary.

Meanwhile, right-wing influencers are organising a protest on Sunday, 20 September, over the removal of Mária Schmidt, former director of the museum. The announcement was made by the Tisza government’s minister of social relations and culture, Zoltán Tarr.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s Telegram channel!

House of Terror to reopen next week

The museum hence was temporarily closed on 15 September after Tarr, but the government subsequently changed its plans for the closure. The House of Terror is due to reopen on Tuesday, 22 September, and will be free to visit for one week. The museum’s official website also confirms the 22 September reopening date.

The exhibition will remain in its current form while the professional review is under way. According to Tarr, the review is being conducted by researchers from the ELTE Institute of Historical Studies and independent experts.

The House of Terror is operated by the Foundation for Research on Central and Eastern European History and Society. The foundation was among the public-interest asset management foundations affected by the government’s decision to wind up a number of such organisations, with their public assets and responsibilities transferred to the state.

Stay up-to-date: Hungary scraps EUR 73 billion motorway deal linked to Orbán-era allies, launches criminal complaints

Peace March postponed as Fidesz announces separate event

The announcement also follows a decision by the Civil Összefogás Fórum (CÖF), a Fidesz-aligned civic organisation, regarding a planned 23 October Békemenet, or Peace March.

CÖF said on Friday that it considered holding the march on 23 October premature and that the next Békemenet would take place at a later date. The decision came after right-wing public figures had announced plans for demonstrations around the House of Terror.

Meanwhile, Prime Minister Péter Magyar criticised the cancellation in a social media post, arguing that the march was being called off because of a lack of interest and public funding. His comments represent his own political interpretation of the decision.

With the Békemenet postponed, the Fidesz announcement establishes the House of Terror as the location for the party’s 23 October commemoration, while debate over the museum’s leadership and professional direction continues.
