World.title: Moving to Hungary costs less than Spain – and newcomers bring twice as much stuff, new data shows
World.content:
New data based on nearly 200 Hungary-related moving quotes suggests people moving to Hungary tend to relocate much larger households than those leaving the country, while Hungarian routes are generally cheaper than the European average.

Moving to Hungary can be significantly cheaper than relocating to Spain from the same European countries, while people moving into Hungary also tend to bring substantially larger household loads, according to new international moving data covering January to September 2026.

The figures come from Finnish international moving company Flyto Relocation, which analysed 7,754 quoted moves across 1,211 international routes. The company says its dataset includes 197 Hungary-related quotes, covering 48 routes and 29 partner countries. All prices cited are median quoted prices excluding VAT.

The data shows that 108 of the Hungary-related quotes were for moves into Hungary, compared with 90 for moves out of the country.

People moving to Hungary bring much larger households

One of the clearest differences is the amount of belongings being moved. The median inbound load to Hungary was 16.75 cubic metres, more than twice the 7.5 cubic metres recorded for outbound moves.

According to Flyto Relocation, a 17 m³ load would typically correspond to a furnished one- to two-bedroom home, while 7.5 m³ is closer to a studio-sized move or a car full of boxes.

The company says the figures suggest that moves into Hungary more often involve people settling into the country with an entire household, while those leaving Hungary tend to move smaller quantities of belongings, potentially reflecting individuals relocating for work.

The largest number of inbound quotes came from the Netherlands and Belgium, with 18 quotes each, followed by Germany with nine, and Greece and Spain with eight each.

For outbound moves, Spain was the most common destination, with 13 quotes, followed by the Netherlands with 10 and Germany with seven. France and Italy each accounted for six quotes.

If you missed it: Reader’s letter: The things I learned to appreciate about Hungary after leaving

Moving to Hungary can be cheaper than Spain

The data also shows a notable difference when comparing Hungary and Spain as destinations.

For a 20–30 m³ household move, the median quoted price from the Netherlands to Hungary was €4,831, compared with €5,690 for a move from the Netherlands to Spain.

For Belgium, the corresponding figures were €3,998 to Hungary and €5,632 to Spain. From Germany, a 20–30 m³ move to Hungary had a median quoted price of €3,406, compared with €5,797 for Spain.

That means the median quoted price for these Hungarian routes was roughly 15% lower from the Netherlands, 29% lower from Belgium and 41% lower from Germany than the comparable Spanish routes.

Hungarian routes also come in below the European average

The company’s broader European data indicates that Hungarian routes can also be cheaper than the European average for comparable move sizes and distances.

For moves of 20–30 m³ travelling 800–1,500 km, the median quoted price on Hungarian routes was €3,754, compared with €4,566 across Europe – around 18% lower.

For smaller moves of 10–20 m³ over the same distance, the median was €2,888 in the Hungary data, compared with €3,297 across Europe, or about 12% less.

However, Flyto Relocation notes that these comparisons are based on relatively small samples of 14 and 17 quotes respectively, meaning they should be treated as indicative rather than representative of the entire moving market.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official Telegram channel!

A typical European move costs thousands of euros

Across the company’s full European dataset, a typical mid-range move of 20–30 m³ over 1,500–2,500 km had a median quoted price of €6,279, excluding VAT. For a smaller 10–20 m³ move travelling less than 800 km, the median was €2,394.

The company also warns that simply dividing the total price by the volume of belongings can give a misleading impression of moving costs.

A 3 m³ move costs around 12 times more per cubic metre than a 50 m³ household move, according to the index. This reflects the fact that fixed costs such as collection, transport arrangements and handling do not increase proportionally with the amount being moved.

Hungarians book moves about two months in advance

The Hungary data suggests that people planning international moves generally give themselves around two months to prepare. The median booking lead time for Hungary-related moves was 58 days, almost identical to the European-wide figure of 57 days.

July to October were the busiest months in the Hungary dataset, together accounting for around 70% of quotes. Budapest featured in roughly one in three Hungary-related quotes, followed by Debrecen and Szeged.

The most common Hungary-related routes in the dataset included the Netherlands to Hungary, with a median quoted price of €4,831 for a 21 m³ move, based on 18 quotes. The median for Belgium to Hungary was €3,998 for 20.5 m³, also based on 18 quotes.

For moves in the opposite direction, Hungary to Spain had a median quoted price of €4,398 for 12 m³, based on 13 quotes, while Hungary to the Netherlands stood at €3,021 for 5 m³, based on 10 quotes.

The figures are based on quoted prices rather than final paid prices, and the Hungary sample represents one company’s customer enquiries rather than official migration data.

World.title: Beautiful European destination could become Budapest Airport’s next novelty
World.content:
Zaragoza could soon be added to Budapest Airport’s European route map, after the Aragón regional government and Zaragoza City Council announced a tender covering 31 potential air routes.

New air connection could link Budapest Airport with Aragón

The scheme could connect the airport serving the capital of Aragón with 15 countries, creating new international links while strengthening existing connections. The tender includes 29 cities in total, seven of them domestic destinations. Among the international routes included in the programme are Budapest, Prague, Bratislava, Warsaw and Kraków.

If the Budapest route goes ahead, Zaragoza would become a new Spanish destination available to travellers from the Hungarian capital. According to the information published about the tender, Zaragoza is currently a significant but unserved potential Spanish destination on Budapest Airport’s European network, reports Budflyer.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s Telegram channel!

A historic Spanish city between Madrid and Barcelona

Zaragoza is the capital of Aragón and Spain’s fifth-largest city. Situated on the banks of the Ebro River, it has a history spanning more than 2,000 years, with Roman, Muslim, Jewish and Christian influences all leaving their mark on the city.

One of Zaragoza’s best-known landmarks is the enormous Baroque Basilica of Our Lady of the Pillar. Other major attractions include La Seo Cathedral, associated with the UNESCO-listed Mudéjar architecture of Aragón, and the Aljafería Palace, a former Moorish palace.

A beautiful city that is somehow still overlooked by some

The city’s location between Madrid and Barcelona has also made it an important transport and economic centre. At the same time, Zaragoza remains less familiar to international tourists than Spain’s best-known major cities. For Hungarian travellers, the city could offer a different side of Spain, with its historic centre, riverside setting, Roman remains and El Tubo district, known for its many tapas bars, writes 24.hu.

The proposed route is part of a wider tender process, meaning a Budapest–Zaragoza flight has not yet been confirmed. However, the inclusion of the Hungarian capital in the plans could open the way for a new direct connection between Budapest and one of Spain’s major inland cities.

Read also: Stress-free autumn travel: motorists face strict parking rules at Budapest Airport

World.title: Social workers protest for pay rise in Budapest, Péter Magyar meets the demonstrators
World.content:
Social sector workers demonstrated outside the Prime Minister’s Office in Budapest on Friday, demanding an immediate 25 per cent pay rise and improved working conditions. Péter Magyar then went out and met them to hear their demands.

Demonstrators call for higher wages and better working conditions

The protest was organised under the slogan, “We pay our utility bills in one go, so we want our pay rise in one go, too.” Workers said the previously promised 20–25 per cent wage increase, which is expected to be introduced in two stages and may also take into account the minimum wage increase and tax relief, falls well short of their expectations.

Ferenc Köves, president of the Trade Union of Workers in the Social Sector, said employees understood that the government had inherited the problems facing the sector from the previous administration. However, he stressed that the current government was the one responsible for finding a solution.

Péter Magyar meets protesters outside Prime Minister’s Office

Prime Minister Péter Magyar went out to the demonstrators and said the government was fully aware of the difficulties facing the social sector. He argued that even another 25 per cent pay rise would not, on its own, provide a meaningful and genuine solution to the sector’s problems.

Köves handed the prime minister the union’s proposed wage table, along with a list of issues it wants to discuss beyond the question of pay. Magyar invited union representatives to talks, but although they thanked him for the invitation, they suggested holding the meeting at a later date.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s Telegram channel!

PM Magyar wants a long-term solution

Addressing the demonstrators, Péter Magyar said the government faced a wide range of responsibilities. He said it had taken over a severely depleted budget and would have to decide whether workers should receive a one-off payment or a pay rise this year.

The government must also determine whether next year’s wage increase should be implemented in one or two stages, he added, asking workers in the social sector for patience.

Read also: Hungary scraps EUR 73 billion motorway deal linked to Orbán-era allies, launches criminal complaints

World.title: Person hit by tram on one of Budapest’s busiest lines
World.content:
A person was hit by a tram on Margaret Boulevard in Budapest’s 2nd district on Friday afternoon, temporarily disrupting services on several lines.

Tram services disrupted after accident

The accident happened near Mammut shopping centre at Széna Square, where the vehicle struck a person, according to Hungary’s National Directorate General for Disaster Management. Firefighters from the Budapest professional fire service were called to the scene.

Following the incident, trams 4 and 6 were temporarily suspended between Jászai Mari Square and Széll Kálmán Square, according to the Budapest Transport Centre (BKK). Replacement buses operated along the affected section while emergency services dealt with the accident.

Tram 17 was also diverted, running as far as Batthyány Square instead of following its normal route. The service did not call at stops between Szent Lukács Spa and Széll Kálmán Square during the disruption.

Services are already restored

The disruption was relatively short-lived. According to the latest information, normal services were restored shortly after 2.30 PM. The accident occurred on one of Budapest’s busiest tram corridors. The 4 and 6 lines run through central Budapest and across Margaret Bridge, connecting Buda and Pest, while the 17 line serves several areas of Buda.

No further information about the condition of the person involved in the accident was provided in the reports.

Read also: Girl taken to hospital with serious limb injury after Budapest bus runs over her leg

World.title: EU President to Skip Serbia and Bosnia on Balkan Tour
World.content:
The European Commission announced on Friday that President Ursula von der Leyen will miss Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina during her trip to the Western Balkans between September 30 and October 2, citing upcoming elections in the two countries.

“In light of the upcoming parliamentary and general elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in Serbia, the president intends to visit these countries at a later date,” a Commission spokesperson, Arianna Podesta, said on Friday.

During the trip, von der Leyen will visit Albania, Kosovo, Montenegro and North Macedonia where she will meet leaders and look at EU-funded projects.

After the EU announcement, Serbia’s President hinted that looming elections were not the only reason for the no-show – hinting at her recent criticism of his administration.

“Ursula von der Leyen is far too wise and intelligent a woman to have any illusions about, or to be unaware of, public opinion in Serbia. So I’m sure she knows very well… [but] let’s not get into that,” Vucic said.

Von der Leyen and other EU officials have condemned Serbia’s government over the glorification of the convicted Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladic, whose funeral in Belgrade on September 7 was attended by ministers and high officials both from Serbia and Bosnia’s Serb-led entity, Republika Srpska.

“I was horrified by the pictures from Ratko Mladic’s funeral in Belgrade last week. He committed the most atrocious crimes against humanity. Glorifying war criminals simply has no place in the European Union,” von der Leyen said on September 16. Serbia is an EU candidate state.

A day after Mladic’s funeral, von der Leyen also wrote on X that “the elements of official support and the presence of some senior Serbian officials at the funeral are deeply regrettable”.

Earlier in September, EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos cancelled her planned visit to Serbia, the day after Mladic’s body was transported on a government plane to Belgrade, where it was met by officials and an army honour guard.

Early parliamentary elections will be held in Serbia on October 25. President Vucic called the elections after a year-and-a-half of anti-government protesters demanding snap elections.

The elections will be Vucic’s most challenging test since he came to power in 2012. The main rival to his ruling Serbian Progressive Party, SNS, is the Student List, a political list formed by Serbian students who have been protesting since November 2024, following the deadly collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad.

Bosnia and Herzegovina will hold presidential ​and parliamentary elections ‌on October 4.

World.title: Week in Review: Campaigns, Crackdowns and Clan Wars
World.content:
Wildfires have blazed across the Balkans over the last couple of months amid another scorching summer. Around the Albanian coastal city of Himara, they forced evacuations, destroyed homes and olive groves.

The Albanian government has identified the growing threat from wildfires as an expected consequence of climate change. But there’s a lack of readiness and coordination to confront the challenge, experts are warning.

World.title: Discontent Simmers in Kosovo as Protesters Denounce Hague War Crimes Verdict
World.content:
The KLA War Veterans’ Organisation, which staged Friday’s protest, called for the dismissal of Justice Minister Donika Gervalla, the repeal or amendment of the Law on the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, unlimited funding for the defence of the four former KLA leaders in their upcoming appeal against the verdict, and the engagement of top international experts for their defence.

Hysni Gucati, head of the organisation, accused minister Gervalla of submitting evidence for the case to the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague.

“We are telling [Prime Minister] Albin Kurti to remove these people from the government starting today; he should not keep them in the government. People who collaborate with the enemy are enemies of my nation, and we do not want them among us,” Gucati said.

“Donika Gervalla has still not come forward to apologise,” he added. Gervalla has not commented publicly about the allegation so far.

World.title: Fining Bosnia’s Parties for Campaign Violations Won’t Deter Them, Expert Warns
World.content:
The unprecedented fines imposed this week by Bosnia’s Central Election Commission won’t stop ruling parties from exploiting state resources to secure votes, Dario Jovanovic, project manager of the fair-elections campaign group Pod Lupom, told BIRN on Friday.

“Parties in Bosnia view these fines as a minor, predictable cost of doing business,” Jovanovic said. “When a ruling party controls millions in public budgets, a few thousand euros will not stop them from exploiting state resources to secure votes.”

The state Election Commission imposed unprecedented penalties exceeding 100,000 euros during a single session in Sarajevo on Thursday, heavily targeting major political entities for premature campaigning and abusing public resources ahead of the polls on October 4.

The primary target of Election Commission’s sanctions was the Alliance of Independent Social Democrats, SNSD, the Bosnian Serb ruling party led by Milorad Dodik.

The SNSD, which holds power in Bosnia’s Serb-led entity, Republika Srpska, was directly fined about 41,900 euros, while individual sanctions against its candidates brought the party’s total penalty to 52,700 euros, effectively accounting for over half of the entire session’s fines.

The regulatory body cited multiple severe violations of Bosnia’s Election Law, focusing on the unlawful exploitation of public infrastructure projects for partisan gain and the illegal use of children for political marketing.

Dodik himself was personally fined around 4,600 euros over an Instagram post in which he took direct credit on behalf of his party for taxpayer-funded public works. A member of the state parliament, Sanja Vulic, was fined 4,100 euros for inaccurate media statements and premature campaigning during a television broadcast.

The financial sweep extended beyond the SNSD. The Drasko Stanivukovic – Safe Srpska Movement coalition received the second-highest cumulative penalty, of some 13,000 euros. Following the ruling, Stanivukovic, mayor of Banja Luka, the main city in Republika Srpska, criticised the decision.

“They are fining us simply for doing our jobs and presenting infrastructure projects to the citizens,” Stanivukovic stated to media. “These decisions are rigid and politically targeted to diminish our campaign visibility.”

Other penalised entities included the Social Democratic Party, SDP, which was fined 8,700 euros, and Nedeljko Stevandic’s United Srpska, at 7,200 euros.

Major political entities from Bosnia’s other entity, the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, including the Party of Democratic Action, SDA and a five-party Croat coalition, were also hit with financial sanctions.

With voters set to elect the state’s tripartite Presidency and entity parliaments in less than three weeks, the watchdog’s latest financial targeting represents an aggressive institutional effort to enforce compliance in a highly polarized race.

World.title: Greece Mourns Margarita Papandreou, Pioneering Feminist
World.content:
Margarita Papandreou with her three sons Photo: Nikos Papandreou/Facebook.

Greek feminist and author Margarita Papandreou, who was the wife of prime minister and centre-left PASOK party founder Andreas Papandreou, died in Athens on Friday. On September 20, she would have turned 103 years old.

Margarita (Margaret) Chant-Papandreou, originally from the US, studied journalism and pursued postgraduate studies in Public Health. Her name became linked to one of the most prominent political dynasties in Greek history, as well as to a series of significant reforms regarding gender equality.

She was the second wife from 1951 to 1989 of Andreas Papandreou; together they had four children, including former PM George Papandreou and PASOK MEP Nikos Papandreou.

“Margarita Papandreou linked her name to the struggle for women’s rights and social progress,” stated PASOK’s current leader, Nikos Androulakis.

Margarita met Andreas in the US in 1948 and the couple moved to Greece in 1961. Following the military takeover and Andreas’s arrest in 1967, she campaigned for his release. They left Greece for Sweden, and then Canada, returning to Greece after the fall of the military junta in 1974, when Andreas announced the founding of PASOK.

Margarita did not remain in her husband’s shadow; in 1976, alongside other women, she founded the Women’s Union of Greece, a women’s non-profit.

She played a pivotal role in promoting, drafting and passing legislation that improved the social status of Greek women. Key measures included the introduction of civil marriage in 1982, the abolition of the dowry system, the legalisation of divorce by mutual consent, the right of women to retain their maiden names after marriage in 1983, and the legalisation of abortion in 1986.

In her book, Love and Power, she recounted her turbulent relationship with her husband – marked by infidelity, their acrimonious divorce and his subsequent marriage to a younger woman.

Her son, Nikos Papandreou, wrote in the preface: “She may have stood by the side of the Greek politician who transformed Greece – Andreas – but she also created and led the country’s most significant feminist movement, the one that exerted the greatest influence regarding women’s rights in Greece.”

World.title: Turkey Arrests Fund Managers Over Stock Market Manipulation Scandal
World.content:
Turkish authorities arrested four suspects on Friday, including investment fund board members, and imposed travel bans on 51 others, as part of an investigation into alleged manipulation of the stock market, Justice Minister Akin Gurlek announced.

Courts have also imposed precautionary measures on accounts and other assets linked to those under investigation, to prevent their transfer, Gurlek said.

“Those who exploit the sweat, labour and savings of our citizens will be held accountable before the law,” he added.

Turkey’s Capital Markets Board, SPK, has filed criminal complaints about alleged manipulative transactions in several funds and listed shares.

In a separate investigation, a court ordered access blocked to 246 social media accounts accused of publishing speculative material capable of causing fear or panic among investors.

Another investigation by prosecutors in Istanbul’s Bakirkoy District has resulted in 16 arrests over social media posts allegedly intended to manipulate capital markets, Gurlek said.

Turkish Interior Minister Mustafa Ciftci on Thursday said operations related to the stock market investigation would continue, suggesting further action is likely.

On Thursday the SPK ordered the liquidation of 130 funds managed by seven portfolio management companies after liquidity problems contributed to sharp market losses.

Trading on Istanbul Stock Exchange was temporarily suspended on Wednesday after the benchmark BIST 100 index fell by more than 6 per cent, triggering a market-wide circuit breaker.

Estimates of the combined size of the 130 funds differ.

According to Reuters, their assets are worth around 21.4 billion US dollars, involving about 353,000 investors. CNBC-e puts the total at about 19.8 billion US dollars and the number of investors at more than 514,000.

Liquidation does not mean that the investors’ money has been confiscated. Instead, banks are being tasked to deliver citizens’ money in these funds. Is Bank has been appointed to handle the liquidation of funds managed by Tera Portfoy, while state-owned Ziraat Bank will oversee funds belonging to the six other managers.

The proceeds will be distributed to investors according to their holdings. However, investors may not recover the last reported value of their holdings, as the final amount will depend on prices achieved when the assets are sold.

The crisis intensified after regulatory changes targeted risks associated with funds concentrated in thinly traded shares.

“It has been observed that some funds have caused price movements that cannot be explained by the financial realities of companies,” the SPK said on Thursday, adding that the new measures were aimed at preventing market manipulation and increasing transparency.

World.title: Expelled by Greece’s Ruling Party, Ex-PM Samaras Plots His Revenge
World.content:
At the beginning of September, former Greek prime minister Antonis Samaras seized on a newspaper report that users of the online platform of the Greek health service were allowed to specify gender options beyond ‘Male’ and ‘Female’, to include ‘Other’ and ‘Undetermined’.

Samaras was expelled from Greece’s ruling New Democracy party last year, and still bears a grudge.

He promptly took to Facebook to accuse the conservative government of promoting a “woke agenda” and echoed erroneous claims that school textbooks were depicting families with same-sex parents.

“The only thing ‘undetermined’ here is the extent of the ideological shift within the ruling party,” Samaras wrote. Greek families “need support, not redefinition”, he claimed.

World.title: EU Should Not Turn a Blind Eye to Montenegro’s Bloody Clan War
World.content:
When Montenegro declared independence in 2006, it identified EU and NATO integration as its strategic priorities. The country applied for EU membership in 2008, accession negotiations began in 2012, and NATO membership followed in 2017.

Yet, beneath the language of democratisation and Europeanisation lies a far less reassuring reality: a country where rival organised crime clans have waged a conflict for more than a decade, with dozens of people murdered, including innocent bystanders – and where allegations of links between criminal groups, police officers, and senior judicial figures have repeatedly surfaced

The question is not merely why Montenegro has struggled to defeat organised crime. It is why this conflict appears to have become increasingly peripheral to the European Union’s public assessment of the country.

The origins of Montenegro’s interclan war are generally traced to a dispute involving the disappearance of almost 200 kilograms of cocaine in Valencia, Spain, in 2014. What followed was a violent confrontation between two criminal groups based in the coastal town of Kotor – the Kavac and Skaljari clans. Most of the country’s organised crime groups eventually aligned themselves with one of the two rival groups.

Kotor itself became a symbol of the problem. The UNESCO World Heritage Site and historic home of both clans was described by then Interior Minister Goran Danilovic as a “hostage town.” Investigations subsequently alleged the existence of surveillance networks used by criminal gangs and the disclosure of confidential police information to members of the Kavac clan.

World.title: If Government Fails to Intervene, Croatia’s Most Expensive Diesel is Coming
World.content:
September the 19th, 2026 – If the government fails to intervene, then Croatia’s most expensive diesel so far is on its way next week.

From next Tuesday, drivers at petrol stations could be met with higher fuel prices. Index reports that according to what currently remains unofficial information, all types of fuel are becoming more expensive, and diesel could reach a historic high in Croatia. These are the prices that will apply if the government fails to properly intervene, reports RTL.

expected price increases

If there is no government intervention, the price of a litre of eurosuper should rise by one cent and amount to €1.74. Eurodiesel would become more expensive by ten cents, so its new price would be €1.95 per litre. The largest price increase is expected for blue diesel, which should rise by 11 cents to €1.51.

historic highs for diesel…

If the government does not make a different decision, the diesel price of €1.95 per litre would be the highest recorded in Croatia’s history. Until now Croatia has had some of the lower fuel prices in Europe, but that could change from next week.

why are diesel and oil prices rising like this?

The background to the new blow to drivers’ pockets lies in the global disruptions caused by the US war against Iran, which has been shaking the world energy market for months. The situation escalated further after drone attacks on the Saudi East-West oil pipeline, a key alternative route for transporting crude oil after navigation through the Strait of Hormuz became unsafe. As a result, Brent crude prices jumped above $100 a barrel, and some deliveries in Europe exceeded $120.

As energy expert Davor Štern warned, the price increases are not only a consequence of a physical shortage of fuel, but primarily of stock-market speculation. “We follow the markets, and the markets do what they do. The exchanges have again returned to their traditional bookmaking methods – it is not so much a real shortage of diesel as expectations that there will not be enough of it that have driven the price up,” Štern explained.

the croatian government’s hands are tied…

On whether the state even has mechanisms with which it could stop this rise, Professor Marijana Ivanov from the Department of Finance at the Faculty of Economics in Zagreb spoke for Index. She warns that the geopolitical circumstances are extremely unfavourable and that the Government is running out of instruments with which it could cushion new blows.

“I think the room for preventing a further rise in fuel prices is quite limited. With excise duties there is almost none, especially with diesel, while with petrol it is also very narrow,” Ivanov points out. Although cutting the VAT rate is often mentioned in public, the economist considers that this would not be a good move: “In principle it is possible to reduce VAT on fuel, but I would not suggest it because public finances are already under pressure from the risk of a larger deficit. A third option would be further cutting of distributors’ margins, but we know that even at these levels they have become unsustainable for small traders.”

World.title: Will Croatia Have Enough Energy Capacities to Match Consumption Growth?
World.content:
September the 19th, 2026 – Will Croatia have enough energy capacities for both the general public and for the economy as consumption increases?

Experts keep on emphasising that without a stronger electricity grid and larger energy storage capacities it will not be possible to keep up with the growth in consumption. The question in many minds now is whether or not Croatia will have enough energy capacities for the economy, the public and new industry, and at competitive prices? Poslovni reports that this was one of the key questions at the ENERGREEN – Energy Security of Croatia 2027 conference.

The focus was primarily placed on the security of gas supply, the LNG terminal on Krk and the Okoli storage facility, as well as the accelerated development of solar and wind power plants, as reported by HRT. Experts emphasise that without a stronger electricity grid and larger energy storage capacities it will not be possible to keep up with the growth in consumption. When it comes to heating, people have no reason to worry. “Croatia has a relatively good energy situation due to its geostrategic position, and the country is home to an LNG terminal, storage, and good transport infrastructure, which means that we will always have enough gas, because now we’re no longer last in line but first,” explained Dalibor Pudić, president of the Croatian Professional Gas Association.

“As you’ve already seen, the 11th package of measures has also been adopted. The government is very much continuing to protect the general public and the concrete economy; in addition, there is also supply stability through certain measures, limiting retail fuel prices, and supply stability is also ensured through the filling of gas storage facilities,” concluded Željko Krevzelj, director of the Energy Directorate at the Ministry of the Economy.

World.title: Renovated University Campus Worth Over €50 Million Opens in Zagreb
World.content:
September the 19th, 2026 – A newly renovated university campus worth over €50 million has opened as part of FER in Zagreb.

After two years of extensive works, Buildings B and C of the campus of the Faculty of Electrical Engineering and Computing of the University of Zagreb (FER) were solemnly opened. The complete renovation amounting to €50 million excluding VAT was co-financed with European Union funds from the Solidarity Fund and the Recovery and Resilience Facility. Poslovni reports that this concerns an area spanning 18,000 square metres in Unska Street that includes five modern amphitheatre lecture halls with a capacity of 900 seats, 153 office rooms and 26 classrooms and laboratories for teaching. The newly opened FER premises were visited by representatives of the state leadership, the City of Zagreb, the University of Zagreb and prominent entrepreneurs, members of the Faculty’s Alumni Board.

FER Dean Prof. Vedran Bilas, PhD, said that the investment in the renovation is the initial phase of the campus development, which was last expanded at the end of the 1980s, when the faculty had almost half as many employees, fewer study programmes and many times fewer research projects than today.

“Generations of professors and students before us built this institution, its competences, significance and values. FER is a synonym of excellence in the Croatian public, academic and business community. This renovation and this ceremony are stations on a path that continues. The Faculty has an experienced and proven team and capacity for the implementation of complex infrastructure projects, ready to continue cooperation with the Ministry of Science, Education and Youth on campus development projects,” Bilas said and announced a new spatial expansion: “The Government of the Republic of Croatia, through a Loan Agreement with the World Bank, is financing the preparation of the main project for the reconstruction of Building A, which will be completed by the end of this year. The reconstructed building will have three underground and nine above-ground floors, five more than now.”

Prime Minister Andrej Plenković praised the Faculty’s results and emphasised its contribution to society.

“By renovating these buildings we aren’t investing merely in space, but in Croatia’s ability to understand, shape and lead the technological changes that in the decades ahead will determine the economic strength, security and technological independence of states. FER is one of the central places where Croatia creates knowledge for the digital age, and we count on its professors, researchers and students also in responding to the challenges of artificial intelligence, cyber security and quantum computing. Our vision is clear: Croatia must not be only a user of other people’s technology, but must develop and export its own high value-added solutions,” said Prime Minister Plenković.

“Through patient work, persistence and joint action we have arrived at a result that benefits our teachers and those most important for our future, and that is our students. I believe that the Faculty in the renovated premises will develop new visions and continue to lead in the IT sector and digital transformation, recognising what society and the state need,” said Rector of the University of Zagreb, Prof. Stjepan Lakušić, PhD.

The FER team responsible for the implementation of the renovation guided representatives of the Government, Prime Minister Plenković, Minister of Construction and State Property Branko Bačić, Minister of the Economy Ante Šušnjar and other high-ranking guests through the newly renovated premises, and the tour ended on the 13th floor with a spectacular panoramic view of the whole of Zagreb. The contractor for the extensive works was the construction company TROMONT d.o.o., and a complete energy, fire-protection and multimedia renovation was carried out.

The programme and celebration of the opening will continue in the afternoon. From 18:00 a parking party for friends, fellow citizens and neighbours is planned on the FER car park in Unska Street, with musicians Duška Brčić, Vjeko Ključarić, Filip Rudan, young up-and-coming bands and the Disco section of KSET.

World.title: “Forever Chemicals” Found in Lika Water Following Waste Scandal
World.content:
September the 19th, 2026 – So-called “forever chemicals” have unfortunately been found in Lika water following the shameful hazardous waste scandal.

The Croatian Institute of Public Health (HZJZ) and the Public Health Institute of Lika-Senj County have published the results of extraordinary water sampling in the Lika area. Index reports that the results have revealed that dangerous PFAS compounds, so-called “forever chemicals,” were found in two private wells downstream from an illegal waste dump near Gospić, but they assure the public that the pollution is exclusively of a local character and that water from the public water supply is not endangered.

the chemicals were found in two wells near the illegal waste dump

According to the HZJZ statement, from the 20th of August to the 9th of September water was sampled from 43 private facilities – 38 wells, three cisterns and two springs. The Institute states that in one well in the immediate vicinity of the dump a concentration of PFAS compounds of 0.3018 µg/L was recorded, which is three times higher than the maximum permitted limit of 0.1 µg/L. In the second well 0.0265 µg/L was measured, which is within the permitted limits. HZJZ claims that the owners of the disputed wells are connected to the public water supply and do not use that water for drinking. As for the other findings, the Institute claims that in 33 facilities only “usual microbiological pollution characteristic of untreated water” was recorded, while elevated physical-chemical values in a further 10 samples are attributed to the natural properties of the karst, and not to the dumped waste.

the people of lika feel betrayed by the government

The statement comes at a moment when the scandal surrounding the illegal burial of as many as 37,000 tonnes of hazardous waste in Divoselo and Benkovačko Selo near Gospić has grown into a first-class political scandal. HZJZ Director Krunoslav Capak personally sits on the newly established Scientific Council of Prime Minister Andrej Plenković, a body that the government formed precisely with the aim of “correctly interpreting” in public the dramatic findings of the USKOK investigation into the pollution of soil and waters in Lika. The documents that Plenković’s Scientific Council is supposed to put into the “correct context” were signed by authorised institutions and are quite exact.

The expert examination by the “Josip Juraj Strossmayer” Water Institute for the Divoselo location established that the water passing immediately under the dump carries 89 percent of the total detected plastic, while upstream it is clean. 737 micrograms of Styrofoam per litre were measured, and the presence of Teflon from the group of “forever chemicals” (PFAS) was also recorded, with the expert’s note that the Lika River is a directly connected water body.

the prime minister is at the council’s helm

Although formally composed of professors from technical and natural science faculties, the Council has been placed under the direct authority of the Prime Minister. According to the government decision, the sessions are convened and chaired by Plenković himself, operational tasks are carried out by his office, and there are no prescribed obligations for the publication of minutes, expert conclusions or any dissenting opinions of members. The entire manoeuvre of forming the Council is taking place at a time when the remediation is only being prepared, and political pressure on the ruling party is growing after a mass protest in Zagreb and a drop in HDZ’s rating.

is there any real reason to panic?

Despite this, HZJZ persists in the claim that there is no reason for panic. They state that the fact that such compounds were not found in other wells across the county proves that it is “pollution of a local character in a narrower circle.” They also repeat that private wells in any case do not fall under regular state supervision and that the responsibility lies with the owners themselves. The Institute finally states that all regular tests confirm that water from the public water supply in the entire Lika-Senj County area, as well as on the islands of Pag and Rab, is completely health-safe and that they will continue monitoring the situation on the ground.

World.title: New Passenger and Hospitality Complex Coming to Split Port
World.content:
September the 18th, 2026 – A brand new passenger and hospitality complex is coming to Split Port, finally giving the entire area a much needed proverbial facelift.

What was once the Dalmacijavino winery, a work by architect Stanko Fabris and a gem of Croatian modern architecture, has over time become a dilapidated, abandoned building in what is definitely one of the most beautiful locations in the entire city. A place where Katalinića brig meets the port, the sea, and the rest of the world.

Morski reports that the Split Port Authority, the manager of that part of the port, has received a permit for the changes. After more than two years of waiting, the Split Port Authority has finally obtained a location permit – a permit for the changes according to which the building will be repurposed, under strict conservation guidelines. The building is under the protection of the Conservation Department of the Ministry of Culture.

After all the necessary studies (economic and legal) in cooperation with the constituents of the University of Split, and according to conservation guidelines, we conducted an international expression of interest from potential concessionaires and submitted all the necessary documentation to the City of Split, and we finally have it.

As part of the city’s project for the arrangement of Split’s Eastern Coast, according to the existing city Master Plan (GUP), two garages with 500 parking spaces can be built at that location, which would solve the problem of stationary traffic in the city port; passenger space can be expanded, accompanying hospitality facilities, and even a hotel with around a hundred rooms.

Now that the location permit has arrived, an international tender will be announced for the concession of the building and the space around it. The significance of this investment can best be shown through numbers, and that is the estimated value of the concession, which totals a massive 600,000,000 euros.

World.title: New Croatian Price Comparison System Coming Next Month
World.content:
September the 18th, 2026 – A brand new Croatian price comparison system is coming next month, with additional technical obligations awaiting traders and service providers.

As of the 1st of October 2026 in Croatia, the prices highlighted on the shelves, in the menus or on the price lists will no longer stand alone. Poslovni reports that alongside the current price an additional, so-called anchor price will also have to be stated. The new obligation applies to all retailers and registered service providers in Croatia. This means that the new rules will not cover only supermarkets, but also clothing and footwear shops, technical goods, furniture and building materials stores, as well as restaurants, cafes, hair and beauty salons, car mechanics, various service workshops and other craftsmen who offer their products or services to consumers.

The anchor price will be the regular price that applied to a particular product or service on 10 September 2026, without promotions, discounts and other special forms of sale. A hair salon will thus have to state, alongside the current price of a haircut or colouring, also the price of the same service on that date; a car mechanic will have to do the same alongside the price of a working hour or a particular service; and a restaurant alongside the prices of food and drinks in the menu or price list.

The anchor price is neither frozen nor the highest permitted price. A trader or craftsman can still change prices, but the consumer will at any moment be able to see how much the current price differs from the one that applied on the 10th of September, explain lawyers Dora Ljevar and Danijel Pribanić. The obligation also applies when advertising prices. If a trader or service provider publishes a price on a leaflet, poster, digital , outdoor advertising space or website, they will also have to highlight the anchor price alongside it. An exception applies to traders who for food, drinks, cosmetics, cleaning agents, toiletries and household products already had to highlight an additional price. For those products the relevant price remains the one that applied on the 2nd of May 2025.

Additional technical obligations await traders and service providers who already have their own website. On it they will have to publish a price list in XML or CSV format, which enables the automatic collection and comparison of data. Traders will update the price list every working day by 08:00 at the latest, and service providers after every price change, also 08:00 on the day of the change at the latest. Previously published price lists will have to remain available for 30 days. Those who do not have their own website are not obliged to set one up solely because of this obligation. Traders and craftsmen should therefore keep proof of the prices that applied on the 10th of September and, by the start of application of the new rules, adapt the price lists in business premises, s and websites.

World.title: Croatia’s Zvijezda Marks 110 Years of Successful Business
World.content:
September the 18th, 2026 – Croatia’s famous brand Zvijezda has celebrated 110 years of doing successful business and engaging in market leadership.

Zvijezda mayonnaise and Zvijezda oil occupy first and second place on the ranking of the strongest brands in Croatia according to Ipsos research. Poslovni reports that the very well known Zvijezda, a market leader and Croatian manufacturing company whose values are founded on tradition, quality and innovativeness, celebrated 110 years of successful business.

The ceremony was held at the Zagreb City Museum, on the day when in 1916 the First Croatian Oil Factory was founded in Zagreb, in the presence of numerous company partners as well as representatives of institutions and the media. Zvijezda’s strong position is also confirmed by data on the habits of Croatian households: every second edible oil used in Croatia is Zvijezda’s, two out of three cakes are baked with Zvijezda margarine, and nine out of ten people, when it comes to mayonnaise, first think of Zvijezda.

According to the BRANDpuls research by the Ipsos agency from spring 2026, as many as five Zvijezda brands are among the 20 strongest brands on the Croatian market, with Zvijezda mayonnaise and Zvijezda oil occupying the first two places.

“I’m proud that we’re the market leader in almost all categories in which we have decided to compete, and the historically high result in the mayonnaise category of more than 70 percent confirms this. Zvijezda has for years been the number 1 brand among all brands of fast-moving consumer goods, and we continuously achieve these results thanks to our consumers, employees and partners,” emphasised Dinko Jurišić, member of the Management Board of Zvijezda. From the very beginnings of production in the First Croatian Oil Factory right up to the present day, the company has over the decades followed the needs of consumers, developed new products and set standards for the domestic food industry.

As such, back in 1956, it became the first producer of margarine in the country, in 1959 it introduced mayonnaise to the market, and in 2016 it launched the production of its own ketchup. The company today operates through the brands Zvijezda, Margo and Omegol. “Today, Zvijezda is a large and modern company, which is best proven by these figures: €150 million in annual revenue, more than 400 employees and presence on more than 15 markets. We look at these 110 years with pride, but even more with a sense of responsibility towards what is coming, therefore we continue to invest in the development of our products, the modernisation of production, the digitalisation of processes and sustainable solutions that will further strengthen Zvijezda’s competitiveness,” stated at the ceremony Karmen Rosan, member of the Management Board of Zvijezda.

Since this year Zvijezda has been operating as part of the Žito Group, one of the leading Croatian food groups. By entering the Žito Group a new development chapter has begun for Zvijezda, directed towards further strengthening of business, market position and the creation of new opportunities for growth.

“Zvijezda is one of the best-known Croatian food brands and a company that for 110 years has had a special place in the lives of generations of consumers. Its entry into the Žito Group represents a great responsibility for us, but also an opportunity to jointly build a new chapter of one of the most successful Croatian business stories, so that in the years to come we remain competitive and recognisable among consumers,” said Josip Bičvić, President of the Supervisory Board of Zvijezda. Zvijezda marked the anniversary also with a donation to the Croatian Down Syndrome Association, with which it has been cooperating for more than ten years, and as part of the cooperation the labels of a special edition of Zvijezda sunflower oil were decorated with drawings by children from the Association.

World.title: Croatian Scientists Concerned by Adriatic Sea Test Results
World.content:
September the 18th, 2026 – Croatian scientists are becoming more and more concerned by Adriatic Sea test results following 75 years of frequent measurements.

Scientists from the Ruđer Bošković Institute have analysed 75 years of measurements showing that the warming and salinisation of the Mediterranean Sea are accelerating, and the changes are becoming increasingly clear even in the deep layers. The Adriatic-Ionian area stands out particularly in this regard. Morski reports that when a warmer sea in summer is discussed, it usually means the temperature that is more or less suitable for swimming near the coastline itself. However, what we see and feel near the surface is only a small part of the story. Below it lie hundreds and thousands of metres of seawater, whose deep layers change much more slowly and are considerably harder to monitor.

It was precisely in these layers of the sea that scientists from the Ruđer Bošković Institute sought an answer to the question of how much the Mediterranean has really changed over the past decades. Dr Elena Terzić and Dr Ivica Vilibić, in a paper published in the leading international geoscience journal Geophysical Research Letters, collected and connected data from different periods, from historical measurements from research vessels to modern autonomous Argo floats that today regularly dive into the depths of the sea. In this manner, they obtained a kind of cross-section of the Mediterranean from 1950 to 2025 and tracked what is happening with the temperature, salinity and density of the sea at different depths. The results show that the Mediterranean is not only warming and becoming saltier, but that the speed of these changes is increasing, and their signal can be tracked hundreds and thousands of metres below the surface.

the sea’s warmth is increasing and the process is accelerating…

We have known for a long time that the sea is warming, and this process is most often described by the average rate of warming, i.e. by how much the sea temperature increases on average over one decade. “The average rate of warming tells us how much the sea temperature changed over some longer period. However, when we describe the entire period with a single average rate, we do not see whether the speed of warming itself is also changing. Our results show that it is increasing, so the average can conceal how much faster the changes of recent decades actually are,” explains Dr Elena Terzić.

In other words, a single straight line showing average warming no longer describes well enough what is happening in the Mediterranean. That is why the scientists also analysed the acceleration of warming, i.e. whether the speed at which the temperature is rising is itself changing. The clearest signal is seen near the surface, but the more interesting part of the story begins when one looks deeper. In the last years of the analysed period the temperature in the first hundred metres or so of the Mediterranean was about two degrees higher than the average of the second half of the 20th century. Warming is clearly visible also between 300 and 1,000 metres, and a measurable signal appears even at depths between one and two kilometres.

This is important because the deep sea does not react quickly to what is happening in the atmosphere. The surface can warm up during one exceptionally hot summer and cool down again a few months later, while changes in the deep sea take place much more slowly. “When the signal of change is no longer seen only near the surface but also deep in the water column, we are talking about a much broader change in the properties of the sea. The deep layers are a kind of memory of what has been happening in the system over a longer period,” emphasises Dr Ivica Vilibić.

why does the adriatic stand out here?

The temperature is not the only thing that is changing, because the Mediterranean Sea is simultaneously becoming saltier as well, especially in its central and eastern parts. Salinity and temperature together determine the density of seawater: the higher the salinity, the denser the water, and the higher the temperature, the lower the density. It is precisely the differences in density that drive the main circulation cells in the sea, i.e. the processes by which water mixes, sinks and transfers heat and salt from one part of the Mediterranean to another. Because of this, changes that begin near the surface do not necessarily stay there.

The Adriatic has a special place in this story because it is one of the areas of the Mediterranean in which dense water is formed. During cold winter periods the surface water can cool strongly, become dense enough and begin to sink. In this way the properties that the water acquired near the surface can be transferred into the deep layers of the Adriatic, and then further towards the deep Ionian Sea and the eastern Mediterranean.

The Adriatic-Ionian system in this research proved to be one of the areas with a particularly pronounced acceleration of changes. In the southern Adriatic a strong signal of accelerated warming appears even at a depth of around 1,000 metres, accompanied by simultaneous changes in salinity. This indicates that areas in which surface water sinks can be important places for the early detection and monitoring of changes that are transferred towards the interior of the sea.

how are measurements from 1950 and 2026 connected?

One of the biggest challenges in the research was to compare the properties of the sea that over the decades were not measured in the same way. In the 1950s and 1960s the data mostly came from research vessels, while today scientists have a network of Argo floats that independently pass through the water column and regularly send data on temperature and salinity. The authors therefore combined several large data sources, checked their quality and specifically tested whether the larger number of modern measurements could introduce bias into the results, i.e. artificially create the impression of acceleration. They repeated the analyses for different time periods and with different statistical approaches, and the basic pattern remained visible.

the wider mediterranean is an early indicator

The Mediterranean is a relatively small and almost closed marine basin that reacts strongly to changes in the atmosphere. Precisely for that reason it can serve scientists as a kind of natural laboratory for understanding what is happening to the oceans in a warmer climate. The research does not give a final answer to the question of which individual process is responsible for the observed acceleration. The changes can be connected with the warming of the atmosphere, evaporation and precipitation, the exchange of water with the Atlantic through Gibraltar, and changes in the circulation of the Mediterranean itself.

For the scientists the next step is to determine the contribution of each of these processes, and what they can already conclude is that the change in the Mediterranean is no longer only a story about a warmer sea surface. The sea is changing ever faster, and the signal of these changes has reached deep below the surface.

World.title: Agricultural Museum renamed MUHK, opens new permanent exhibition
World.content:
Starting Friday, the Estonian Agricultural Museum in Ülenurme, Tartu County, will operate under a new name: Maaelu uudishimukeskus (Rural Curiosity Center), or MUHK. The new name reflects the museum's expanding scope.

Alongside the history of Estonian rural life and agriculture, the museum will now place greater emphasis on the present and the future, exploring connections between the past, today's questions, and tomorrow's possibilities.

For decades, the Agricultural Museum has collected, preserved, and showcased Estonia's rural and agricultural heritage. That mission will not disappear with the old name. MUHK will retain its history, collections, artifacts, machinery, stories, and skills — but the way rural life is presented will change.

According to Kadri Valner, head of the SA Eesti Maaelumuuseumid (Estonian Rural Life Museums Foundation), the museum has long moved beyond focusing solely on the past.

MUHK headquarters. Source: Anna Mishina/Raadio 4

"The museum doesn't just talk about history — it also looks to the future. Our new exhibition covers everyday rural topics, food security, and even the future of our dinner table. As the Rural Curiosity Center, we will bring contemporary and forward‑looking perspectives alongside the museum's traditional historical approach," Valner said.

The name change is one of the most visible milestones in a broader transformation, and the new approach will gradually shape all of the center's activities.

On Friday, MUHK will open a new permanent exhibition of more than 600 square meters titled "Why Do I Need Soil?! From Seed to Harvest, From Harrow to Robot." The exhibition also blends history, the present, and the future, moving from the world of soil through agriculture and food production to satellites, robots, artificial intelligence, and the future of food.

The name and structure of the Estonian Rural Life Museums Foundation will not change. The foundation will continue to operate three sites: MUHK (Rural Curiosity Center) in Ülenurme, the C. R. Jakobson Farm Museum in Kurgja, and the Tori Horse Breeding Farm in Tori.

World.title: Tartu Illustration Festival back for third year with European guests
World.content:
Tartu Illustration Festival (TIF) is back September 25–26, bringing together creators from Estonia and beyond for two days of workshops, talks, a market and more.

The third TIF will be held at Aparaaditehas, with this year's theme, "Playful Patterns," exploring and challenging texture, repetition, modularity and rhythm.

Throughout the two-day festival, visitors can take part in hands-on workshops, hear talks and join a panel discussion, as well as browse an international exhibition and an illustrators' market.

Activities include designing and screen printing a board game, speed meetings between writers and illustrators, drawing dogs and creating Annelinn-inspired collages.

This year's festival also features several award-winning guests, including Finnish pattern designer Lotta Maija, whose work includes designs for Marimekko; British graphic artist and illustrator Ryan Chapman, whose work has appeared in The New York Times, The Economist and The Atlantic; Slovenian children's book illustrator Damijan Stepančič; and Estonian graphic designer and creative director Helene Vetik.

Tartu Illustration Festival (TIF) at Aparaaditehas. Source: Kerttu Kruusla

Hobbyists and pros alike welcome

Organizers Helena Pass and Liina Lember said TIF is intended as a meeting place for anyone interested in visual storytelling, creative experimentation and illustration culture, from professionals and students to hobbyists and curious visitors.

"Playfulness gives us the chance to move beyond familiar solutions and see illustration in a new light," they said. "TIF 2026 invites us to experiment with materials, techniques and ideas and discover unexpected connections."

The festival's program also includes the international exhibition "Bright Memory," hosted at the University of Tartu Library, which brings together classic Estonian illustration and contemporary work by artists from other countries.

The show explores the link between images, memory and visual storytelling, placing illustration in a broader cultural and international context.

World.title: Estonia and the U.S. seek rare‑earth agreement
World.content:
Estonia and the United States are working toward an agreement on rare earth elements to strengthen supply security. The talks are not about Estonia's mineral deposits; the goal is to develop local industry and attract new investment, says Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna. On Thursday, Lithuania signed a similar agreement with the U.S.

The global rare‑earth market is largely controlled by China, which in recent years has significantly restricted exports. As a result, the U.S. is trying to diversify supply and secure its supply chains by striking agreements with other partners. Estonia, for its part, has one of Europe's largest rare‑earth production and processing capacities. Both sides are interested in closer cooperation, but negotiations are still in the early stages.

"Our interest is to establish in Estonia at least Europe's largest knowledge and development center. And likewise to bring broader‑scale investments to Estonia and strengthen Estonia's role in the rare‑earth network — and certainly also for security‑policy reasons. We are not negotiating over Estonia's mineral resources," Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said.

Countries already involved in the U.S. initiative include Poland, the United Kingdom and Japan. On Thursday, Lithuania's foreign minister, who visited Washington, signed a cooperation agreement.

"This is currently our second foreign‑policy priority — the first is security. We must face these economic challenges, build a strategic partnership with the world's leading power, the United States, and create a resilient and strong supply chain," said Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys.

"Supply and processing security for rare earth elements is a foundation of the 21st‑century economy. This has been discussed before. It is essential for our economy and for defense. Lithuania, for example, has a global leadership role in photonics," said U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

The agreement was discussed extensively with Lithuanian companies, who believe it could lead to several major projects. Over the next six months, Lithuania and the U.S. will decide which initiatives are worth pursuing. Funding is expected to come from both government and private sources.

World.title: AI professor: Today's chatbots will not end civilization
World.content:
In recent weeks, leading figures in the tech world have grown increasingly vocal in warning about the risks posed by the rapid development of artificial intelligence. However, University of Tartu Professor of Artificial Intelligence Meelis Kull says there is currently no existential risk.

The debate gained momentum when executives at several major corporations urged engineers to slow down the development of new systems. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, for example, warned on his blog that the current pace of development carries excessive risks. At the same time, U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk called on countries to take swift action to rein in the new technology. One expert in the field estimated that there is a greater than 10 percent chance that artificial intelligence could destroy civilization.

In Kull's view, society first needs a clear picture of what machines are actually capable of today. The chatbots people use every day are still powered by large language models that wait for instructions from humans and only then search the web for information.

"Right now, we are talking about the most extreme danger — a threat to civilization and all of humanity. I would emphasize from the outset that with the capabilities AI has today, I do not see such a threat. It is close to zero," Kull said.

Scientists are much more concerned about the future when code begins improving itself. The human role in training models is steadily diminishing and in the future algorithms may be able to create increasingly intelligent versions of themselves without human assistance.

"The danger arises when we build AI systems that are vastly more intelligent. If a superintelligence emerges that is vastly more intelligent than humans in every respect, then managing and controlling it and guaranteeing that nothing can go wrong will be very difficult," the professor explained.

A catastrophe would not even require an attacker with malicious intentions. It would be enough for engineers to give a machine a noble goal but fail to define its limits precisely. For example, an algorithm instructed to stop global warming could conclude that the most effective solution would be to immediately shut down all oil platforms worldwide, along with economic activity more broadly.

"The danger also arises when a person has no intention of doing anything bad and simply wants to use AI for a good purpose — even in that case, a superintelligence could behave in ways we would not want," Kull said.

To prevent such scenarios, programmers need to give their digital assistants clear ethical boundaries. In practice, however, ruling out every possible loophole is simply beyond human capabilities.

"The problem with human error is that when assigning a task to AI, it is very difficult to define the conditions and set the boundaries precisely enough to completely eliminate the risks," the professor said.

An incident at OpenAI's labs this summer provides a good illustration of the potential cost of mistakes. Developers asked a virtual agent to test an internal network for security vulnerabilities. Unexpectedly, however, the program broke out of the controlled environment. The model was able to establish a means of communication through a message board on a public website and began attacking the servers of another company, Hugging Face.

The safeguards created by humans failed because the machine chose a path to solving the problem that engineers had not anticipated. Such dangerous incidents are encouraged by cutthroat competition in the technology sector where companies race to be the first to bring new products to market.

Stricter external oversight could help address the situation.

"First, there needs to be agreement on the processes used to mitigate risks. Independent experts can primarily verify whether those processes are being followed. When the pace of development is too fast, the processes are not followed precisely because of carelessness and that is exactly what increases the risks," Kull emphasized.

The global race also worries experts because computing power is becoming concentrated in the hands of a small number of organizations. A handful of U.S. technology giants currently dictate the pace of development worldwide. They have the money and servers that smaller startups could never afford.

With major corporations firmly in control, Europe has largely been left watching the digital race from the sidelines. Researchers and engineers in Europe lack resources comparable to those available to U.S. labs.

"Europe's serious problem is that we do not have anything comparable to the cutting-edge capabilities of U.S. companies. The strongest models in Europe are currently being trained by the French company Mistral, but its models are still slightly weaker than those of OpenAI and Anthropic in the U.S.," the professor said.

However, Kull said Europe's lag and the global risks should not deter small countries from embracing innovation. The energy consumption of artificial intelligence, for example, is steadily declining and an algorithm now requires 10 to 100 times less energy to perform the same computation than it did a couple of years ago. More efficient models could instead help organizations achieve their green transition goals.

If Estonian companies turn their backs on intelligent algorithms, they will give their competitors a huge advantage in international markets.

"If the question is whether these kinds of risks should prompt us in Estonia to restrict the use of AI, my answer is: absolutely not. Estonia has every reason to adopt AI more and more widely. It gives us economic advantages and increases our competitiveness," Kull said.

World.content:
Construction on the Tallinn–Pärnu section will continue, but work on other segments can be postponed, says infrastructure minister Kuldar Leis.

Intense work is underway along the Rail Baltica route in Estonia. Builders have so far operated under the assumption that trains must be running by 2030.

The government's message on Thursday — that the railway's completion deadline may be pushed back by four years — saddened construction company TREV-2's CEO Sven Pertens.

"From a builder's perspective, it's very unfortunate," said Pertens. "Construction companies have built up their resources assuming the market would remain more or less stable. If there's no work, we simply cannot keep people on payroll waiting for the possibility that maybe years later something will come up."

About ten kilometers away, another builder Verston has carved the rail corridor through more than ten meters of limestone and is preparing to cross a bog. On such difficult terrain, extra time could allow for more cost‑effective solutions, said Verston Group CEO Veiko Veskimäe.

Construction of the Rail Baltica Ülemiste Terminal in Tallinn. Source: Siim Lõvi / ERR

Tallinn-Pärnu section is the most mature

"I just visited the project office and asked the site manager what the biggest problem is right now. Naturally, he said they're short on trucks," Veskimäe noted.

Rail Baltic Estonia believes that extending deadlines could cool the construction market and allow the project to rely more on EU funding.

"A longer construction period would certainly ease the situation, making it possible to build kilometers at a more reasonable price," said Rail Baltic Estonia board member Lauri Ulm.

A delay would also affect train procurement. After the failure of its first tender, Elron is preparing a new one. Elron CEO Lauri Betlem wants new trains to begin operating within Estonia by 2030.

"I think we should stick to the proposed deadline, mainly because the project becomes more expensive with each passing year," Betlem said.

Although Latvia's construction pace gives little hope that trains could run beyond Ikla by 2030, the Tallinn–Pärnu section could be completed by the end of the decade.

"The Tallinn–Pärnu section is the most mature. Construction is underway across nearly the entire stretch," Ulm said.

Kuldar Leis. Source: Priit Mürk/ERR

Minister: We must decide what's sensible

Estonia's infrastructure minister Kuldar Leis said that revising the plan requires approval from Brussels.

"On Sunday and Monday, the three Baltic transport ministers will meet in Ireland at the gathering of European transport ministers. We'll discuss this again to ensure all three Baltic states act in the same way," Leis said.

"We must look at the entire process as one whole and bring all components together. First, whether Estonia is capable of finishing by 2030. Second, our southern neighbor Latvia has not given a clear signal about their ability to continue building. Third, the EU funding period is 2028–2034. If we truly finished by 2030, a large portion of EU support would go unused. Putting all this together, it makes sense to slow the pace now," Leis explained.

The minister said the plan remains to finish the domestic section — Tallinn to Pärnu — earlier. "The regional train tender will be relaunched immediately. We are not slowing down work on the entire route. Since construction on the Tallinn–Pärnu stretch is progressing very rapidly — over 100 kilometers where work is actively underway — that will continue. But south of Pärnu, and also from Ülemiste terminal toward the port in Tallinn, we can delay the start of work."

Leis added that early next week the Baltic prime ministers will also meet to discuss Rail Baltic's new timeline. "Much depends on Latvia — whether they will specify a year or not. Once the three Baltic states agree on our shared capability, we will negotiate with the European Commission on the pace of Rail Baltica. The European view is: agree among yourselves, say what you can deliver, and complete Rail Baltica."

World.title: Day of Countryside Living organizer says rural life best suits active people
World.content:
Reve Lambur, the lead organizer of Day of Countryside Living, said that anyone interested in rural life should definitely go meet the vibrant communities who are eager to welcome new residents.

Rural living is best suited for active people, because there are so many opportunities to create something new yourself, she added.

"There are two ideas behind organizing Day of Countryside Living. One is to show that living in the countryside is very pleasant, and to give people who have thought about moving there a chance to see what the local community is like — whether there is work, whether there is housing," said coordinator Reve Lambur.

The second idea is to show local residents what their municipality looks like. "Maybe new people have moved in — it's a chance to introduce them to the community, and for the community to feel proud of their municipality, to see that it's such a great place to live," Lambur said.

This year, 26 rural municipalities are participating. "In previous years, the municipality itself had to be the main contact point, but this year communities could take the lead as well, so we wouldn't take away the opportunity from communities that are actively looking for new residents," Lambur said.

The pandemic, she noted, encouraged many people to move to the countryside — and stay. "Many of them are families with children, because rural living is safe. The downside is that services aren't always close at hand. Families definitely need a car. When visiting communities, you can ask directly about the pros and cons of living there," Lambur explained.

"You don't just move into a house — you move into a community. That's the message of the day. Rural life suits active people. There are so many opportunities to create and do things yourself, to become a spark‑person — someone whose actions matter to others," Lambur said.

This year's Day of Countryside Living will take place on September 19.
