World.title: 'Western values' and 'national pride' underpin Coalition's education reform plans
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The Coalition has unveiled its plan for "root and branch" reform of Australia's education system, that would include subjects on "Western values", and less time spent on Indigenous history.

Speaking in Sydney's west, Shadow Education Minister Julian Leeser said the reforms would also see the Australian flag flown in all schools to foster more national pride.

He declared that the Coalition's policy would "restore excellence" in education, amid plummeting academic standards.

"Our academic performance is worse than ever. Our boys are disengaged and falling behind, our classrooms are disrupted and, in some cases, dangerous," Mr Leeser said.

To address rising classroom disruption, Mr Leeser floated the idea of teaching pathways for military veterans.

"When I think about the need for better classroom behaviour and more discipline in our classrooms, and the need for more support for Australian values, it seems to make sense," he said.

Make Indigenous history 'discrete' subject

Mr Leeser, who is also the shadow minister for Indigenous Australians, said children should learn about Indigenous heritage, "just like they learn about our British foundation and multicultural character".

Global results show Aussie students' struggles Australian students have recorded their lowest-ever scores in maths and reading in international testing, but improved on their science results.

Advocating for a shorter national curriculum that "returns time to teachers", he said the Coalition would remove cross-curricular priorities — which are areas of learning embedded across the curriculum, rather than as separate subjects.

These include Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander histories and culture, Asia and Australia's engagement with Asia, and sustainability.

"All three topics are important … but that doesn't mean they should be delivered thematically to our children as cross-curricular priorities," he said.

"Teach them as discrete, carefully planned topics that fit properly within geography or history or science classes."

'Western values' to underpin curriculum

The Coalition's curriculum overhaul also calls for students to "specifically learn" about Western values and culture.

"That includes basics like democracy, the rule of law, a fair go, the development by Australians of our system of constitutional monarchy and federation," Mr Leeser said.

"But I would also like to see Australian students taught and exposed to …classical works of literature, art, music and philosophy that underpin and enrich the ideas that have shaped our country."

The shadow minister said the Coalition's "root and branch" reforms would build a sense of national pride, which he said was lacking.

"Let every school have a flag and let every student take pride in it, its history and the values for which it stands."

Faster pathways for teachers

In addition to potentially streamlining teaching pathways for soldiers, a Coalition government would also slash qualification timelines.

Coalition's teacher claims spark backlash A teacher's union has fired back, labelling remarks by Angus Taylor and Matt Canavan "fundamentally incorrect".

Mr Leeser pledged a Coalition government would support a return to a one-year teacher accreditation system.

"Until the early 2010s, teachers in Australia were generally accredited on the basis of one-year teacher training courses," he said.

"In 2023, the NSW Productivity Commission released data showing that the shift to the longer qualification led to 9,000 teachers not entering the profession between 2015 and 2022."

The Coalition's policy would also include a framework to help all Australian schools develop "a clear statement of behavioural expectations" for students, amid rising instances of abuse towards teachers.

World.title: Mother charged over hidden recording device in son's clothing
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

A Gippsland mother has been charged by police after allegedly sewing a recording device into her non-verbal son's clothing after he began refusing to go to school.

Skye Cooper says her seven-year-old son came home from school one day last year with what looked like bruises.

He had been attending Churchill Primary School in the state's east since February 2025, but it was only around a month into his time there when he began acting distressed during the morning school run.

"He would not get out of the car. He started screaming, he started begging for me," Ms Cooper said.

"He just got more and more emotionally distressed… [and] would not be left in a room with anyone other than me. He was traumatised."

Her son has severe epilepsy, autism level three, global development delay and severe language delay. He is also non-verbal.

Ms Cooper said she was prompted to act when she noticed bruising on her son's arm. (ABC News: supplied)

Ms Cooper said she had multiple meetings with the school to express her concerns about her son's experience but didn't feel that her concerns were being addressed.

Worried, Ms Cooper approached a disability advocate for advice and was advised to sew a recording device into his clothes.

Each night, she listened back to the audio — until she heard an aide telling her son "you hurt me, I'll hurt you".

"Once I heard her on the recording threatening him, saying that she'll hurt him … I ended up pulling him out [of the school]," Ms Cooper said.

Charges laid over recording device

The alleged use of a recording device was reported to police and Ms Cooper has since been charged with Regulation of Installation, Use and Maintenance of a Listening Device.

She said she is shocked by the turn of events.

"I was trying to protect my child," she said.

"I just couldn't make sense of it, that … the tables have been turned on me."

She said she's been told by police that if she admits to the charges and makes a donation of $300 to a suitable charity, she won't have a criminal record.

Ms Cooper is receiving legal advice over her next steps.

She has also started a petition calling for the aide's removal and for the Education Minister to push for change in the Surveillance Devices Act to protect parents who use covert recording devices in suspected cases of abuse.

Ms Cooper doesn't believe her concerns have been addressed. (ABC News: Danielle Kutchel)

Earlier this year Ms Cooper received a formal written apology from the aide, which said she did "not specifically recall the exchange" but was "extremely remorseful that such a statement was made".

"I take full responsibility for the language used and am using this as an opportunity to reflect on my communication style under stress," the letter said.

"I clearly used words that I should not have used. While they would not have been intended as a threat or a literal statement, I recognise that language expressed that way is inappropriate."

Recording device 'only recourse you've got'

Julie Phillips is the disability advocate who has been assisting Ms Cooper and who recommended placing a recording device in the child's clothes.

She said she would still recommend it to others, while also warning of the possible consequences.

"But if there's no other way of finding out, what else can you do?" Ms Phillips said.

Julie Phillips advised Skye Cooper to use a recording device. (ABC News: supplied)

She said Ms Cooper's descriptions of her son's behaviour during his time at the school immediately raised red flags.

"One of the common issues with kids who can't use speech to communicate is when their behaviour deteriorates and there is bruising, usually something is going on that's traumatic for them," she said.

"Obviously it shouldn't be that [using a recording device] is the only recourse you've got, but with non-verbal people it is the only recourse you've got.

"The consequences have been experienced by a mother whose number one priority is the safety of her child, who can't communicate with her. If that's not completely backwards, I don't know what is."

Ms Phillips said abuse of children with disabilities in schools is extensive.

"When you take away any options that parents have to find out what is going on at school, your children are in a very dangerous position," she said.

She believes Ms Cooper's use of a listening device was justified and could even be legally defended if it can be proven that there was a threat to assault her son.

"If children can't be safe in government schools, it's a sad reflection on our society."

Ms Cooper said the Disability Workers Commission is investigating the issue.

World.title: Victorian Greens MP Tim Read dies aged 64
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Victorian Greens MP Tim Read has died aged 64, following a high-profile battle with metastatic cancer.

Dr Read, who announced his retirement from the Victorian parliament in January, used his final year as the Member for Brunswick to fight against the Allan government's decision to close VicHealth, described as the world's first health promotion foundation.

The former general practitioner told the ABC in January that VicHealth had helped pioneer sun safety messaging that could have helped him reduce his cancer risk if promoted when he was younger.

Mr Read delivered his valedictory speech to the Victorian parliament earlier this year. (AAP: James Ross)

Paying tribute to Dr Read on social media today, Victorian Greens leader Ellen Sandell said the Brunswick MP was the most liked MP in the state parliament.

"Tim was a brilliant local MP, doctor and scientist — but to those who knew him, he was also the kindest, funniest and most fundamentally decent of people," Ms Sandell said.

"Tim never held back from speaking truth to power, whether it was getting arrested for spray-painting health messages on tobacco billboards prior to getting elected or taking it up to the Premier in Question Time.

"Yet, he was also the most liked MP in state parliament, respected across the community for that rarest combination in a politician: conviction, integrity, wit and genuine humility."

Ms Sandell said Dr Read's advocacy led to legislative reforms over pill testing, tobacco licensing, the abolition of public drunkenness laws and a statewide plan to eradicate congenital syphilis and HIV transmission.

She said his work also led to gay men being allowed to donate blood, and a statutory ban on solitary confinement in prisons.

Victorian Premier Ben Carroll said he spoke with Dr Read earlier this week and was "deeply touched by that conversation".

"We spoke about something on which we have always agreed: integrity in public life and the need for reform," Mr Carroll said.

"Despite his health challenges, he was positive and optimistic for a better world.

"I always valued his intelligent and humane contributions to the public debate."

Victorian Opposition Leader Jess Wilson said Dr Read "was a man of conviction and a thoroughly decent person".

"He brought sincerity, compassion and a strong sense of public duty to his work, earning respect across the parliament," she said.

The Greens MP was a doctor before being elected to the Victorian parliament eight years ago. (ABC News: Simon Tucci)

"His commitment to integrity in public life was unwavering. Through his leadership of parliament's Integrity and Oversight Committee and his advocacy for stronger anti-corruption laws, Tim worked to ensure those entrusted with power were held accountable."

Ms Wilson said parliament often required negotiation and compromise.

" I always enjoyed working with Tim. He was an honest broker, someone who listened, engaged in good faith and approached every discussion with respect and integrity. "

Born in 1962, Dr Read completed a PhD while working as a medical practitioner in a public HIV and sexual health clinic.

His research included HIV prevention and treatment and how best to treat antibiotic-resistant sexually transmitted infections.

Dr Read's political activism started in his early 20s, as a participant in the Billboard-Utilising Graffitists Against Unhealthy Promotions group, comically known as BUGA-UP.

Medical students including a young Tim Read took part in a graffiti campaign in the mid-1980s, when cigarette advertising was still legal on public billboards. (Supplied)

The politician first ran for a parliamentary seat at a federal level, running as the Greens candidate at the 2013 election in former prime minister Bob Hawke's seat of Wills, which overlaps with the state electorate of Brunswick.

The following year, he stood as the Greens candidate for Brunswick in the Victorian election before ultimately winning the seat on his second attempt in 2018.

The Greens hold the inner suburban constituency with a two-candidate preferred margin of 13.7 per cent against Labor.

A by-election for the Brunswick electorate will not be necessary as Victoria is already scheduled to go to the polls on November 28.

Last year, Dr Read told the ABC he had noticed his leg was swollen while getting ready for work.

Scans revealed cancer had spread throughout his body. Dr Read first had a melanoma removed from his leg seven years ago.

His initial diagnosis was grim, forcing the Brunswick MP to retire ahead of the November state election.

Victorian Premier John Cain established VicHealth in 1987. (ABC News)

In January, Dr Read said closing VicHealth would create a "false economy" — an apparent saving that would in fact lead to more spending.

"We need to be strengthening health promotion, not weakening it," he told the ABC.

VicHealth was set up in 1987 by Labor premier John Cain and his health minister David White with bipartisan political support.

The policy banned outdoor tobacco advertising and used taxes from cigarette sales to promote health, including warning about the dangers of cigarettes.

Revenue was used to fund the arts and sport, which until then had relied heavily on tobacco sponsorship.

In his valedictory speech, Dr Read called for stronger NSW-style anti-corruption oversight in Victoria and bolstered rental controls, similar to those of the Australian Capital Territory.

"Despite the theatrics, most of us are here for the right reasons," he said.

"Politicians are unfairly maligned, and for me, politics is the work you do to improve people’s circumstances, not just now but in the future.

World.title: Demons claim top spot as Cats maintain winning ways
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Melbourne is the only unbeaten side after six rounds of the AFLW season, producing a statement 34-point win over Carlton at Casey Fields.

But the Demons may count the cost of Saturday's 8.10 (58) to 3.6 (24) win after star forward Georgia Gall limped off in the third quarter with an ankle injury.

A day after Hawthorn manufactured an upset to topple defending premiers North Melbourne, the Demons knew a win over the Blues would lift them into top spot on the ladder and establish a 6-0 (win-loss) start to their campaign.

The Blues were spirited in the opening half, but Melbourne slotted four straight goals in the third quarter to set up the victory.

Midfielder Olivia Purcell (26 disposals) was at the centre of the blitz, slotting two majors, while Jorja Livingstone scored on debut in the final quarter.

Tyla Hanks (32 disposals, one goal) also excelled, but it came as Gall sustained her injury.

It is the second consecutive loss for the Blues (4-2) and dents their top-four aspirations, although midfielder Claudia Whitfort was typically busy with 24 disposals.

Cats in fifth straight win

Aishling Moloney produced a goal-of-the-year contender to help Geelong to a 14.6 (90) to 7.7 (49) triumph over Collingwood at Victoria Park.

Knowing a victory would shore up their position inside the top eight, the Cats (5-1) were given a scare when the winless Magpies levelled scores minutes after the main break.

But the visitors flicked a switch, finding six goals in an electrifying third quarter to take a 31-point lead into the final break.

One of those majors was from Moloney, who booted the ball from halfway before it took a favourable flurry of bounces and crept into the goal.

The Cats tightened the screws in the final quarter, keeping Collingwood goal-less to seal their fifth straight win.

Midfielders Nina Morrison (30 disposals), Mikayla Bowen (29 disposals) and Georgie Prespakis (12 clearances) were prolific for the Cats, while Moloney and Chloe Scheer grabbed three and four majors respectively.

While the loss kept the Magpies (0-6) winless, they enjoyed a highlight when half-forward Olivia Lewis booted a goal on her AFLW debut after shifting from Super Netball's Melbourne Mavericks to the Magpies.

Lewis was a late call-up on Saturday morning because midfielder Bri Davey was ill.

Swans move clear in top four

Chloe Molloy continued her glittering goal-scoring form, spearheading Sydney to a 14-point victory over Port Adelaide.

Chloe Molloy played a starring role for the Swans. (Getty Images: Mark Brake)

The Swans (5-1) knew a win at Alberton Oval would move them four points clear of the fifth-placed Blues.

Molloy was instrumental in helping the visitors secure the precious 5.11 (41) to 3.9 (27) victory, booting three goals.

Her dazzling display came despite the Power keeping Sydney's usually dynamic attack at bay in the first half, with the scores locked at 16-16 at the main break.

The Swans stepped up in the third quarter, with Molloy booting a crucial goal, although a late major by Gemma Houghton kept the Power in the contest.

Leading by four points at three-quarter time, young Swans forward Cynthia Hamilton snagged a settling major, before Molloy kicked another to open up a match-winning advantage.

Swans defender Zippy Fish was typically influential, picking up 26 disposals, while midfielder Montana Ham had 16 possessions.

Midfielder Abbey Dowrick was a shining light for the Power (2-4), racking up a match-high 27 disposals and 415 metres gained.

Triumphant Bulldogs

The Western Bulldogs held firm to claim a 6.4 (40) to 4.6 (30) victory over Fremantle.

Looking to jump into the top eight, the Bulldogs (4-2) were kept scoreless in the opening term in Perth but kicked four unanswered majors in the second quarter to lead by 11 points at half-time.

The Dockers tightened their defence in the third quarter, holding the visitors to just one point as they surged back after Hayley Miller and Kiara Bowers found goals.

But just 17 seconds into the final quarter, a series of slick handballs led to Bulldogs forward Heidi Woodley slotting a major, before Sarah Hartwig nailed a goal to help her team move up to seventh on the ladder.

The Dockers (3-3) missed an opportunity to cement themselves inside the top eight, although Bowers (23 disposals, eight tackles and one goal) was busy, while midfielders Gabrielle Newton and Aisling McCarthy posted 24 possessions each.

Defender Jess Fitzgerald (25 disposals) shone for the Bulldogs, and midfielder Isabelle Pritchard jagged 21 disposals and a goal.

AAP

World.title: Helicopter winches family to safety after Whitsundays yacht crash
World.content:
Two children are among four people winched to safety by a rescue helicopter after their yacht struck a reef off the Queensland coast.

The family of four had been sailing a 10-metre vessel about 120 kilometres off the mainland when the yacht became stuck on Elizabeth Reef in the Whitsundays about 4am on Saturday.

The parents — along with their nine-year-old and 12-year-old — remained on board the damaged yacht until a rescue helicopter could arrive.

A spokesperson for CQ Rescue Helicopters said a crew from Mackay arrived about sunrise.

The helicopter maintained a steady hover while a swimmer was lowered to rescue each family member. (Supplied: BMA CQ Rescue)

"In a highly complex operation, the helicopter hovered above the vessel while a rescue swimmer was lowered to assist," the spokesperson said.

"Each person was secured and winched into the helicopter one at a time."

Once on board the helicopter, the family was transferred to the Whitsunday Airport.

The father was treated on board for head injuries before being taken to Proserpine Hospital for further medical attention.

CQ Rescue CEO Tim Healee said the challenging operation on an isolated reef required immense skill.

"Our crew had to maintain a precise and stable hover while the family were rescued," he said. "The precision and teamwork required cannot be overstated."

World.title: Live: Lions down Hawks in epic to reach fourth-straight grand final
World.content:
Kai Lohmann drills the set shot after the siren after Ashcroft found him inside 50, oh my goodness.

Boos ring all around the MCG at that holding the ball call on Impey, the Hawks fans are absolutely SEETHING.

Hawks fans have thrown bottles onto the playing surface in protest after that call.

It was a huge call from the umpire, a brave call, and as unpopular as it may be, I think it was there.

It's just one of those calls you don't usually see the umpires make in that position at that stage of the game.

Sam Mitchell has his side in a huddle on the ground, he's got to be proud of their effort when that game looked absolutely gone.

Nick Watson, I'm comfortable enough saying, is the most terrifying small forward this game has ever seen.

When the Hawks looked gone for all money, he pulled them out of the fire and gave them a chance.

Josh Ward with 25 touches and 11 clearances just turned into an absolute demon to get the Hawks back in it.

But this Brisbane side has won the last two flags for a reason.

Where other teams would've dropped the bundle, they kept trusting their process, and they are through to their fourth straight grand final!

World.title: Hynes off as Collins goes in for Roosters

Hynes off as Collins goes in for Roosters

Nicho Hynes was forced from the field in the opening minutes for a HIA moments after Lindsay Collins scored the first try of the night.

World.title: NRL finals LIVE updates: Roosters lead Sharks after Hynes ruled out with concussion
World.content:
Kick-off time, and the Roosters get things started tonight, Braydon Trindall bringing down the kick and sending Addin Fonua-Blake on his way for the game’s first hit-up.

Trindall is the one who gets the kick away on the last tackle, and he’s hit hard in the process by Victor Radley – who manages to avoid giving away a penalty despite the officials’ focus on late tackles on kickers this season.

Even better for the Roosters, they quickly earn the game’s first line break through Salesi Foketi down the left. One tackle later the Tricolours swing the ball to the right, Daly Cherry-Evans sending Lindsay Collins over for the game’s opening try after just a couple of minutes.

And Nicho Hynes has gone off for a HIA after going low in a tackle on Foketi and copping a knock to the head.

What a start for the Chooks. Disaster for Cronulla.

Roosters 6, Sharks 0 after three minutes

World.title: Bar manager banned after hundreds of unwanted calls, graphic images
World.content:
NationalNSWSex, sleaze and hospitality Bar manager banned after hundreds of unwanted calls, graphic images Harriet Alexander September 19, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Sydney bar owner who sent inappropriate text messages and made hundreds of unwanted phone calls to staff members has been banned from managing a licensed venue and faces criminal charges, amid a regulatory crackdown on sexual harassment in the hospitality industry. Jake Samuel-Brennan, 39, the former owner and chef at OG’s Kitchen and Bar in Cronulla, was alleged to have sent dozens of unwanted text messages to staff members, including images of his genitalia, over two separate events in July and December last year. Jake Samuel-Brennan was the owner and licensee of OG’s Kitchen & Bar in Cronulla. The Independent Liquor and Gaming Authority [ILGA] disqualified him from holding a liquor licence or being involved in the management of licensed venues for five years after finding that he was not a fit and proper person to hold a position of responsibility in the liquor industry. Police have charged him with five counts of stalking and intimidation and one count of using a carriage service to menace or offend. His bail conditions include not approaching the complainants, not entering the suburb of Cronulla and reporting daily to Springwood police station.



The prosecution comes as the NSW government has made it easier for ILGA to remove individuals from the industry or cancel or suspend venues notorious for inappropriate behaviour, following a Herald investigation into sleaze in the hospitality industry. Related Investigation

Sex, sleaze and hospitality Sex, sleaze and hospitality However, the complaint by NSW Police to ILGA pre-dated reforms that allow the authority to strip individuals of their Responsible Service of Alcohol certificates for harmful behaviours such as sexual assault, and thereby prevent them from being re-employed at a different venue. OG’s Kitchen and Bar is no longer in business. Liquor and Gaming NSW executive director Dimitri Agreres said the decision reinforced the expectation that hospitality venues were safe places to work. The recent legislative changes expanded the disciplinary grounds available to ILGA for sexual harassment and sexual violence, he said.



“People who hold positions of authority in licensed venues are expected to demonstrate integrity, professionalism and respect,” Agreres said. ILGA found that Samuel-Brennan called one staff member 50 times and another staff member 23 times, none of which were answered, and sent more than 100 inappropriate messages to their phones over several hours between July 17-18 last year. He deluged the same staff members again with more than 100 phone calls and dozens of inappropriate text messages between the hours of 4am and 9am on December 28, and asked one of them to come to his house. On the same occasion, he called a third staff member 124 times and sent her 58 text messages, all of which were unanswered, and called a fourth staff member more than 20 times, asking her to send the first complainant to his house. Later that day, three of the complainants reported his behaviour to Cronulla Police, and Samuel-Brennan was arrested and charged with stalking and harassment.



ILGA reported that Samuel-Brennan acknowledged his behaviour was harassing and made admissions. But he later submitted that he had never intended to threaten, harass or harm anyone, nor to make them feel uncomfortable or unsafe. He told the authority that the period of imprisonment he had served in connection to the matter had led to “significant personal growth and meaningful changes” in his life. He was engaged in a wellbeing program and had taken steps to improve his stability and decision-making in future. Samuel-Brennan also pointed to his 25 years in the industry and unblemished criminal record. He has pleaded not guilty to the charges.

World.title: Woman dies after being stabbed in Bondi apartment
World.content:
Breaking NationalNSWCrime Woman dies after being stabbed in Bondi apartment Rachel Rasker Updated September 19, 2026 — 7:58pm ,first published 7:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A woman has died after she was stabbed in a Bondi apartment on Saturday, just metres from a busy pedestrian thoroughfare and the beach. A 47-year-old man has been arrested after police were called to the unit in Chambers Avenue about 5.15pm on Saturday, following reports of a stabbing. A man has been arrested after a woman aged in her 90s died at a Bondi home. TNV Officers attached to Eastern Suburbs Police Area Command attended and found a woman aged in her 90s with significant injuries. She was treated by NSW Ambulance paramedics but died at the scene.



The man, who is believed to have been known to the woman, was arrested and has been taken to Surry Hills police station. Police have established a crime scene at 10 Chambers Avenue, Bondi. George Chan Earlier on Saturday, at a home in Kooringal, a suburb of Wagga Wagga, a 23-year-old woman was also fatally stabbed in a private home. Emergency services responded about 11.45am on Saturday morning.



NSW Ambulance paramedics and police officers performed CPR on the woman but she died at the home. Related Article Opinion

Domestic violence My neighbour was almost murdered by her partner. The police response left me disheartened Amber Schultz Reporter An 18-year-old was arrested at the scene, while police are still searching for a second man, who fled the residence before the arrival of emergency services. All three people are believed to have been known to each other. One woman was killed every 11 days in 2024–25, according to recent data from the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare.



Of the 98 domestic homicide victims in 2024–25, 46 were killed by an intimate partner, 52 were killed by a family member, 20 victims were the child of the offender and 21 were the parent of the offender. Police have established a crime scene at both locations and detectives have commenced inquiries. Anyone with information is urged to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic and Family Violence Counselling Service (1800RESPECT) on 1800 737 732. Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Hamer hammers her Liberal stake into Malvern’s blue-ribbon heartland
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaAmelia Hamer Hamer hammers her Liberal stake into Malvern’s blue-ribbon heartland Christine Lacy September 19, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Amelia Hamer, the Liberal candidate for the blue-ribbon seat of Malvern in November’s state election, will launch her campaign on Sunday afternoon. But driving around the leafy streets of the electorate the 33-year-old Oxford graduate hopes to represent, you’d think her official campaign had been up and running for weeks. Hamer’s corflutes are mushrooming on mansions across Toorak, Armadale and Malvern. A campaign source not authorised to speak publicly said nearly 200 had been erected so far, with Hamer’s signature royal blue Liberal for Malvern signage suggesting youthful, albeit conservative, enthusiasm. It’s the second crack Hamer, who ditched her safety net when she finished her job as a research analyst at Ord Minnett a fortnight ago, has had at running for public office. Amelia Hamer election material is popping up all over the Malvern electorate. PENNY STEPHENS Last year she narrowly failed in her tilt to win back the historically blue-ribbon federal seat of Kooyong from incumbent teal Monique Ryan, who in May 2022 ousted former Liberal treasurer Josh Frydenberg.



During the May 2025 federal campaign, billionaire Lindsay Fox and his wife Paula gave permission for a Hamer billboard to be attached to the high fence of their Irving Road, Toorak mansion. The rich-listers’ granddaughter went to school with Hamer at nearby exclusive girls’ school St Catherine’s. Amelia Hamer is hoping to win the blue-ribbon Liberal seat of Malvern Simon Schluter So far this time around, there is no such electioneering affixed to the Fox compound – but many other powerful and wealthy residents of the electorate have fallen in behind Hamer. Ten weeks out from election day, chairman of investment bank Flagstaff Partners Tony Burgess, who lives on prestigious Toorak boulevard Hopetoun Road, has a Hamer corflute on his fence, as does the Clendon Road, Toorak, home owned by listed fund manager and fintech group Netwealth CEO Michael Heine, and a Heyington Place, Toorak mansion owned by millionaire neurosurgeon Richard Bittar. Even former Victorian Liberal Party treasurer and millionaire businessman Andrew Abercrombie, who was recently seen at a fundraiser for Pauline Hanson’s One Nation, is behind Hamer, sporting a corflute on his prominent St Georges Road, Toorak, estate.



Thus far, however, there are some notable exceptions amid what are awkward dynamics between local party powerbrokers. Related Article Updated

Liberal Party Amelia Hamer holds off rivals to win Malvern preselection Hamer won Malvern preselection over local party identity Jacquie Blackwell, who is chair of both the Liberal Women’s Council of Victoria and of the party’s Kooyong federal electorate branch – as well as being treasurer of the party’s Malvern state electorate branch. Blackwell was backed in the race by Frydenberg, who has history with Hamer too. After she won preselection for his old seat in March 2024, speculation built that Frydenberg might seek a political comeback in Kooyong. A backlash erupted at the prospect of him displacing a preselected female candidate, until he publicly ruled out a return and confirmed his support for Hamer. Graciously, Frydenberg has donated a signed copy of his memoir, A Grateful Son, to be auctioned at Sunday’s event, while Blackwell has been out on the campaign trail with Hamer. On Saturday morning Blackwell (sporting a Hawks scarf and Hamer T-shirt) was streetside at a “listening post” with Hamer talking to voters and handing out materials.



“Amelia is a great candidate, and she will make a fabulous member for Malvern,” Blackwell told The Age. “I am 100 per cent behind her and am enjoying working closely with her.” Related Article Battle for Kooyong Old family links put a Fox among the Liberals in Kooyong Blackwell’s husband is Richard Murray, the former executive at billionaire Solomon Lew’s Premier Investments and now chief financial officer at Sigma Healthcare. Like his wife, Murray is a Liberal powerbroker in his own right, now as a director of party fundraising vehicle the Higgins Foundation. Returns lodged with the Australian Electoral Commission for the 2025 financial year show the vehicle brought in just under $680,000 in the year and paid out almost $410,000, for an effective surplus of more than $270,000. A party source not authorised to speak publicly told The Age that the Higgins Foundation would not be providing any funding for Hamer’s Malvern campaign, with monies earmarked for the next federal election.



Almost 200 corflutes promoting Liberal candidate for Malvern Amelia Hamer have already been erected. PENNY STEPHENS The power couple live in a historic, recently renovated mansion in Armadale. Their wrought-iron fence has been emblazoned with a billboard supporting Hawthorn’s tilt at the 2026 AFL premiership. Blackwell says when the season is over, the sign will be replaced by one promoting Hamer. Likewise, no sign is yet to be seen at the Toorak homes of Murray’s fellow directors on the Higgins Foundation board, former Australian Bankers Association boss Alan Cullen and Alinta Energy chair Robert Nicholson. Former Victorian premier Jeff Kennett, who was a key backer of Hamer’s federal preselection in November last year, will be at Toorak Park Pavilion in Malvern for Sunday’s event to speak in support of her candidacy. Kennett told The Age that Hamer, who is a grandniece of former Victorian premier Sir Rupert “Dick” Hamer and granddaughter of former Liberal senator for Victoria David Hamer, represented a key part of what Malvern and Victoria needed.



“She’s young, she’s highly academically qualified, she’s commercially experienced for a young person and she is a good communicator,” he said. Related Article Liberal Party Amelia Hamer embraces Millennial renter tag with stamp duty housing pitch Kennett said application of Hamer’s “good values” into the community would be an important ingredient towards making Victoria a better state. Hamer is running a disciplined campaign. She declined to speak at length ahead of her launch, but told The Age her early footslog revealed an appetite for change. “Malvern residents are sick and tired of a Labor government that has failed to deliver for Victorians,” she said. “The roads are full of potholes, crime is out of control and costs just keep going up.



“From all the doors I’ve knocked on across the electorate, one message is clear: the people of Malvern want a fresh start for Victoria.” Hamer’s quest follows the retirement of one-time state treasurer and opposition leader Michael O’Brien, who has held the safe, inner-Melbourne seat for the Liberals for two decades – a seat that is now held by a margin of 6 per cent. O’Brien has been actively supporting Hamer’s candidacy, making sure she is invited to the right functions and introduced to the right people. Amelia Hamer corflutes are appearing on multimillion-dollar Toorak mansions. Penny Stephens Hamer fundraised $1.8 million to drive her 2025 Kooyong campaign and spent it all. A Liberal source said a candidate running in a hotly contested state seat might expect to spend up to $300,000, but this time around Hamer is expected to spend much less than that to win the safe seat. Her campaign, having raised more than it needs, is expected to help fund less financially flush Liberal candidates elsewhere in Victoria towards November. “Amelia comes as a candidate in Malvern having already campaigned in Kooyong where … she worked very hard,” Kennett said. “I think there is a lot to be said for candidates who get out there and do the work, candidates whether they’re existing members of parliament or new have to earn the right to be employed for four years, and Amelia has done that with energy and enthusiasm.”



Kennett, along with several others including Victorian senator Jane Hume, for whom Hamer worked as staffer, have emerged as key advisers. Related Article Interview

Jeff Kennett What Jeff Kennett really thinks of Julia Gillard, Daniel Andrews – and death Hume, who unsuccessfully ran for preselection in Malvern in 2006 before she became a senator, will speak at Hamer’s campaign launch, which will be hosted by Liberal deputy leader David Southwick. More than 200 supporters are expected to attend, making it one of the largest Liberal campaign launches in the unfolding Victorian campaign. “[Hamer] has a number of people who she talks to and asks advice from, and I am one of those,” Kennett said. “She reaches out, she is a good listener, but, unlike many, she will act on that advice. A lot of people, particularly in politics, will listen and be very personable and engaging … but with very little follow-up. “She has earned the respect of those who have gone before and those who are there because of her own effort and her personality. There is no doubt that Amelia has worked very hard.”



Kennett is “absolutely” confident Hamer will win come November 28. “I think Amelia will win, deserves to win and will win comfortably,” he said. “That will be a reflection of what’s going to happen throughout the state. “I think she’s going to be one of a small army of people who are new to the parliament – they will be on the conservative side, not the Labor side.” Victorians, he predicted, would vote for change. “I think the public’s had a gutful, they can’t afford to continue to live the way they are,” he said.



“The public are increasingly aware of the condition of the state and who they blame. The government is seen to have run out of steam and not governed well, there is the added layer of corruption and other ingredients that tell me … a whole lot of traditional Labor seats are going to lose support.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Bar manager banned after hundreds of unwanted calls, graphic images
World.content:
NationalNSWSex, sleaze and hospitality Bar manager banned after hundreds of unwanted calls, graphic images Harriet Alexander September 19, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Sydney bar owner who sent inappropriate text messages and made hundreds of unwanted phone calls to staff members has been banned from managing a licensed venue and faces criminal charges, amid a regulatory crackdown on sexual harassment in the hospitality industry. Jake Samuel-Brennan, 39, the former owner and chef at OG’s Kitchen and Bar in Cronulla, was alleged to have sent dozens of unwanted text messages to staff members, including images of his genitalia, over two separate events in July and December last year. Jake Samuel-Brennan was the owner and licensee of OG’s Kitchen & Bar in Cronulla. The Independent Liquor and Gaming Authority [ILGA] disqualified him from holding a liquor licence or being involved in the management of licensed venues for five years after finding that he was not a fit and proper person to hold a position of responsibility in the liquor industry. Police have charged him with five counts of stalking and intimidation and one count of using a carriage service to menace or offend. His bail conditions include not approaching the complainants, not entering the suburb of Cronulla and reporting daily to Springwood police station.



The prosecution comes as the NSW government has made it easier for ILGA to remove individuals from the industry or cancel or suspend venues notorious for inappropriate behaviour, following a Herald investigation into sleaze in the hospitality industry. Related Investigation

Sex, sleaze and hospitality Sex, sleaze and hospitality However, the complaint by NSW Police to ILGA pre-dated reforms that allow the authority to strip individuals of their Responsible Service of Alcohol certificates for harmful behaviours such as sexual assault, and thereby prevent them from being re-employed at a different venue. OG’s Kitchen and Bar is no longer in business. Liquor and Gaming NSW executive director Dimitri Agreres said the decision reinforced the expectation that hospitality venues were safe places to work. The recent legislative changes expanded the disciplinary grounds available to ILGA for sexual harassment and sexual violence, he said.



“People who hold positions of authority in licensed venues are expected to demonstrate integrity, professionalism and respect,” Agreres said. ILGA found that Samuel-Brennan called one staff member 50 times and another staff member 23 times, none of which were answered, and sent more than 100 inappropriate messages to their phones over several hours between July 17-18 last year. He deluged the same staff members again with more than 100 phone calls and dozens of inappropriate text messages between the hours of 4am and 9am on December 28, and asked one of them to come to his house. On the same occasion, he called a third staff member 124 times and sent her 58 text messages, all of which were unanswered, and called a fourth staff member more than 20 times, asking her to send the first complainant to his house. Later that day, three of the complainants reported his behaviour to Cronulla Police, and Samuel-Brennan was arrested and charged with stalking and harassment.



ILGA reported that Samuel-Brennan acknowledged his behaviour was harassing and made admissions. But he later submitted that he had never intended to threaten, harass or harm anyone, nor to make them feel uncomfortable or unsafe. He told the authority that the period of imprisonment he had served in connection to the matter had led to “significant personal growth and meaningful changes” in his life. He was engaged in a wellbeing program and had taken steps to improve his stability and decision-making in future. Samuel-Brennan also pointed to his 25 years in the industry and unblemished criminal record. He has pleaded not guilty to the charges.

World.title: Demolishing homes is not looking after the vulnerable
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Demolishing homes is not looking after the vulnerable September 19, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Photo: Matt Golding To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. Richmond clearances

The removal of 220 families and the imminent demolition of their Richmond homes is another chapter in the clearing out of the not-so-well-off from valuable inner-city real estate. In the 1950s and 1960s the Housing Commission of Victoria compulsory acquired many thousands of small inner-city holdings, the homes of many not so well off, and stacked those people into high-rise towers, while the land fell into other hands. In many instances, the HCV acquired for the price of land only if the house could be declared ″⁣sub-standard″⁣, leaving the home owner with never enough to buy elsewhere, so they were forced into rental.

Now the estate will be converted into ″⁣build-to-rent″⁣ residences with the rental way out of reach of those previous residents. They will lose their inner-city location and be forced out into the sticks, with transport issues and no local employment.

Ironically, all this from a Labor government.

John Marks, Werribee Where’s social justice?

The state government appears hell-bent on destroying Victoria’s public housing system with the proposed demolition of the 44 high-rise towers across Melbourne. The replacement of the Highett Street, Richmond, flats is a case in point. The government had announced that 220 public tenant units will be replaced by only 150social housing dwellings while 650 will be built as private build-to-rent apartments for middle to high income earners. With this outrageous plan how will the 69,000 people on the public housing waiting list ever be housed? Where has our tradition of social justice gone?

Jeff Fiedler, Castlemaine Grim present and future

Richard Flanagan’s article “Albanese is selling out Australia to AI colonists as artists face ruin” (18/9) is hard-hitting and dares to tell the truth about where Australia is today. I, like him in 1974 had optimistic hopes for our country.

Unfortunately, I agree with his critique and am not only angry and disappointed with what might have been but sad that the country has descended into a toxic culture, likely with AI and the rich tech companies extinguishing us all at some point.

Geraldine Lakha, Balwyn North



PM, protect artists

Your correspondent (Letters, 19/9) is right to call out the government’s sell-out of creative artists in not sufficiently protecting original works through strong copyright laws. Fill in a few lyrics or even just submit a topic to any number of songwriting apps and a song will be created in a few minutes.

These songs are built from the blood, sweat and tears of thousands of songwriters and artists from around the world without their knowledge or permission.

Proper copyright laws are essential if we are to protect original works created by hardworking musicians, writers and artists.

The government is letting our talented and creative artists down by not implementing strong copyright laws.

Freedom of expression is one thing but stealing work from others is not on.

Graeme Lechte, Pascoe Vale Words of a child

ABC news report on Thursday night of the Labor government’s plans to curb migration was followed by a story of children escaping the rubble of a collapsed building in Gaza. Our seven-year-old daughter immediately sensing the irony in our country seeking to keep people out during a time of global conflict and record numbers of forcibly displaced people asked to write a letter to the prime minister.

While we carefully frame these stories to ensure they’re as safe as possible for young viewers, our daughter’s plea that “we have room” and that these kids “have done nothing wrong” were all her words. If our daughter is to grow up in an egalitarian society and a liberal democracy, our government must do better than pander to rightwing social media algorithms and nativist populism.

Tim Wright, Point Lonsdale Freight train blues

Your correspondent (Letters, 18/9) has correctly identified that a major cause of road surface deterioration and potholes is the plethora of heavier vehicles on the roads, compared with earlier decades. In addition to the rectification of road surfaces and pothole removal, a desirable alternative solution is the redirection of heavy freight volumes to the logical alternative – freight rail. Yet the prime minister this year decreed that the long overdue for completion inland freight rail, between Melbourne (Australia’s largest port) and Queensland, be suspended. More freight on country and interstate roads – more potholes and surface deterioration. Time to get the goods back on (the rail) track.

Brian Kidd, Mt Waverley Going south

With the ongoing debate over East Brighton or Brighton East, among others, I am looking forward to the following discussions; Korea South, Sudan South and Africa South or even America South.

Phil Labrum, Trentham Hidden agenda

I can’t believe that the federal Labor government has plans to introduce new legislation regarding visas and migrants without the knowledge of the devastating impact these rules will have on rural and regional Australia.

I believe that they know exactly what they are doing and that after some parliamentary and committee biffo they’ll be largely withdrawn and all that will be left is a policy to engage actively in deporting ″⁣overstayers″⁣.

Why? Because this tactic serves to wedge One Nation and the Nationals and bleed votes from those affected negatively by the migration policies as they stand, if not to the ALP then to Greens and Independents, parliamentarians with whom I’m sure the ALP would rather deal.

Simon Clegg, Donvale



Hanson, open the mind

Pauline Hanson’s public comments that First Nations people are the most primitive on Earth and have achieved nothing is as disdainful as claiming all redheads are ignorant. There isn’t enough column space to acknowledge the awesome contributions First Nations people have made to sport, dance, literature, music, journalism, art, and politics. I would encourage Hanson to read any book by one of the many talented Indigenous writers and open her mind to their history being told through music and dance.

Knowledge is no burden to carry. An intractable ignorance on the other hand, diminishes her.

Linda Grace, Mitcham It’s all Trumps

Donald Trump tells Americans, “When you vote, pretend that Trump is on the ballot!”

Democrats tell Americans, “When you vote, pretend that Trump is on the ballot!“

Stuart McArthur, Carlton North Band together

When politicians ban news organisations from news conferences (Pauline Hanson and Donald Trump) it would be good if all other organisations banded together and refused to also attend.

Michael Brinkman, Ventnor Carney’s vision

It’s a joy to hear a politician whose words are memorable. ″⁣We believe that a strong economy is not an end in itself but the means to a just society.″⁣ – Mark Carney, speaking to the European Parliament. So much wrapped up in one sentence. So much addressed in one speech.

Alison Fraser, Ascot Vale Falling behind

I spend almost every waking moment trying to “help mitigate climate change”. And yet, seeing the climate becoming more chaotic and governments and major polluting companies continuing their climate-damaging behaviours, I fear we all fall into the “not-doing-enough” category.

Lesley Walker, Northcote

World.title: Hamer hammers her Liberal stake into Malvern’s blue-ribbon heartland
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaAmelia Hamer Hamer hammers her Liberal stake into Malvern’s blue-ribbon heartland Christine Lacy September 19, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Amelia Hamer, the Liberal candidate for the blue-ribbon seat of Malvern in November’s state election, will launch her campaign on Sunday afternoon. But driving around the leafy streets of the electorate the 33-year-old Oxford graduate hopes to represent, you’d think her official campaign had been up and running for weeks. Hamer’s corflutes are mushrooming on mansions across Toorak, Armadale and Malvern. A campaign source not authorised to speak publicly said nearly 200 had been erected so far, with Hamer’s signature royal blue Liberal for Malvern signage suggesting youthful, albeit conservative, enthusiasm. It’s the second crack Hamer, who ditched her safety net when she finished her job as a research analyst at Ord Minnett a fortnight ago, has had at running for public office. Amelia Hamer election material is popping up all over the Malvern electorate. PENNY STEPHENS Last year she narrowly failed in her tilt to win back the historically blue-ribbon federal seat of Kooyong from incumbent teal Monique Ryan, who in May 2022 ousted former Liberal treasurer Josh Frydenberg.



During the May 2025 federal campaign, billionaire Lindsay Fox and his wife Paula gave permission for a Hamer billboard to be attached to the high fence of their Irving Road, Toorak mansion. The rich-listers’ granddaughter went to school with Hamer at nearby exclusive girls’ school St Catherine’s. Amelia Hamer is hoping to win the blue-ribbon Liberal seat of Malvern Simon Schluter So far this time around, there is no such electioneering affixed to the Fox compound – but many other powerful and wealthy residents of the electorate have fallen in behind Hamer. Ten weeks out from election day, chairman of investment bank Flagstaff Partners Tony Burgess, who lives on prestigious Toorak boulevard Hopetoun Road, has a Hamer corflute on his fence, as does the Clendon Road, Toorak, home owned by listed fund manager and fintech group Netwealth CEO Michael Heine, and a Heyington Place, Toorak mansion owned by millionaire neurosurgeon Richard Bittar. Even former Victorian Liberal Party treasurer and millionaire businessman Andrew Abercrombie, who was recently seen at a fundraiser for Pauline Hanson’s One Nation, is behind Hamer, sporting a corflute on his prominent St Georges Road, Toorak, estate.



Thus far, however, there are some notable exceptions amid what are awkward dynamics between local party powerbrokers. Related Article Updated

Liberal Party Amelia Hamer holds off rivals to win Malvern preselection Hamer won Malvern preselection over local party identity Jacquie Blackwell, who is chair of both the Liberal Women’s Council of Victoria and of the party’s Kooyong federal electorate branch – as well as being treasurer of the party’s Malvern state electorate branch. Blackwell was backed in the race by Frydenberg, who has history with Hamer too. After she won preselection for his old seat in March 2024, speculation built that Frydenberg might seek a political comeback in Kooyong. A backlash erupted at the prospect of him displacing a preselected female candidate, until he publicly ruled out a return and confirmed his support for Hamer. Graciously, Frydenberg has donated a signed copy of his memoir, A Grateful Son, to be auctioned at Sunday’s event, while Blackwell has been out on the campaign trail with Hamer. On Saturday morning Blackwell (sporting a Hawks scarf and Hamer T-shirt) was streetside at a “listening post” with Hamer talking to voters and handing out materials.



“Amelia is a great candidate, and she will make a fabulous member for Malvern,” Blackwell told The Age. “I am 100 per cent behind her and am enjoying working closely with her.” Related Article Battle for Kooyong Old family links put a Fox among the Liberals in Kooyong Blackwell’s husband is Richard Murray, the former executive at billionaire Solomon Lew’s Premier Investments and now chief financial officer at Sigma Healthcare. Like his wife, Murray is a Liberal powerbroker in his own right, now as a director of party fundraising vehicle the Higgins Foundation. Returns lodged with the Australian Electoral Commission for the 2025 financial year show the vehicle brought in just under $680,000 in the year and paid out almost $410,000, for an effective surplus of more than $270,000. A party source not authorised to speak publicly told The Age that the Higgins Foundation would not be providing any funding for Hamer’s Malvern campaign, with monies earmarked for the next federal election.



Almost 200 corflutes promoting Liberal candidate for Malvern Amelia Hamer have already been erected. PENNY STEPHENS The power couple live in a historic, recently renovated mansion in Armadale. Their wrought-iron fence has been emblazoned with a billboard supporting Hawthorn’s tilt at the 2026 AFL premiership. Blackwell says when the season is over, the sign will be replaced by one promoting Hamer. Likewise, no sign is yet to be seen at the Toorak homes of Murray’s fellow directors on the Higgins Foundation board, former Australian Bankers Association boss Alan Cullen and Alinta Energy chair Robert Nicholson. Former Victorian premier Jeff Kennett, who was a key backer of Hamer’s federal preselection in November last year, will be at Toorak Park Pavilion in Malvern for Sunday’s event to speak in support of her candidacy. Kennett told The Age that Hamer, who is a grandniece of former Victorian premier Sir Rupert “Dick” Hamer and granddaughter of former Liberal senator for Victoria David Hamer, represented a key part of what Malvern and Victoria needed.



“She’s young, she’s highly academically qualified, she’s commercially experienced for a young person and she is a good communicator,” he said. Related Article Liberal Party Amelia Hamer embraces Millennial renter tag with stamp duty housing pitch Kennett said application of Hamer’s “good values” into the community would be an important ingredient towards making Victoria a better state. Hamer is running a disciplined campaign. She declined to speak at length ahead of her launch, but told The Age her early footslog revealed an appetite for change. “Malvern residents are sick and tired of a Labor government that has failed to deliver for Victorians,” she said. “The roads are full of potholes, crime is out of control and costs just keep going up.



“From all the doors I’ve knocked on across the electorate, one message is clear: the people of Malvern want a fresh start for Victoria.” Hamer’s quest follows the retirement of one-time state treasurer and opposition leader Michael O’Brien, who has held the safe, inner-Melbourne seat for the Liberals for two decades – a seat that is now held by a margin of 6 per cent. O’Brien has been actively supporting Hamer’s candidacy, making sure she is invited to the right functions and introduced to the right people. Amelia Hamer corflutes are appearing on multimillion-dollar Toorak mansions. Penny Stephens Hamer fundraised $1.8 million to drive her 2025 Kooyong campaign and spent it all. A Liberal source said a candidate running in a hotly contested state seat might expect to spend up to $300,000, but this time around Hamer is expected to spend much less than that to win the safe seat. Her campaign, having raised more than it needs, is expected to help fund less financially flush Liberal candidates elsewhere in Victoria towards November. “Amelia comes as a candidate in Malvern having already campaigned in Kooyong where … she worked very hard,” Kennett said. “I think there is a lot to be said for candidates who get out there and do the work, candidates whether they’re existing members of parliament or new have to earn the right to be employed for four years, and Amelia has done that with energy and enthusiasm.”



Kennett, along with several others including Victorian senator Jane Hume, for whom Hamer worked as staffer, have emerged as key advisers. Related Article Interview

Jeff Kennett What Jeff Kennett really thinks of Julia Gillard, Daniel Andrews – and death Hume, who unsuccessfully ran for preselection in Malvern in 2006 before she became a senator, will speak at Hamer’s campaign launch, which will be hosted by Liberal deputy leader David Southwick. More than 200 supporters are expected to attend, making it one of the largest Liberal campaign launches in the unfolding Victorian campaign. “[Hamer] has a number of people who she talks to and asks advice from, and I am one of those,” Kennett said. “She reaches out, she is a good listener, but, unlike many, she will act on that advice. A lot of people, particularly in politics, will listen and be very personable and engaging … but with very little follow-up. “She has earned the respect of those who have gone before and those who are there because of her own effort and her personality. There is no doubt that Amelia has worked very hard.”



Kennett is “absolutely” confident Hamer will win come November 28. “I think Amelia will win, deserves to win and will win comfortably,” he said. “That will be a reflection of what’s going to happen throughout the state. “I think she’s going to be one of a small army of people who are new to the parliament – they will be on the conservative side, not the Labor side.” Victorians, he predicted, would vote for change. “I think the public’s had a gutful, they can’t afford to continue to live the way they are,” he said.



“The public are increasingly aware of the condition of the state and who they blame. The government is seen to have run out of steam and not governed well, there is the added layer of corruption and other ingredients that tell me … a whole lot of traditional Labor seats are going to lose support.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.
